She wishes she had reached SSLC. All three children attend the village government school in Kannada medium; the school has four teachers for eight classes, so Classes 6 and 7 share one room. Renuka passed SSLC in 2026 with 62 percent under the new 33-percent aggregate rule and joined first-year PUC science stream at Saundatti, hoping to reach nursing college. The Rs 1,500 bus fare each month was a burden until the student pass began, and Lata worries about textbook and tuition costs. Kavitha is bright but sometimes absent when the anganwadi closes or Lata is ill. Lata has heard of the Morarji Desai residential school and KGBVs but does not know the admission process. She receives Gruha Lakshmi—Rs 2,000 monthly when it arrives—and uses part of it for the children's notebooks, uniforms and shoes.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Lata and her family depend on the primary health centre at Saundatti, fourteen kilometres return by bus. Her mother-in-law's arthritis requires monthly painkillers and occasional referral to Belagavi district hospital, costing the family Rs 1,500 to Rs 2,000 each trip for transport, tests and medicines not available free. Lata herself suffers from anaemia—she was told her haemoglobin was eight during Kavitha's pregnancy—and chronic back pain from years of heavy work, but she rarely seeks care. Renuka began menstruating at thirteen and Lata bought her sanitary napkins from the ration shop when available, otherwise cloth. The village borewell water has a salty taste and some neighbours complain of joint pain, though no one has tested for fluoride. Dengue and diarrhoea cases rise in the monsoon; Kavitha had fever and loose motions in September 2026 and Lata took her to a private clinic in Saundatti, spending Rs 800. Basappa drinks occasionally and has had minor injuries on construction sites in Goa but no major illness. The family is enrolled in Ayushman Bharat but Lata has never used the card. She worries about the cost of any serious illness and the debt it would bring.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Lata's family belongs to the Kuruba community, listed as OBC Category 1 in Karnataka. Kurubas in the village work as labourers and small farmers; some families own two or three acres, most less. The village has a mix of Kuruba, Lingayat and SC Madiga households, and a small Maratha presence. Lata speaks Kannada at home and knows a few Marathi phrases from her mother-in-law, who grew up near the Maharashtra border. The family worships at the village Hanuman temple and once a year makes the pilgrimage to the Yellamma temple at Saundatti during the Bharat Hunnime fair in November, though Lata knows the devadasi history and is glad the practice is now unlawful. Her mother-in-law believes in the Mailara jatra and herbal remedies from the local vaidya. Lata participates in a women's self-help group organized by a local NGO; the group saves Rs 100 per member monthly and has taken a Rs 50,000 bank loan for joint ventures, though Lata's share was used to repay the moneylender. She has little contact with the gram panchayat beyond ration-card updates. Caste tensions are muted in daily life but Lata has heard of Panchamasali agitations in Belagavi and Kuruba families' demand for ST status, which she supports because it might help Manjunath get a quota seat.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Lata's household receives five kilograms of rice per person under Anna Bhagya, though the ration shop sometimes runs short and opens irregularly. She enrolled for Gruha Lakshmi in June 2023 and receives Rs 2,000 monthly, but payments have been delayed by two months twice in the past year; she uses the money for children's school costs and loan repayment. Renuka now travels free on NWKRTC buses under the student pass announced in June 2026, a relief Lata praises aloud. The family has a BPL ration card and Ayushman Bharat coverage but no land title—Basappa's father held the acre on a decades-old arrangement with a Lingayat landlord and the family has no patta. She has heard of the Kittur Rani Chennamma schemes but does not know what they fund. The anganwadi supervisor visits monthly and Lata must maintain records and cleanliness, but supplies of rice, dal and oil are often delayed. She wishes the gram panchayat would fix the village road and the hand-pump near her house. Basappa has worked ten days under MGNREGA this year at Rs 309 per day, paid after six weeks. Lata does not follow state politics closely but knows there is a new chief minister, Shivakumar, since June 2026, and hopes the government will not stop the guarantees.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Lata is proud that Renuka passed SSLC and reached PU college, something neither parent managed, and she is determined that Kavitha will study at least that far. She worries constantly about money—the unpaid anganwadi salary, the moneylender's interest, the cost of Renuka's textbooks and the question of where Manjunath will study after Class 10. Lata blames middlemen and the government for the low price of jowar and groundnut, and she resents that Gruha Lakshmi payments are delayed while the scheme is advertised on TV. Lata feels the government listens more to Belagavi city and Hubballi than to Saundatti taluk villages, and she has heard people say that Kalyana Karnataka gets special money under some central rule while Kittur Karnataka is ignored. She does not understand the politics but agrees something is unfair. She wishes her daughter could study without fear, her son could reach degree, and the family could clear its debt. What she wants from the government is regular payment of wages and Gruha Lakshmi, a proper bus service to Saundatti, a high school closer to the village, and a doctor at the PHC who is present when needed.

personas.name: Laxmi
personas.definition: Laxmi is a composite portrait of an anganwadi worker in Jamkhandi taluk, Bagalkote district, navigating precarious employment, household debt and the schooling hopes of a family facing seasonal floods and drought. She embodies the pressures on women balancing care work, agricultural livelihoods and community responsibilities in the Krishna-Malaprabha belt.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Laxmi works as an anganwadi helper in a centre serving two hamlets outside Jamkhandi town, earning a monthly honorarium of around Rs 5,500 that arrives irregularly. Her day begins at six, preparing a breakfast of jowar rotti and shenga chutney before cycling four kilometres to the centre, where she weighs children, serves the midday meal of rice and sambar, and helps the main worker with immunisation records and preschool activities. Her husband Basavaraj owns three acres of black-soil land where they grow jowar, cotton and gram; hired labour and tractor costs mount to about Rs 25,000 each season. The 2023 drought cut cotton yields by half, forcing them to borrow Rs 40,000 from a Jamkhandi moneylender at three per cent monthly interest. Flood relief after the Krishna rose in 2024 paid only Rs 8,500 per hectare, far less than the actual loss. Evenings she cooks, tends the two buffaloes and repairs torn school uniforms. Her anganwadi wage barely covers groceries; the farm income is consumed by input costs, loan repayments and two children's school fees.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Laxmi lives with her husband Basavaraj, two children, her widowed mother-in-law and Basavaraj's unmarried younger brother in a tiled house near the Jamkhandi-Bilagi road. Her daughter Pavitra is fourteen and in Class 9 at the government high school in Jamkhandi; her son Sharan is eleven and in Class 6 at the same school. Laxmi was married at nineteen after completing SSLC; Basavaraj finished Class 10 but never went further. Pavitra dreams of becoming a nurse, and Laxmi insists she stay in school despite relatives suggesting she help at home or marry early. Gender roles are fixed: Laxmi cooks all meals, fetches water from the shared borewell, manages the anganwadi work and buffaloes, while Basavaraj and his brother handle field labour and trips to the APMC. Her mother-in-law, now frail, once worked as a daily-wage labourer and receives a widow pension of Rs 1,000 monthly.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Laxmi herself passed SSLC from a Kuruba hostel in Jamkhandi in 2007, the first girl in her family to complete secondary school; her parents pulled her out after tenth because they could not afford the bus fare to Bagalkote for PU. Pavitra studies in the Kannada-medium government high school where textbooks are free under the government scheme, but Laxmi pays around Rs 1,200 yearly for the uniform, notebooks and a private mathematics tutor who charges Rs 300 monthly. Sharan attends the same school and brings home midday-meal benefits; both children receive Shakti bus passes, sparing the family about Rs 400 monthly in transport costs. Laxmi dreams of sending Pavitra to the nursing college in Bagalkote after SSLC and PU, which would cost perhaps Rs 60,000 yearly for fees and hostel.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Laxmi's mother-in-law suffers from joint pain and occasional breathlessness; the nearest primary health centre is six kilometres away in Jamkhandi, and doctors refer serious cases to Bagalkote district hospital, a forty-kilometre bus ride costing Rs 150 return. Laxmi herself is anaemic—her haemoglobin was 9.8 g/dL at the last anganwadi check—and tires easily, though she rarely rests. Pavitra complains of stomach pain during exams, which Laxmi attributes to exam stress and irregular meals when money is short. The anganwadi distributes iron tablets and deworming doses, but many mothers skip follow-up visits. Laxmi worries about fluoride in the borewell water; neighbours speak of dental stains and joint problems, though no one has money for water filters. Dengue struck the hamlet in the 2024 monsoon, and one child was hospitalised in Bagalkote for a week; the family borrowed Rs 12,000 for treatment despite Ayushman Bharat coverage, because they had to pay upfront and wait for reimbursement. Health expenses deepen debt faster than any other shock.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Laxmi's family belongs to the Kuruba community, traditionally shepherds and now mostly small farmers and labourers in Bagalkote; Kurubas form a significant part of the district's population and many identify with the Kaginele Kanaka Guru Peetha. Laxmi visits the Banashankari temple in Badami once a year during the jatra, a half-day trip by bus with Pavitra and her mother-in-law, seeking blessings for the children's education and the farm's prosperity. Caste shapes social ties: Laxmi's anganwadi serves Kuruba, Lingayat and SC Holeya families, and she navigates caste sensitivities around seating and utensils diplomatically, though upper-caste parents sometimes complain. Her husband attends Kuruba community meetings in Jamkhandi where leaders discuss the demand for Scheduled Tribe status and political alignments; some support Congress, others BJP. Festivals such as Ugadi and Deepavali are marked with new clothes if money permits; Sharan participates in Huttari, the jowar harvest festival. The anganwadi also runs SHG meetings where women discuss microfinance loans, though Laxmi has not joined, fearing she cannot repay another instalment.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Laxmi receives her anganwadi honorarium through direct bank transfer, though delays of two or three months are routine, forcing her to borrow for groceries. Pavitra and Sharan hold Shakti bus passes issued in mid-2026, which save the family considerable expense; Laxmi herself uses Shakti for the rare trip to Bagalkote, marvelling that women can now travel without paying, though she hears the NWKRTC complains of unpaid dues. The family has a yellow ration card and collects ten kilograms of rice monthly under Anna Bhagya; Laxmi would prefer cash, as neighbours do, to buy jowar flour instead, but the system is rigid. Gruha Lakshmi payments began reaching her account in late 2023, Rs 2,000 monthly, but instalments have been delayed since mid-2025; she tracks the news anxiously because that money pays the tutor. Flood relief in 2024 came months late and covered only part of the cotton loss. The gram panchayat is dominated by Lingayat leaders; Kuruba voices are fewer, though the taluk panchayat member is Kuruba. Laxmi has attended one Janaspandana grievance day but got no response about the anganwadi building's leaking roof.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Laxmi worries most about keeping Pavitra in school until she finishes PU and enters nursing college; every rupee of debt and every delayed wage threatens that dream. She resents that Kalyana Karnataka districts receive Article 371(J) funds and a Kalaburagi secretariat while Bagalkote, equally poor, gets nothing beyond Belagavi's ten-day winter session, which feels like a symbolic gesture. She blames both drought and government for the farm crisis: Almatti dam's height has not been raised, Malaprabha canal water comes irregularly, and crop insurance pays a pittance. She fears Pavitra will marry early if money runs out, and that Sharan will migrate to Goa or Pune for work, leaving the farm and the old to fend for themselves.

personas.name: Shankar
personas.definition: Shankar is a composite portrait of a handloom weaver in Ilkal town, Bagalkote district, navigating the sharp decline of a craft once supported by thousands of looms but now reduced to about two hundred working units. He represents the generation caught between pride in Ilkal's GI-tagged kasuti border sarees and the daily economic pressures that push families toward powerloom conversion, migration, or withdrawing children from school to cut costs.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Shankar works a pit loom in a small shed behind his house in the Devanga colony near Ilkal's bus stand. He begins before dawn, warping and weaving for eight to ten hours to complete one saree every two to three days, depending on the intricacy of the kasuti border and the tope-teni join that marks genuine Ilkal work. A finished saree fetches him between Rs 1,500 and Rs 3,000 from the master weaver who supplies the yarn and takes the piece to the Ilkal cooperative or to traders in Hubballi and Belagavi. After the master weaver's cut and the cost of warp preparation, Shankar's daily earnings settle around Rs 300 to Rs 400, far below what a powerloom operator or a construction worker in Bagalkote town can make. Orders have thinned over the past decade; cheaper polyester sarees flood the market, and even wedding customers now hesitate at the Rs 8,000 to Rs 15,000 price for a pure-silk Ilkal. The 2025 GI tag brought brief publicity but no price premium or bulk orders. Shankar borrows from the cooperative society and from a private financier at two per cent monthly interest to buy groceries and to pay school fees. Electricity cuts interrupt the single bulb that lights his loom in the evening, and his eyesight has weakened from years of close work without proper glasses.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Shankar lives with his wife Renuka, their three children—a daughter in second-year PU at the government composite college in Ilkal, a son in Class 9 at the Kannada-medium high school, and a younger daughter in Class 6—and his widowed mother, who is seventy and receives a Rs 1,000 monthly pension. Renuka winds bobbins, helps with the warp, and runs the household on a budget that rarely exceeds Rs 8,000 a month. She also works two hours each morning at a neighbour's chilli-sorting shed during the December-March season, earning Rs 100 a day. The eldest daughter wants to study B.Com in Bagalkote and then attempt the KPSC exam, an ambition that fills Shankar with both pride and dread because hostel and tuition fees in Bagalkote will cost at least Rs 5,000 a month. His son is less interested in studies and has started spending afternoons at a friend's motorcycle-repair shop near the bus stand, a drift that worries both parents. Renuka's brother works in a powerloom unit in Ilkal and has offered to teach the boy the trade, an offer Shankar resists because he still hopes his children will escape the loom. Gender roles are traditional: Renuka manages all housework, cooking on a two-burner LPG stove, and Shankar makes the financial decisions, though he consults her on the children's schooling. His mother, frail and arthritic, spends her days on a cot in the front room, recalling the 1980s when every house in the colony had two looms and work never stopped.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Shankar completed Class 7 at the Kannada-medium primary school in Ilkal and then left to learn weaving from his father; Renuka studied up to Class 5. Both are determined that their children will finish at least SSLC and, if possible, PU. The eldest daughter attends the government composite PU college in Ilkal, travelling one kilometre by bicycle; her arts stream fees are nominal, but textbooks, notebooks, and the compulsory college uniform cost about Rs 3,000 a year, and she takes private tuition in English and Economics for Rs 1,200 a month in a tutor's house near the market. The Class 9 son studies at the town high school; his fees are covered under the midday-meal and textbook schemes, but Shankar pays Rs 800 a month for maths and science tuition because the school's teacher turnover is high and the boy's marks have slipped. The younger daughter attends the nearby primary school and needs no extra tuition yet. Shankar received the first two instalments of Gruha Lakshmi on time, which helped pay the PU daughter's college fees, but the August 2026 payment was delayed, forcing him to borrow Rs 2,000 from the financier. The family hopes the eldest will pass second PU in 2027, gain a government seat in Bagalkote for B.Com, and eventually secure a government job or bank post. That hope justifies every rupee spent on her education, even as the household's income remains precarious.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Shankar suffers from chronic lower-back pain and weakening eyesight, both occupational hazards of pit-loom weaving. He consulted the taluk hospital in Ilkal two years ago and was prescribed reading glasses, which he bought for Rs 400 from a vendor at the weekly market, and painkillers, which he takes sporadically because they upset his stomach. He has not followed up with an ophthalmologist in Bagalkote because the consultation, travel, and spectacles would cost more than Rs 2,000. Renuka has mild anaemia, diagnosed during a government health camp, but she rarely takes the iron tablets because they cause nausea. The eldest daughter is healthy, though she complains of fatigue during exams. The younger children had fever and loose motions during the September 2026 rains; Shankar took them to a private clinic in Ilkal, spending Rs 800 on consultation and medicines, because the taluk hospital's outpatient queue was three hours long. His mother has osteoarthritis and high blood pressure; she receives subsidised medicines under the Arogya Karnataka scheme from the taluk hospital, but the family worries about a fall or a sudden illness that would require admission to the district hospital in Bagalkote, thirty kilometres away, where even a subsidised bed would mean lost wages, travel, and food costs. Fluorosis is endemic in parts of Bagalkote district, and several neighbours have dental fluorosis, though Shankar's family drinks filtered water from a community tap that he believes is safer. No one in the household has health insurance beyond the Ayushman Bharat-Arogya Karnataka card, which Shankar has never needed to use. The family's diet is dominated by jowar bhakri, dal, and seasonal vegetables; milk, eggs, and chicken are rare luxuries, reserved for festivals.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Shankar belongs to the Devanga weaving community, historically associated with handloom cotton and silk work and classified as OBC in Karnataka. The Devanga colony in Ilkal has about sixty weaving families, most now struggling with the same decline that has closed looms across the town. Community ties are strong: families lend each other warp yarn, share master-weaver contacts, and gather for life-cycle rituals. Shankar is a Lingayat by faith, initiated as a child, and wears a linga in a silver case around his neck. The family visits the Kalamma temple in Ilkal on Fridays and the Banashankari temple in Badami once a year during the January jatra, a daylong trip by NWKRTC bus. Renuka observes Monday fasts for Shiva and lights a lamp at the small household shrine each evening. Shankar occasionally attends satsangs at a Lingayat math in Bagalkote, where the swami offers dasoha free meals and spiritual talks, though he has no regular discipleship. The community's historical pride in weaving is now shadowed by economic humiliation: younger Devangas in Ilkal increasingly describe themselves simply as OBC or avoid mentioning their caste occupation. Shankar resents the stereotype that weavers are backward or uneducated; he points to the craft's artistic complexity and the GI recognition, though he concedes that recognition has brought no rescue. Relations with the neighbouring Valmiki and Muslim colonies are cordial but separate; children play together, but social and marriage networks remain endogamous. Shankar has little involvement in formal caste or community organisations, though he contributed Rs 500 to a Devanga sangha effort in 2024 to petition the state for a weaver welfare package, which went unanswered.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He is cynical about local politicians, who visit the Devanga colony before elections with promises of loom-shed upgrades, yarn subsidies, and marketing support but rarely return afterward. The Ilkal town panchayat repaired the main road through the colony in 2025, but the community tap still runs dry for three hours each afternoon, and the streetlights are erratic. Shankar accessed a Rs 10,000 emergency loan from the Ilkal weavers' cooperative society in 2024, repaying it in monthly instalments of Rs 1,000; the cooperative also runs a small showroom, but it stocks mostly powerloom sarees now. He enrolled for a subsidised yarn supply under a state handloom-welfare scheme in 2023, but the yarn arrived eight months late and the colours were not what he had ordered. He has a ration card (BPL, though the family's income sometimes exceeds the threshold) and receives five kilograms of rice per person per month under Anna Bhagya, which Renuka collects from the fair-price shop. The family has an Ayushman Bharat card but no other insurance. Shankar has never met his MLA, though he knows the legislator is from Bagalkote taluk and belongs to the Congress. He has heard of the Kittur Rani Chennamma development board proposal and wonders, with little optimism, whether it might bring funds to revive Ilkal's handloom sector. He blames both the central and state governments for allowing cheap polyester imports and for failing to enforce the Handloom Reservation Act.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Shankar is proud of Ilkal's saree tradition—the crimson-and-black temple borders, the tope-teni technique, the 2025 GI tag—but he fears he may be among the last generation to practise it. He worries daily about money: paying the tuition fees, clearing the debt with the financier, meeting a medical emergency, keeping his children in school. His greatest anxiety is that his son will quit after SSLC and join a powerloom or a Bagalkote garage, closing the door to a salaried future. He is determined that his eldest daughter will not be married off at seventeen, as some neighbours have done, but will finish PU and attempt college; this determination borders on defiance, given the household's shaky finances. He resents that NWKRTC's Shakti scheme benefits women travelling to Hubballi but does not help him get his sarees to market more cheaply. He sees the Gruha Lakshmi payments as genuine help, though the delays frustrate him. He admires his daughter's ambition and discipline, and he draws his own resilience from the need to support her dreams, even as the loom's earnings shrink year by year.

personas.name: Raju
personas.definition: Raju is a composite portrait of a skilled foundry mould-maker in Vijayapura city, navigating the pressures of industrial work, rising household costs, and the aspiration to see his children finish schooling in a district where dropout rates and economic volatility test even stable working families. He belongs to the Ganiga sub-caste of Lingayats, a community historically associated with oil-pressing and now spread across trades, farming and wage labour in Vijayapura.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Raju works at a small foundry near the APMC Road that casts agricultural pump parts and motor housings. His day begins at seven-thirty; he prepares sand moulds, pours molten metal under a tin-roofed shed where the heat in summer months is brutal, and finishes moulds by hand with files and scrapers. The foundry employs eight men; wages are paid weekly, about Rs 14,000 a month for Raju, sometimes delayed when orders slow. Metal prices and farmer demand swing with the monsoon: a drought year like 2023 or the feared declaration in 2026 means fewer pump orders and shorter weeks. Diesel, groceries and school fees have all climbed; his wife's ration card helps with rice under Anna Bhagya, but vegetables, kerosene and clinic visits eat into savings. Raju keeps a modest emergency fund in a post-office account and borrowed Rs 40,000 two years ago from a local finance company to repair the house roof; monthly instalments of Rs 2,200 continue. He rides a fifteen-year-old TVS motorcycle to work, shares tea at a stall outside the foundry gate, and returns home by seven in the evening, hands blackened and shoulders aching.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Raju lives in a two-room house with a small courtyard in a Ganiga-majority lane near the railway crossing. His wife Renuka manages the household, cooks on an LPG stove, draws water from a street tap that runs for two hours each morning, and washes clothes by hand. They have three children: a daughter aged eighteen who passed SSLC last year and now stays home helping with housework and younger siblings; a son aged fifteen in Class 10 at a Kannada-medium government high school; and a younger daughter aged eleven in Class 6. Raju's mother, now seventy-two and widowed, lives with them; she suffers joint pain and relies on him for medicines and clinic visits. His elder brother farms a small dryland plot in a village twelve kilometres away; they meet on festival days and sometimes share costs for family ceremonies. Gender roles are traditional: Renuka does not work outside the home, though she once stitched blouses for neighbours; Raju decides major expenses, but Renuka manages the ration card, Gruha Lakshmi instalments and children's clothing. The eldest daughter's marriage is on his mind; arranging it will require a loan or pledging gold.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Raju completed Class 7 in his native village; his parents needed him to work, and schooling ended. He is determined his children will do better. His son Suresh studies at the government boys' high school a kilometre away; fees are low, but notebooks, uniform and a second-hand bicycle cost about Rs 3,000 a year, and Suresh attends evening tuition for mathematics and science at Rs 500 a month. Suresh wants to study PU and join a polytechnic or ITI; Raju hopes he will, though PU college fees, hostel costs and two years without earnings worry him. His younger daughter Kavita studies at a Kannada-medium primary school; she is bright and regular. The eldest, Lata, passed SSLC with 60 per cent but did not continue; Raju could not afford college fees and believed marriage was the next step, a decision he now half-regrets.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Raju's main health concern is his mother's arthritis and his own occasional chest pain from foundry smoke and metal dust. The family uses a government primary health centre for fevers and minor ailments; serious cases mean a trip to the district hospital or a private clinic where consultation and medicines cost Rs 800 to Rs 1,500. His mother's pills for blood pressure cost Rs 300 a month. Raju enrolled in Ayushman Bharat-Arogya Karnataka two years ago after a neighbour's hospitalisation; he has not used it yet but keeps the card. Renuka is anaemic, a common issue among women in Vijayapura district according to clinic posters, but she has not had blood tests or regular treatment. Drinking water from the tap sometimes smells of chlorine; during summer, diarrhoea cases rise in the lane, especially among children. Vijayapura's NFHS-5 data show high levels of child stunting and anaemia, though Raju does not follow statistics. Heat is exhausting; last summer he fainted once at the foundry and was given oral rehydration salts. The family has no health insurance beyond Ayushman, and a major illness or accident would mean debt. His mother occasionally visits a traditional bonesetter and uses herbal oil for joint pain, distrusting hospital queues and costs.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Raju belongs to the Ganiga sub-caste within the Lingayat fold, historically oil-pressers, now a small OBC community in Vijayapura. His family visits the Murusavira Math and the Tontadarya Math on festival days and receives prasada. He wears the linga; his wife and mother observe Somavara vrata on Mondays. The lane where he lives is mixed—Ganiga, Kuruba, a few Muslim families—but socialising mostly happens within caste lines. Community ties matter for loans, job leads and marriage arrangements; a Ganiga sangha in the city organises an annual fair and sometimes provides school scholarships, though Raju's children have not received one. He respects the mutt's authority and attended a Panchamasali rally in Belagavi in 2024, though as Ganiga he is not part of that agitation. His Muslim neighbour's son is a friend of Suresh; they play cricket in the street, but Raju would not consider an inter-religious marriage. Renuka participates in a women's self-help group linked to a local NGO; it offers small savings and loans at lower interest than private moneylenders. Raju's trust is in mutts, cooperative banks and kin networks more than government offices, which he finds slow and indifferent.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He has a ration card under the National Food Security Act, receiving rice and some sugar; the Gruha Lakshmi Rs 2,000 monthly payment to Renuka has been irregular—delayed twice this year, causing frustration. Shakti free bus travel helped his eldest daughter visit relatives in a nearby village, though city buses are few. Raju has never applied for MGNREGA; it is for villagers, he believes. He once visited the taluk office to get an income certificate for his son's school fee concession; it took three visits and a small payment to a typist. He knows the corporator by face and has asked him twice to fix the street tap; the second time it was done. Raju hears about the Kittur Karnataka development board demand, the winter session at Belagavi's Suvarna Soudha, and complaints that Kalyana Karnataka gets Article 371(J) funds while Kittur Karnataka is ignored; he agrees broadly but does not join rallies. His encounters with police are few and wary; once his motorcycle documents were checked and he paid a small fine. Govt schemes feel distant—forms, delays, and favouritism—but the ration card and Ayushman card are tangible.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Raju worries most about money: keeping his son in school, marrying his daughter without crushing debt, and his mother's health. He is proud to be Lingayat, proud of Vijayapura's history—Adil Shahi monuments, Basavanna's vachana legacy—and proud that his children speak Kannada. He resents that Bengaluru and Mysuru get attention, Kalyana Karnataka gets funds, and Kittur Karnataka is left with speeches and a ten-day winter session. Drought, he says, is the city's curse; when rains fail, pump orders vanish, water is rationed, and tempers fray. He blames government negligence for Mahadayi's delay—"Why should Goa get our river?"—and believes Kalasa-Banduri would transform Vijayapura's dry lands, though he is vague on the details. He respects mutts, distrusts politicians equally across parties, and believes hard work and education are the only escape. Outsiders, he says, confuse Vijayapura with the Kalyana or lump it with Belagavi's Marathi politics, missing that it is a Kannada city with its own struggles. He demands Mahadayi water, a Kittur board with real funds, and fair crop prices; he expects little and plans accordingly.

personas.name: Nasreen
personas.definition: Nasreen is a composite portrait of a Bidriware artisan and workshop assistant from Bidar city, Bidar district, in the Kalyana Karnataka region. She represents the lived experience of women in traditional craft families navigating workshop labour, household responsibilities, children's schooling aspirations and the economic pressures facing Bidar's centuries-old silver-inlay metalwork trade.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Nasreen works in her family's small Bidriware workshop in one of the old neighbourhoods near Bidar Fort, where the craft has been practised for generations. She assists with the black-oxidation finishing and polishing stages after the men complete the inlay work, earning around four to five thousand rupees a month when orders are steady. The workshop depends on government emporium orders, tourist purchases and occasional export consignments arranged through craft cooperatives, but demand has become unpredictable. Her husband, also a Bidriware craftsman, works on the silver-wire inlay, and together they manage household expenses that include rent, food, children's school fees and healthcare. Mornings begin early with cooking and sending the children to school, then she reaches the workshop by nine. Work continues until late afternoon, interrupted by breaks for namaz at home. She buys vegetables and provisions from the weekly market near the Dargah-e-Shareef, where Dakhni Urdu is the common language of bargaining. Income fluctuates with tourist seasons and craft-fair bookings, and the family has taken small loans from relatives during lean months when orders dry up.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Nasreen lives with her husband, two daughters aged twelve and nine, and a seven-year-old son in a rented two-room house in Bidar city's old quarter. Her husband's elderly mother lives with them and helps with cooking and minding the younger child when Nasreen is at the workshop. Marriage was arranged when Nasreen was nineteen, and she moved from her parents' home in a nearby lane to her husband's household. Her own schooling stopped after Class 7 when her parents needed her to help at home and saw no path forward for girls in their community beyond marriage. She is determined that her daughters finish at least their SSLC and perhaps continue to PUC, though the costs worry her. Her older daughter attends the government Urdu-medium high school nearby, and Nasreen walks her there each morning before heading to work. Her son studies at a Kannada-medium school that charges a small fee, chosen because the family hopes he might find government work someday. Household chores—cooking, washing, fetching water when the tap runs dry—fall mostly to Nasreen and her mother-in-law. Her husband's income is pooled with hers, but decisions about spending rest largely with him and his mother.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Nasreen's own schooling ended at Class 7 in an Urdu-medium government school, a common path for girls in her neighbourhood at the time. She can read Urdu fluently and some Kannada, and she regrets not continuing to high school, feeling it limits her ability to help her children with homework or navigate official forms. Her older daughter, in Class 7 now, attends the same government Urdu-medium girls' high school Nasreen once did, and the girl is a good student, regularly bringing home marks above seventy percent. The school charges no tuition, but Nasreen pays for textbooks, uniform cloth and the annual exam fee, amounting to around two thousand rupees a year. She dreams her daughter might study further, perhaps become a teacher, though the cost of PUC college and the question of whether the family can spare her labour at home loom large. Her younger daughter, in Class 4, studies at the same school. Her son, in Class 2, attends a nearby Kannada-medium school that charges a nominal fee; Nasreen and her husband chose Kannada for him hoping it opens government-job pathways under the Article 371(J) local-recruitment quota.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Nasreen delivered all three children at the government district hospital in Bidar city, and she takes them there for vaccinations and when they fall ill, though she sometimes consults a local Unani practitioner for minor ailments. The hospital is within walking distance, but waiting times are long and medicines often need to be purchased from outside pharmacies. Her mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure, managed with tablets from the government hospital's outpatient clinic, though the family sometimes struggles to afford the prescribed diet. Nasreen herself has experienced recurrent back pain from long hours bending over workshop tasks, but she rarely takes time off to see a doctor unless the pain becomes unbearable. The family is enrolled under Ayushman Bharat, and the card came in useful when her husband needed minor surgery two years ago, covering much of the hospital bill. Drinking water comes from a municipal tap in the lane, and Nasreen boils it during summer when stomach infections spread. She worries about her daughters' health as they grow older, particularly menstrual hygiene, which is rarely discussed openly at home. The workshop's dust and chemical fumes bother her lungs sometimes, but she has no protective equipment and considers it part of the craft's unavoidable conditions.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Nasreen's family belongs to Bidar's Muslim community, which has lived in the city for generations, tracing roots back to the Bahmani Sultanate period and the city's centuries as a Deccani cultural centre. The neighbourhood around the Bidar Fort and the old bazaar lanes is predominantly Muslim, with Urdu and Dakhni spoken at home and in the market. Her family visits the Dargah-e-Shareef of Khwaja Bande Nawaz in Kalaburagi once a year during the urs, a journey by KKRTC bus that the whole household looks forward to. Daily prayers structure the rhythm of life: her mother-in-law prays five times a day at home, and Nasreen joins for Fajr and Maghrib when workshop hours allow. Her husband sometimes attends Friday prayers at the neighbourhood mosque. Community ties are dense—relatives live within walking distance, and the lane's families have known each other for decades. Weddings, Eid celebrations and condolence gatherings bring everyone together. Nasreen's circle includes other Bidriware artisan families, and women gather in the afternoons to chat, share news and help with each other's children. She is acutely aware of the stereotypes that outsiders sometimes hold about the region being "not really Kannada" because of its multilingual character, and she feels both pride in Bidar's Deccani heritage and frustration that this history is sometimes read as foreignness rather than as rooted Karnataka identity.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Nasreen has a ration card and an Aadhaar card, and the family collects subsidised rice and kerosene each month from the ration shop near the market. She enrolled for the Gruha Lakshmi scheme when it was announced, and the monthly two thousand rupees deposited directly into her bank account has become an important cushion for household expenses, though she wishes it were indexed to inflation. The family's Ayushman Bharat card came through the local Asha worker's help, and Nasreen keeps it carefully for hospital visits. She has heard of Article 371(J) and the special status meant for Kalyana Karnataka, and she hopes her son might one day benefit from the local-recruitment quota in government jobs, though she does not fully understand the domicile-certificate process. Her husband applied for a loan under a craft-cooperative scheme, but the paperwork took months and the amount granted was less than hoped. Nasreen has never voted separately from her family's collective decision, usually guided by her husband and his brothers, though she is registered as a voter. She is aware of the annual September 17th event marked by some as Liberation Day and by others in her community as Integration Day, and the contested framings of Hyderabad State's end make her wary of political rhetoric that pits one memory against another. She has little direct interaction with the taluk office or the municipal corporation, except when renewing ration-card details or getting a birth certificate for her youngest child.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Nasreen worries most about money—whether the workshop will get enough orders, whether the children's school fees can be paid on time, whether a medical emergency will force the family into debt. She is proud of her craft and the centuries of skill it represents, but frustrated that Bidriware's reputation does not translate into steady income for artisans like her family. She wants her daughters to have choices she did not, and she is determined they finish schooling even if it means tight budgets and borrowing from relatives. She blames the government for not doing enough to support traditional crafts beyond token awards and exhibitions, and for letting tourist interest wane without serious marketing. She resents the way Bidar and the larger Kalyana Karnataka region are labelled "most backward" in reports, a phrase that feels like an insult rather than a diagnosis calling for remedy. She sees the multilingual, multi-faith character of her neighbourhood as a strength, not a deficit, and she bristles when outsiders imply the region is less authentically Kannadiga because Urdu and Dakhni are spoken here. She takes pride in Bidar Fort, the city's heritage and the memory of the Bahmani court, and she wishes her children knew more of this history in their textbooks. She hopes Article 371(J) will eventually deliver real opportunities for local youth, but she has seen enough schemes come and go to remain cautious. Above all, she wants her children to have a stable future, whether through education, craft or government work, and she is prepared to work as hard as necessary to give them that chance.

personas.name: Shanmukha
personas.definition: Shanmukha is a composite portrait of a thirty-four-year-old Kuruba man working as a truck operator at a limestone quarry near Basavakalyan town in Bidar district, Kalyana Karnataka. He represents the working lives of men in and around this historic temple town who rely on the cement-linked stone economy for their livelihoods, while maintaining deep roots in a community marked by seasonal herding traditions and pride in Basavakalyan's Sharana heritage.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Shanmukha drives a tipper truck ferrying limestone from a quarry west of Basavakalyan to a cement plant near Shahabad, making three or four trips a day depending on load times and road conditions. He earns around twelve thousand rupees a month on contract, paid per trip rather than a fixed salary, so a breakdown or a rain closure cuts directly into his income. The quarry is noisy and dusty; he wraps a cloth over his nose and mouth but still coughs through most evenings. Diesel costs, tyre repairs and the occasional bribe to overloading checkpoints eat into what he takes home. He starts before sunrise to beat the heat and the crowded roads, returning by mid-afternoon when the quarry shuts for blasting. On Sundays and festival days he helps his brother tend their small field of jowar and tur on the edge of town, work that feels less pressured but brings in little cash. His wife manages the household budget tightly, stretching every rupee between rent, school fees and groceries. He dreams of owning his own truck one day, though the down-payment for a used vehicle is far beyond his savings.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Shanmukha lives with his wife, two sons aged ten and six, and his widowed mother in a rented two-room house in one of Basavakalyan's older neighbourhoods, near the main road to Humnabad. His wife, trained up to seventh standard, stays home to cook, clean and care for his mother, who has joint pain and rarely leaves the house. His elder brother farms the family's ancestral two-acre plot on the town's outskirts and lives there with his own family; the brothers share the harvest but not daily expenses. Shanmukha married at twenty-three, in a simple ceremony arranged by his uncles within the Kuruba community, and his wife brought no dowry beyond clothes and a few gold bangles. He sees his role as provider and his wife's as homemaker, a division neither questions aloud. His mother, widowed young, ran the household when he and his brother were boys, working as a farm labourer; now he insists she rest. His sons are his pride, and he is determined they will finish school and find salaried work, not the dust and uncertainty he has known.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Shanmukha studied up to eighth standard at a government Kannada-medium school in Basavakalyan before dropping out to help his brother in the fields after their father's sudden death. He regrets not finishing tenth, knowing it limits his chances for formal employment, but at the time there was no choice. His elder son is in fifth standard and his younger in first, both attending the same government primary school where fees are waived but books, uniforms and noon-meal contributions add up. The school is a fifteen-minute walk from home, manageable for now, but Shanmukha worries about the transition to high school, which will mean either a longer commute or boarding in Bidar if the nearby high school's quality does not improve. He wants his boys to pass SSLC and go on to a diploma or degree, something with a certificate that opens doors. His wife, though less educated, insists they attend every day and helps them with simple homework in the evenings. The idea that his children might work with their hands as he does feels like failure to him; education is the only ladder he can see.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Shanmukha's persistent cough, legacy of years breathing quarry dust, has never been formally diagnosed; he takes over-the-counter cough syrup when it worsens but has never visited the government hospital in Bidar for a chest check. His mother's joint pain is treated with balms and occasional paracetamol; a doctor once suggested an X-ray, but the cost and the daylong trip put it off. His wife delivered both sons at the government maternity hospital in Basavakalyan; the first birth was difficult, and she was referred to Bidar, but the second went smoothly. Immunisations for the children are up to date, tracked through the anganwadi, and his younger son recovered quickly from a bout of fever last monsoon. Shanmukha knows men in the quarry who have silicosis—hacking coughs that never stop—and he fears the same fate, but quitting would mean no income. The 108 ambulance is known to everyone, though he has never had to call it. Ayushman Bharat cards were issued to the family two years ago, but he has not used his; he is not sure what it covers or whether the hospital will honour it without hassle.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Shanmukha is Kuruba, a Scheduled Caste community with a herding past, though his family has farmed and laboured for two generations and no longer keeps sheep. His neighbourhood is mixed—Kuruba, Madiga, Lingayat and Muslim families side by side—and daily exchanges are cordial, but marriages and temple festivals remain community-bound. He and his family visit the Basaveshwara temple in Basavakalyan town regularly, a site marking the twelfth-century Sharana saint's teaching, and he feels quiet pride that his town holds such a place in Karnataka's history. His mother lights a lamp at home every evening and observes the Kuruba community's festival of Huttari, though it has become modest over the years. Shanmukha does not attend community meetings often—work leaves him too tired—but he contributed money last year when the Kuruba Sangha organised a function at the temple. He sees the Khwaja Bande Nawaz urs procession pass through town each year and respects the tradition, though he does not visit the dargah himself. For him, faith is habit and heritage, not fervour.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Shanmukha holds a ration card, an Aadhaar card and an Ayushman Bharat card, though he is unsure how to use the last one beyond showing it at a hospital counter. His family receives subsidised rice and kerosene through the PDS shop near his house, and his wife collects it monthly without fail. He has not applied for MGNREGA work because the quarry job, insecure as it is, pays better than hundred-day labour. He hears neighbours talk about the Gruha Jyothi scheme reducing electricity bills and his wife mentions that she now travels free on KSRTC buses under Shakti, a small relief when she visits her parents in Humnabad taluk. Shanmukha has never met the gram panchayat president of the revenue village his field falls under, though his brother attends occasional meetings. He does not follow state or national politics closely but knows Basavakalyan's history matters to larger debates about Kalyana Karnataka and the funds the region is supposed to receive; he is sceptical anything will change. Officials, in his experience, ask for papers, make him wait and rarely solve problems. He respects the idea of government schemes but expects little and is rarely disappointed.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Shanmukha worries most about his health, knowing the quarry dust is stealing years from his life, and about money—whether his salary will stretch, whether the truck will break down, whether his sons will finish school or be pulled out by circumstance as he was. He is proud of Basavakalyan's place in Sharana history and feels a quiet bond with the town, but he also knows it offers no future for his children beyond the quarry or the fields. He wants his sons to study, find salaried jobs with Saturdays off, and live in a place with cleaner air. He resents that Kalyana Karnataka is labelled backward and yet sees little of the special funds or opportunities he hears mentioned in the news; to him, it feels like the government forgets this region once the speeches are done. He blames no community or person for his struggles, only a vague sense that people like him are expected to manage on their own. What he demands, quietly and without expectation, is that his children get a fair chance—a good school nearby, a hospital that works, a government job if they study hard enough—and that his cough does not become the kind that never stops.

personas.name: Vasantha
personas.definition: Vasantha is a composite portrait of a Lingayat woman running a small groundnut oil-pressing operation in Deodurga taluk, Raichur district, Kalyana Karnataka. She represents the region's women entrepreneurs balancing agricultural trade, household management, and the challenges of educating children in a district that ranks among Karnataka's most backward under the Nanjundappa Committee framework.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Vasantha runs a small oil-pressing unit inherited from her father-in-law in the Deodurga market yard, where farmers bring groundnut and sunflower seed from the surrounding dryland taluks. She opens the shop by seven in the morning, sorting seed by quality, running the mechanical expeller, and bottling oil in recycled plastic containers for local retail and hotel supply. Her husband drives their second-hand tempo to deliver orders across Deodurga and Lingsugur taluks. The work is seasonal: peak demand runs from November through February after the kharif groundnut harvest, then slows until sunflower arrives in April. Income fluctuates sharply with seed prices and diesel costs for transport. A good month brings fifteen to eighteen thousand rupees in profit; a bad one barely covers the electricity bill and labour for the helper boy they employ during harvest season. Vasantha keeps accounts in a lined notebook, tracking credit extended to repeat customers and outstanding payments, a constant worry in a trade built on trust and delayed settlement.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Vasantha lives in a two-room house behind the oil mill with her husband, two daughters aged thirteen and nine, and her mother-in-law, who is seventy and partially blind from untreated cataracts. Her husband's younger brother migrated to Hyderabad for construction work and sends money irregularly. Vasantha married at nineteen, shortly after completing her second PUC, and her mother-in-law often reminds her that she studied longer than most women in the family. Gender roles are negotiated daily: Vasantha manages the shop's money and customer relations, but her husband makes all major business decisions and handles travel. She wakes at five to prepare breakfast and tiffin for the children, works at the mill until midday, then returns home to cook lunch before reopening in the afternoon. Her mother-in-law helps with housework when her eyesight permits, but cannot be left alone. Vasantha's elder daughter has begun to resent the expectation that she will cook and care for her grandmother after school, a tension Vasantha tries to mediate without openly contradicting her mother-in-law.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Vasantha completed her second PUC at the government junior college in Deodurga town, an achievement she is quietly proud of; few women of her generation in the family went beyond Class 7. Her elder daughter attends the government high school in Deodurga and is preparing for her SSLC this year. Vasantha insists she will send her to PU college in Raichur city if she passes, despite her mother-in-law's objections about the cost and the propriety of a girl travelling so far. The younger daughter studies at the nearby Kannada-medium primary school. School fees are minimal under Anna Bhagya and other state schemes, but Vasantha spends nearly two thousand rupees a term on books, uniforms, and private tuition for mathematics and science, which the government high school barely covers. She dreams of her daughters studying for government jobs under the Article 371(J) local quota, a pathway she believes offers security this volatile trade cannot. The family hopes the elder girl will qualify for the Kalyana Karnataka Regional Development Board scholarship if she scores well, though Vasantha has heard stories of delayed payments and domicile-certificate disputes that make her anxious.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Vasantha's mother-in-law needs cataract surgery, but the waiting list at Raichur Institute of Medical Sciences stretches months, and private clinics in Raichur charge fees the family cannot afford upfront. Vasantha herself suffers recurring joint pain in her knees and lower back from years of standing at the mill and lifting seed sacks, but she rarely takes time off or consults a doctor. The family enrolled in Ayushman Bharat two years ago, though Vasantha is unsure what it covers and has never needed to use the card. Her daughters are healthier than she was at their age, but the younger one had a prolonged fever last monsoon that required a week of private-clinic visits and antibiotics, costing nearly three thousand rupees. Vasantha worries about fluoride in the borewell water they drink at home; neighbours speak of dental staining and bone pain, and a government survey team visited once but never returned with results. The 108 ambulance took her mother-in-law to Raichur during a fainting episode last year, but the emergency-room wait was six hours, and they were sent home with no follow-up. Vasantha sees health as something to manage with home remedies and prayer until a crisis forces hospital expense.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Vasantha's family belongs to the Lingayat community, and they observe Sharana tradition with daily prayers at the household shrine and annual visits to the Basavanna temple during Shivaratri. The local Lingayat mutt in Deodurga provides some social cohesion, organizing festivals and offering informal advice on disputes, though Vasantha herself rarely attends its gatherings, constrained by work and household duties. She speaks Kannada at home and in the market, though many of her Muslim customers speak Dakhni Urdu, and she has picked up enough to manage business greetings and accounts. Community ties are both a source of support and pressure: relatives expect loans, favours, and participation in life-cycle rituals that strain the family's time and budget. Vasantha draws strength from the memory of Basavanna's teachings on equality and work, and she quietly resents caste and gender hierarchies, though she seldom voices this openly. She respects her mother-in-law's authority at home and defers to her husband in public, while managing most practical decisions on her own. The shop's reputation depends on trust, and Vasantha is meticulous about fair weights and honest dealings, a pride she considers both spiritual duty and business necessity.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Vasantha has little direct interaction with local government beyond registering the oil mill for a trade licence and occasional visits from food-safety inspectors, who sometimes demand payments she considers unofficial. The family received a Gruha Jyothi electricity subsidy that reduced their household bill, though the mill's commercial connection does not qualify. Her elder daughter travels to school on the KKRTC bus under the Shakti free-travel scheme, a benefit Vasantha credits with making her willing to send the girl farther for PU college. She applied for a KKRDB scholarship for her daughter last year, but the process required multiple trips to the taluk office and a domicile certificate that took months to secure. She has heard of Article 371(J) guarantees for local jobs and education, but sees the benefits as captured by those with connections or the literacy to navigate bureaucracy. The idea of approaching a gram panchayat or taluk official for help feels remote; she expects officials to serve those who already have influence, not people like her.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Vasantha is proud that she runs her own business and educates her daughters, though she worries constantly about money, her mother-in-law's health, and whether the oil mill can sustain the family if seed prices spike or transport costs climb further. She blames poor rains, fluctuating groundnut prices, and the lack of government support for oilseed farmers for the trade's instability, and she resents that Raichur district is labelled backward without visible improvement in infrastructure or schools. Vasantha insists her daughters will not marry until they finish their education, but she feels the pressure of relatives and neighbours who think she is allowing them too much freedom. She is quietly proud of Kalyana Karnataka's Sharana heritage and the special constitutional status under Article 371(J), though she sees little of the promised funds reaching Deodurga. She worries that her elder daughter's ambition to study in Raichur city will expose her to risks Vasantha cannot control, yet she refuses to let fear trap the girl in the same limits she herself accepted. What Vasantha wants most is stability: reliable income, affordable healthcare for her mother-in-law, and a government job for at least one daughter, so the next generation does not have to wake each morning wondering if the market will cover the day's costs.

personas.name: Sharif
personas.definition: Sharif is a composite portrait of a Muslim working-class man from Manvi taluk in Raichur district, employed in the stone-crushing industry along the Tungabhadra Left Bank Canal command. He represents the mix of irrigated-agriculture opportunity and quarry-labour risk that shapes livelihoods in this corner of Kalyana Karnataka.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Sharif loads crushed stone onto tractors at a small quarry near Manvi town, earning around eight thousand rupees a month when work is steady. During the irrigation season he also drives a tractor for a local farmer who grows paddy on ten acres under the Tungabhadra Left Bank Canal, adding another three to four thousand rupees across those months. The quarry work is dusty and hard on his chest; he coughs often and has heard older workers talk about silicosis, though he has never been screened for it. The tractor-driving brings him into the canal-command paddy belt where water flows predictably, unlike the dryland cotton and jowar patches further from the canal. His income is seasonal and unpredictable: the quarry shuts when orders drop and the tractor work lasts only as long as the canal runs. He leaves home before dawn, returns after dark, and spends Fridays at the mosque in Manvi town. Economic pressure is constant; every month he calculates what is left after rent, groceries and his children's school fees.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Sharif lives with his wife Naseema, their two sons aged ten and seven, and his widowed mother in a rented two-room house on the edge of Manvi town. Naseema stitches blouses and petticoats at home for a local tailor, earning around two thousand rupees a month, and manages all the household cooking, cleaning and caregiving. His mother, in her sixties, helps mind the younger boy when Naseema is busy with orders. Sharif's father died five years ago from a heart attack; there was no insurance and the family borrowed heavily for the funeral. Sharif himself married at twenty-two, shortly after his father arranged the match with Naseema's family from a village near Sindhanur. Gender roles are traditional: Naseema does not work outside the home, and Sharif makes all major financial decisions. He worries about finding enough money for his sons' future—both their schooling now and, later, their marriages. His mother receives a widow's pension of six hundred rupees a month, which helps with groceries but covers little else.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Sharif studied until Class 7 in a government Urdu-medium school in Manvi, then dropped out to help his father with farm labour. He can read Urdu script and simple Kannada, and speaks Dakhni Urdu at home and broken Kannada at work. His two sons attend the government Urdu-medium primary school in Manvi town, walking fifteen minutes each way. The school is free under the RTE Act, but Sharif pays for books, uniforms and the boys' mid-day snacks, totalling around fifteen hundred rupees a year. He dreams of keeping them in school through SSLC and perhaps into a diploma course, ideally something that leads to a government job under the Article 371(J) local quota that everyone talks about. His wife, who studied only until Class 5, insists the boys must study further than their parents did. The older boy is bright and enjoys school; the younger one is less interested and sometimes skips classes to play cricket.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Sharif's persistent cough worries him, but he has never visited a doctor for it because the nearest government hospital is in Raichur town, an hour away by bus, and he cannot afford to lose a day's wages. His wife once suggested he get a chest X-ray, but he dismissed it as too expensive. Naseema and the boys are generally healthy, though the younger son had a bad fever last year and they spent two thousand rupees at a private clinic in Manvi for tests and medicines. His mother has joint pain and mild diabetes, managed with tablets from a local pharmacy; she has never seen a specialist. The family drinks water from a borewell shared with neighbours; Sharif has heard talk of fluoride in the groundwater in some parts of Raichur district, but does not know if it affects Manvi. They are enrolled in Ayushman Bharat, but Sharif is unclear about what it covers and has never tried to use it. Dust from the quarry settles in his lungs and on his skin; he knows men who have collapsed at work, but no one has ever explained silicosis to him in detail. Healthcare feels distant and costly, something to avoid unless absolutely necessary.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Sharif is Muslim, part of the substantial Muslim population in Raichur district with roots going back to the Hyderabad State period. He prays five times a day when work allows, always attends Friday prayers at the Jama Masjid in Manvi town, and observes Ramadan strictly. His family speaks Dakhni Urdu at home, the everyday language of Muslims in this part of Kalyana Karnataka, though he uses Kannada when dealing with quarry supervisors and tractor owners. The mosque is a social hub: after prayers he discusses work, water shortages and children's schooling with other men. He respects the Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah in Kalaburagi, though he has visited it only twice in his life. His neighbourhood in Manvi is mixed—Muslims, Lingayats and Scheduled Castes—but socialising mostly stays within community lines. He feels a strong sense of Muslim identity and is alert to any slight or exclusion, though he does not talk about it much. Naseema and his mother fast, cook for Eid and maintain strict halal practice. Sharif sees himself as a believer and a provider, trying to live a decent life in difficult circumstances.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He knows about Article 371(J) special status and the local-job reservation it promises, and he pins his hopes on it for his sons' future. He hears people talk about the Kalyana Karnataka Regional Development Board and funds that are supposed to come to the region, but he has not seen any direct benefit—no new roads, no better school buildings in Manvi. He receives Anna Bhagya rations every month, ten kilograms of rice that he collects from the ration shop without fail. His wife uses the Shakti free-bus scheme to visit her parents in Sindhanur, saving the family a few hundred rupees a month. Sharif has never dealt with the taluk office or applied for any scheme beyond his ration card and Ayushman card. He is wary of officials, whom he sees as indifferent or corrupt. He knows the local corporator by sight but has never approached him. Government feels distant, something that announces programs but delivers little to men like him.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Sharif worries most about money—whether there will be quarry work next month, whether the tractor owner will call him, whether he can keep paying school fees. He is proud of working hard and staying honest, and he resents the stereotype that Muslims are backward or uneducated; he points to his sons' schooling as proof that his family is trying. He feels Kalyana Karnataka has been neglected by the state government for decades, left behind while Bengaluru and the south prosper, and he is glad the region finally has Article 371(J), even if he does not yet see much change. He blames quarry owners for not caring about workers' lungs, blames the irrigation department when the canal runs dry too early, and blames middlemen for cheating farmers. He is frustrated that people assume Dakhni Urdu speakers are not "real" Kannadigas, when his family has lived here for generations. He dreams of his sons getting government jobs under the local quota, marrying well, and living more securely than he does. He rarely complains out loud, but he carries a steady, low-level anger at how hard everything is.

personas.name: Renuka
personas.definition: Renuka is a composite portrait of a Scheduled Caste woman working in Gangavathi's groundnut and oilseed processing economy, navigating daily wage insecurity, school costs for three children, and the gap between Article 371(J) promises and lived opportunity in Koppal district. She represents the tension between canal-irrigated prosperity along the Tungabhadra Left Bank and the Scheduled Caste households who process the harvest but rarely own the land.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Renuka works the sorting and bagging line at a small groundnut oil mill on the Gangavathi-Munirabad road, six days a week when the mill runs at full capacity during the November-to-March crushing season. She earns two hundred and twenty rupees for an eight-hour shift, though the owner sometimes stretches the day to ten hours without extra pay when a large farmer's lorry arrives. In the lean months she takes daily-wage work weeding sunflower fields or loading onion sacks at the APMC yard, earning one-eighty to two hundred rupees a day. Her husband drives a rented auto-rickshaw on the Gangavathi town routes; on a good day he clears three hundred rupees after fuel and the daily rental of one-fifty to the owner. The household's joint income sits around twelve to fourteen thousand rupees a month during the oil-crushing season, dropping to eight or nine thousand in the summer lean months. They have no savings account with any real balance; every rupee is allocated before it arrives. Renuka leaves home at seven in the morning, returns by six, then cooks, helps her eldest daughter with schoolwork, and falls asleep by ten.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Renuka lives with her husband, their three children—a daughter in Class 10 at the government high school in Gangavathi town, a son in Class 7 at the same school, and a younger daughter in Class 3 at the primary school in their colony—and her mother-in-law, who is in her late sixties and can no longer work. The household rents a one-room asbestos-roofed house with a shared tap and toilet in a Scheduled Caste colony on the edge of Gangavathi, paying twelve hundred rupees a month. Renuka was married at sixteen, shortly after she stopped school in Class 8; her own schooling ended because her parents needed her to work and saw no future return in keeping a daughter in school. She hopes her eldest daughter will finish SSLC and perhaps study further, though the cost and the pressure to marry her off early weigh on every conversation. Her husband's income is unpredictable, and his drinking on some evenings cuts into the week's budget. Renuka manages all the household money, plans every meal around the cheapest dal and vegetables, and absorbs the blame when there is not enough. Her mother-in-law helps with the younger children when Renuka is at work, but her health is declining and she needs medicines the household struggles to afford.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Renuka's own schooling ended in Class 8 when her parents, both agricultural labourers, could not see the point of continuing and needed her to work. She can read Kannada slowly and write her name and basic lists, but she regrets not finishing school and is determined that her children, especially her daughters, will study further. Her eldest daughter attends the government high school in Gangavathi town, a four-kilometre ride on the KKRTC bus each day; the Shakti free-travel scheme has made that possible, saving the family about six hundred rupees a month in bus fare. The school charges no tuition, but Renuka spends around fifteen hundred rupees a term on books, uniforms, and exam fees. Her daughter is a steady student, ranking in the top half of her class, and dreams of becoming a teacher. Renuka has heard about the Article 371(J) reservation for college seats and government jobs, and the family hopes that quota will give her a chance. The youngest daughter attends the colony primary school, where the mid-day meal is often the best meal of her day. Renuka herself cannot help with homework beyond Class 5 level, so her eldest daughter tutors the younger two. The cost of private tuition, which many better-off families use, is completely out of reach.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Renuka suffers from chronic lower-back pain, a legacy of years standing on the mill floor and bending to load sacks, but she has never taken a full day off for it because she cannot afford to lose the wage. She has an Ayushman Bharat card, but the nearest empanelled hospital is in Hosapete, over thirty kilometres away, and the cost and time of traveling there for anything less than an emergency feels impossible. For fever, stomach pain, or her back, she goes to a private clinic in Gangavathi where the doctor charges one-fifty for a consultation and writes a prescription she fills at the pharmacy next door, usually spending another two to three hundred rupees. Her mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure; the government hospital in Gangavathi gives her medicines some months but not others, and when the stock runs out Renuka has to buy them at full price, which can cost six hundred rupees. Her eldest daughter had severe anaemia two years ago, diagnosed at a free school health camp; the anganwadi worker insisted Renuka get iron tablets, but sustaining the treatment and improving her diet proved difficult. Renuka herself has not had a full health check-up in years. She worries about her husband's drinking and the toll it takes on his liver and their household peace, but talking about it only leads to fights. The 108 ambulance service is known in the colony, but people say it is slow to arrive and sometimes does not come at all.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Renuka is Madiga, part of Gangavathi's substantial Scheduled Caste population working in the oilseed economy, construction labour and sanitation work. Her colony is exclusively Scheduled Caste, spatially separated from the main town and the dominant-caste neighborhoods; the colony has a shared water tap, irregular electricity, and a small Ambedkar statue at the entrance that the community gathers around on Ambedkar Jayanti every year. Renuka's family worships both Ambedkar and the village deity, and she visits the Anjaneya temple on the edge of town for her children's health and exam success. She is not deeply religious, but she observes the festivals—Ugadi, Diwali, Ambedkar Jayanti—and fasts occasionally for her children's well-being. The anganwadi worker in the colony is a helpful presence, running the feeding programme and connecting families to government schemes, though Renuka finds the paperwork for most schemes overwhelming. Caste shapes every dimension of her life: where she lives, the kind of work she can get, the way upper-caste people speak to her in the market, and her daughter's experience in a mixed-caste classroom. Renuka has heard about Basavanna and the Sharana movement's rejection of caste, taught as local pride in school textbooks, but she sees little of that equality in daily life.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Renuka has a ration card, an Ayushman Bharat card, and her children's Aadhaar cards, but navigating the welfare system feels like a continuous maze of incomplete information and lost paperwork. The family receives subsidized rice and kerosene through the PDS, though the shop sometimes runs out or opens late. She has heard about the Kalyana Karnataka Region Development Board and Article 371(J) funds, but she has no sense of what that money has actually built in Gangavathi beyond a few school buildings and a hostel she has never seen inside. The local anganwadi worker helps her understand some schemes, but most government programmes feel designed for people who already know the system and have time to visit offices repeatedly. Renuka's husband once tried to get a loan under a self-employment scheme to buy his own auto, but the paperwork and the need for a guarantor defeated him. She respects the local MLA because he is seen in the town, but she has never met him or attended a party meeting. Renuka does not follow state politics closely, but she listens when neighbors talk about reservation quotas, job recruitment, and whether Scheduled Caste families are actually getting the promised share. She feels that the government talks about Kalyana Karnataka being special and backward, but the daily experience is just wage work, school fees, and waiting.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Renuka's deepest worry is her eldest daughter's future: whether she will finish SSLC with good marks, whether the family can afford to send her to college in Gangavathi or Hosapete, whether the Article 371(J) reservation will actually open a government job or college seat for a Scheduled Caste girl from a labour household, and whether they can hold off marriage pressure from relatives long enough for her to study. She is proud that her daughter is the first in the family to reach high school and determined that she will not repeat Renuka's own truncated schooling. She worries about money every single day—the rent, the monthly school costs, the medicines, the price of onions and dal, and what will happen when her mother-in-law needs serious medical care they cannot afford. She resents the way upper-caste people in Gangavathi still treat her and her family, the spatial segregation of the colony, and the gap between the Constitution's promise of equality and the reality of her daughter being made to sit separately in one classroom incident she will never forget. She blames the oil mill owner for underpaying workers, her husband for drinking, and the government for announcing schemes that never seem to reach her household in full. Renuka demands better: a permanent job with a real salary, her daughter's education funded properly, a hospital in Gangavathi that actually works, and respect in public spaces. She sees Gangavathi's irrigated wealth and wonders why her family, working in the heart of the groundnut economy, lives in a rented asbestos room with no savings and no security.
