personas.name: Imran
personas.definition: Imran is a composite portrait of a dal mill floor supervisor in Yelburga town, Koppal district, Kalyana Karnataka region. He represents Muslim working men in the tur-dal processing economy that makes Koppal and neighbouring Kalaburagi districts central to India's pigeon-pea trade.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Imran supervises the sorting and bagging lines at a medium-sized dal mill on the edge of Yelburga town, where tur-dal brought from APMC yards across Koppal and Kalaburagi is cleaned, split and graded. He arrives at five in the morning during peak milling season—October through February—when lorries queue outside and the machines run two shifts. His day is spent checking moisture meters, managing the women who hand-sort the split dal, and keeping the packaging line moving to meet wholesale orders bound for Bengaluru and the coast. The mill pays him a monthly salary of around fourteen thousand rupees, with a small seasonal bonus if tonnage targets are met. Income is steady compared to farming, but the work is exhausting and the air thick with dal dust. The mill owner is a Lingayat trader who runs three units across the district; Imran has worked for him for sixteen years, rising from the bagging crew. During the lean months—June to September—milling slows and his hours are cut, so the household tightens its budget. His wife stitches blouses at home for a neighbourhood tailor, adding three to four thousand rupees a month. They live in a rented two-room house near the old bus stand, within walking distance of the mill and the town mosque.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Imran's household includes his wife Farhana, their three children—two daughters aged seventeen and fourteen, and a son aged ten—and his widowed mother, who is in her late sixties. His father, a bullock-cart driver, died eight years ago, and his mother now lives with them, spending her days in prayer and helping with the younger children. Farhana manages the home, cooks, and does piecework tailoring when orders come in; she attended school only until Class 5. The older daughter completed her SSLC last year at the government high school in Yelburga and now stays at home, helping her mother and waiting while the family considers whether to let her continue to PUC or arrange her marriage. The younger daughter is in Class 9 at the same school. The son is in Class 5 at the Urdu-medium primary school attached to the town mosque. Imran's two brothers live in Koppal town; one drives an auto-rickshaw and the other works as a shop assistant. The brothers gather for Eid and weddings but do not share household expenses. Gender roles are clear: Farhana handles all domestic work and childcare, Imran earns and manages money, and his mother's authority in religious and family matters is respected.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Imran himself studied up to Class 7 at the Urdu-medium school in Yelburga before leaving to work in the dal mills as a teenager; his family needed the income and saw no route forward in further schooling. He can read Urdu and enough Kannada to manage mill paperwork. His older daughter passed her SSLC in the Kannada-medium government high school with a second-class mark; the family is proud but unsure whether sending her to PUC college in Yelburga is worth the cost and risk, given that girls from their neighbourhood rarely continue past SSLC and marriage is expected. The younger daughter is a good student, and Imran wants her to finish at least SSLC. His son attends the Urdu-medium primary school because Imran and Farhana wanted him to learn to read the Quran properly; they plan to shift him to Kannada-medium for high school so he can compete for government jobs under the 371(J) quota if his marks are strong. School fees are low—around five hundred rupees a year for each child in government schools—but books, uniforms, and the PUC college fee would add up. Imran hopes his son will study further, perhaps get a diploma or a government job, and not spend his life breathing dal dust.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Imran has a persistent cough—common among dal-mill workers—from years of inhaling grain dust; he has never been formally diagnosed but knows it worsens in peak season. The family uses the government taluk hospital in Yelburga for fevers and minor illnesses; they wait hours but pay little. His mother has joint pain and high blood pressure; she takes tablets from the hospital and sees a local Unani hakim for herbal remedies. Farhana had a difficult delivery with their youngest child and was referred to the district hospital in Koppal town; the 108 ambulance took her, and she recovered, but the episode left the family in debt for two years. The children are vaccinated and generally healthy. Imran worries about his cough and what will happen if he cannot work, but he has no health insurance—only an Ayushman Bharat card that the family has never used. The drinking water in their neighbourhood comes from a borewell; they boil it after hearing of fluoride problems in some Koppal villages. No one in the household smokes, but Imran chews gutka occasionally during long shifts, a habit he knows he should stop. The older daughter's health and marriage prospects weigh on Farhana's mind.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Imran's family belongs to Yelburga's Muslim community, which makes up a significant share of the town's population and is part of the Dakhni Urdu-speaking network across Kalyana Karnataka. They pray five times a day, and Imran attends Friday prayers at the town mosque whenever his mill shift allows. Farhana observes purdah loosely—she covers her head in public but moves freely within the neighbourhood. Ramzan and Eid are the most important festivals; the family fasts, prepares biryani and sheer khurma, and visits relatives in Koppal town. Imran's mother insists on reading the Quran daily and teaching the grandson. The family has never visited the Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah in Kalaburagi, though they know of its importance and hope to go someday. Social ties are dense within the Muslim neighbourhood—neighbours help each other with loans, childcare, and wedding expenses. Imran is not active in any political organisation but feels the community's interests are often ignored. Caste is not a category he uses within the Muslim fold, but he is acutely aware of the economic distance between his mill-supervisor job and the Lingayat and Vokkaliga dal traders who own the mills and the land.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He has never approached the taluk office or a local MLA for help. The family receives ten kilograms of rice per month under Anna Bhagya, which makes a real difference to the household budget. Farhana uses the Shakti free-bus scheme to visit her mother in a nearby village, a trip she could not have afforded regularly before. Imran knows about Article 371(J) and the local-recruitment quota but does not understand the details; he hopes it will help his son get a government job someday if he studies well. He has heard of the Kalyana Karnataka Regional Development Board but does not know what it has built in Yelburga. The town's streets are poorly maintained, and the neighbourhood's drainage is a mess during the monsoon. Imran blames local contractors and officials for siphoning funds but does not expect anything to change. The dal mill is not registered under any labour welfare scheme, and he has no provident fund or pension. Politics feels distant—something decided by powerful people in Bengaluru and Koppal town.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Imran is proud of his steady job and his climb from mill labourer to supervisor, and he takes satisfaction in providing for his family without depending on anyone. But he worries constantly—about his cough and his ability to keep working, about his older daughter's future and whether they will find a decent match without a heavy dowry, about his son's education and whether the boy will have better opportunities than he did. He resents the fact that decades of dal-milling wealth have enriched a handful of trader families while workers like him remain trapped in rented houses, and he is frustrated that Koppal's schools and hospital lag so far behind what he hears about Bengaluru. He sees the 371(J) quota as a rare chance for his son but doubts it will amount to much if the boy cannot afford coaching or if the system is rigged by people with connections. Imran does not blame his community or religion for the family's struggles; he blames a lack of opportunity, unequal access to education, and an indifferent government. He wants his children to study, his daughters to marry into secure families, and his son to escape the dal dust. He believes in hard work, prayer, and looking after one's own family, but he has no faith that the state or the district administration will ever do much for people like him.

personas.name: Nirmala
personas.definition: Nirmala is a composite portrait of a woman who sorts red chillies at the Byadgi APMC yard during the harvest and milling season, lives in a Kuruba hamlet near Mundargi town, and balances piece-rate work with household farming and care responsibilities. She embodies the economic pressures facing dryland farming families in Gadag district, where cotton, onion and chilli price crashes push women into seasonal wage labour while children's schooling becomes a fragile hope stretched across drought years and harvest debts.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Nirmala sorts chillies at the Byadgi APMC yard from November through March, the peak milling season when lorries arrive from across Karnataka and beyond to buy the prized deep-red Byadgi variety. She earns between one hundred and one hundred fifty rupees for an eight-hour shift, seated on a tarpaulin under a tin shed, fingers stained crimson, eyes stinging from the capsaicin dust that hangs in the air. The work is piece-rate and irregular; some weeks she gets four days, some weeks none, depending on the merchant's stock and the weather. At home she tends a three-acre rainfed plot her husband inherited, where they grow cotton, jowar and onion. The 2023 drought withered the cotton, and the March 2024 chilli price crash—from twenty thousand to eight thousand rupees per quintal overnight—left the family with debts to the commission agent and the cooperative bank. Her husband drives a tractor on hire during the sowing and harvest seasons, but diesel costs and repairs eat into his earnings. The household runs on her chilli wages, his tractor days, a small sale of jowar, and the occasional MGNREGA work card, which she has not been able to use this year because the panchayat says no work is sanctioned.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Nirmala lives with her husband, her mother-in-law, two daughters aged fifteen and twelve, and a son aged nine. Her husband is the eldest of three brothers; the younger two have migrated to Hubballi and Pune for construction work, sending money home irregularly. Her mother-in-law, now in her seventies, looks after the goats and cooks the midday meal—jolada rotti, ennegai, shenga chutney—while Nirmala is at the APMC or in the field. Nirmala was married at seventeen, soon after failing her SSLC, and her first daughter was born the following year. She worries that her elder daughter, now in Class 10 at the government high school in Mundargi, will face the same pressure to marry if she does not pass the exam or if the family cannot afford the fees for pre-university college. Her younger daughter is in Class 7 at the same school, and her son studies in Class 4 at the Kannada-medium primary school in the hamlet. Nirmala's own mother, widowed, lives in a neighbouring village and depends on a small pension and help from Nirmala's brother. Gender roles are clear: Nirmala manages the house, the children's schooling and the goats, while her husband controls the land and tractor income, though both discuss major expenses together.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Nirmala studied up to Class 10 in the government Kannada-medium school in her natal village near Gadag town, but failed the SSLC in 1999 and did not attempt again because her family needed her labour and her marriage was arranged shortly after. She regrets not finishing, and is determined that her daughters will not repeat her fate. Her elder daughter walks four kilometres each way to the high school in Mundargi town; there is no school bus for the hamlet. The girl is bright and wants to study further, perhaps become a teacher or join a nursing course in Gadag. The school charges no tuition under the government scheme, but Nirmala spends about five hundred rupees a term on books, uniforms, pens and the occasional private tuition class in Mundargi for mathematics and science, taught by a retired teacher. Her younger daughter and son study without much difficulty so far, though the boy sometimes misses school during the cotton-picking season when Nirmala needs him to help carry water to the field. The midday meal of rice, sambar and an egg twice a week keeps them in school, but Nirmala has heard that high-school children will soon get a free bus pass, and she hopes it will reach them in time for her elder daughter's PU admission.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Nirmala suffers from chronic back pain and joint stiffness from years of bending over chilli heaps and farm work, and her fingers are scarred and hypersensitive from capsaicin exposure. She has not seen a doctor for herself in years; when the pain is severe she buys a strip of painkillers from the medical shop in Mundargi for twenty or thirty rupees. Her mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure, and receives subsidised tablets from the primary health centre in the hamlet, though the ANM visits irregularly and the centre often runs out of stock. When serious illness strikes—a fever that will not break, a child's infection, her mother-in-law's blood-sugar crisis—the family goes to the government hospital in Gadag town, ten kilometres away, or to a private clinic in Mundargi that charges consultation fees and expensive tests. The family is enrolled in Ayushman Bharat-Arogya Karnataka, but Nirmala does not fully understand the coverage and has never needed hospitalisation. Her children are immunised, but her younger daughter is visibly thin and was told by the anganwadi worker two years ago that she is anaemic; Nirmala tries to give her jaggery and greens when she can afford them. Fluoride in the borewells is a known problem in parts of Gadag; Nirmala has heard of dental fluorosis in neighbouring villages, and she worries about the water they drink. Heat, dust and drought take a toll: in summer the hamlet's hand-pump runs dry, and women walk a kilometre to a borewell that the panchayat sunk with MGNREGA funds.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Nirmala's family belongs to the Kuruba community, a shepherding and farming caste classified as OBC in Karnataka and long associated with the Kaginele Kanaka Guru Peetha, which advocates for Kuruba rights and ST status. The hamlet is mixed—Kuruba, Lingayat, SC Holeya families—but most social life is organised by caste and kinship. Nirmala's mother-in-law is devout, visiting the Tontadarya Math in Gadag town once a year for the annual jatra, and the household keeps a small shrine with pictures of Kanaka Dasa, Yellamma and a Hanuman idol. Nirmala herself prays daily, lighting incense and asking for good rains, her children's success and her husband's safety on the road. The hamlet celebrates Ugadi, Ganesh Chaturthi and Deepavali together, and the Devaragudda Mailara jatra, about twenty kilometres away in Haveri district, draws families from across the region; Nirmala went three years ago with her mother-in-law and daughters. Caste shapes opportunity: Kuruba families here own some land but lack the capital and political connections of the larger Lingayat farmers, and Nirmala sees how SC families in the hamlet get the least MGNREGA work and the worst plots. She respects the Kanaka Guru Peetha's demand for ST status, which she believes would bring her children reservation in education and jobs, though she does not follow politics closely. The community comes together for weddings, funerals and cooperative labour during harvest, and Nirmala's reputation as a hard worker and a responsible mother matters more to her than any formal social capital.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Nirmala's direct encounters with government are few and frustrating. She has a ration card—BPL, revised two years ago—that entitles the family to rice, wheat, sugar and kerosene at the fair-price shop in Mundargi; under the Anna Bhagya scheme she now receives ten kilograms of rice per person per month, which is a significant help. She has heard of the Gruha Lakshmi scheme—two thousand rupees a month to women heads of household—but does not receive it; she applied through the anganwadi worker but was told she did not meet some criterion she does not understand, and the panchayat office gave her no clear answer. Her MGNREGA card has not been activated this year. She has never met the taluk or district officials, and the gram panchayat is dominated by a Lingayat member whom she does not trust to listen to Kuruba or SC complaints. She does not attend gram sabha meetings—too much work, and women are not encouraged to speak—but she hears from neighbours about disputes over panchayat funds, road repair and drinking-water borewells. The aanganwadi in the hamlet provides eggs and nutrition for her youngest child, and the helper is a distant relative, which creates some trust. Nirmala has no experience of police, courts or the tahsildar's office, and regards all government offices as places where you need money, connections or both to get anything done.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Nirmala worries most about money: the debt to the commission agent, the coming expense of her elder daughter's PU fees and hostel, the cost of a wedding dowry if the girl does not finish her studies, and the daily struggle to feed the household when chilli work dries up and the rains fail. She is proud that her daughters study, that her elder girl is clever and wants to become something, and that the family has held on to its three acres despite the droughts. She blames no one in particular for the chilli price crash or the water scarcity—these are seen as bad luck, market forces beyond anyone's control—but she resents that government schemes are announced with fanfare and then do not reach families like hers. She is sceptical of the Kittur Karnataka board demand she has heard about on the radio; she does not see how a new board will change the price of chilli or bring rain to Mundargi. She hopes her son will study well and get a government job, and that her daughters will marry educated men who will not stop them from working. She fears drought, illness, her husband's temper when money is short, and the prospect of her elder daughter's schooling ending before it has really begun. She sees herself as a small person in a large, indifferent system, doing her best with what she has, and she draws strength from her mother-in-law's prayers, her daughters' bright faces and the quiet solidarity of the women she works with at the chilli yard.

personas.name: Irfan
personas.definition: Irfan is a composite portrait of a Muslim man in his mid-thirties who operates carding machinery in one of Lakshmeshwar's small wool and blanket units, navigating irregular work, household debt and the schooling of three children. He represents a generation raised in Urdu-medium schools who now watch their children study in Kannada medium, hoping for salaried futures their own craft town no longer promises.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Irfan runs a carding machine in a shed near the Lakshmeshwar bus stand, cleaning and combing raw wool that arrives from Bagalkote and Hubballi markets for local blanket weavers. The unit belongs to his maternal uncle and employs four workers; Irfan earns around nine thousand rupees a month when orders are steady, but orders have thinned since cheap synthetic blankets flooded the market. He starts at seven in the morning, breaking for namaz at the nearby mosque, and finishes by six unless a rush order keeps him late. Dust fills his lungs and the carding drum's whine follows him home. His wife Shahana stitches blouse pieces at home for a tailor in the market, adding another two thousand rupees most months. They rent two rooms in a lane behind the taluk office. Diesel, flour and onion prices press hard; they buy vegetables from the Thursday bazaar and ration rice under Anna Bhagya. The unit has no ESI and his uncle pays cash weekly. Irfan once thought of learning two-wheeler repair but the fees and lost wages made it impossible. He watches younger men leave for Hubballi's Gokul Road workshops or Bengaluru's garment districts, but moving the whole family feels like gambling rent and school mid-year.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Irfan lives with Shahana, whom he married twelve years ago in a neighbourhood nikah, and their three children: Ayesha is ten and in Class 5, Amir is eight and in Class 3, and baby Zara is two. Shahana manages the kitchen, the children's homework and her stitching work, rising before the azan to pack breakfast and tiffin. Her mother lives in Gadag town and visits during Ramzan; his own mother passed away four years ago and his father, a retired handloom weaver, lives with Irfan's elder brother in Ron. The brother drives an auto-rickshaw and they meet only at Eid. Shahana wants Ayesha to finish high school at least—she herself studied only until Class 7—and she insists the girl help less in the kitchen than she did. Irfan agrees but worries about the cost of PU college if Ayesha clears SSLC. Amir is livelier and sometimes skips homework for cricket in the lane; Irfan scolds him but sees his own restless childhood in the boy. Zara attends the anganwadi two streets away. Shahana's stitching money pays for milk and the children's clothes; Irfan's wages cover rent, flour and school expenses. Neither set of grandparents can help with cash. They borrowed twenty thousand from a local moneylender two years ago when Shahana needed a caesarean for Zara, and they are still repaying five hundred rupees a month.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Irfan studied in the town's Urdu-medium primary school and went to the government high school, where he scraped through Urdu-medium SSLC in 2007 with a second class. He remembers the school as crowded and the teachers as indifferent; Kannada felt like a wall he could not scale. He wanted to study further but his father's loom work was failing and he joined his uncle's carding unit at seventeen. Ayesha and Amir both go to the Kannada-medium government primary school near the taluk office; the school has six teachers for about two hundred children and the classrooms are noisy but the midday meal is regular. Ayesha is a steady student—she brings home praise from her teacher and completed her Class 4 exams with distinction—and Irfan dreams she might become a teacher or a nurse, jobs with respect and a salary. The school charges no fees but notebooks, uniforms, bags and the annual sports-day contribution add up to three thousand rupees a year. Amir is less interested; his teacher says he talks too much and his handwriting is poor. Irfan worries he will lose interest after Class 7 when the work gets harder. Shahana wants Ayesha to continue and says the Shakti bus pass will help, but Irfan knows adolescence and marriage talk will come soon. Tuition costs two hundred rupees a month per child in Lakshmeshwar and they have not started it yet. He wishes there were an Urdu high school with hostel support, but the nearest is in Gadag town. His hope is that Kannada medium will open doors his own schooling never did.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Irfan has a persistent cough from wool dust; he tried a government hospital doctor in Gadag two years ago who gave him an inhaler and advised him to wear a mask, but masks are hot and he forgets. Shahana has mild anaemia—she felt dizzy during her last pregnancy and the ANM gave iron tablets—but she rarely follows up unless she feels faint. The children have been healthy apart from seasonal fevers and a bout of diarrhoea last monsoon when the ward's water tank was contaminated. They go to a private clinic in the market for fevers because the government primary health centre has irregular doctor visits and long waits. A consultation costs one hundred and fifty rupees and medicines another two hundred; they avoid it unless necessary. Zara received her vaccines at the anganwadi and the ANM visits occasionally. Ayesha once had an ear infection that needed a week of antibiotics. For anything serious they would have to go to the GIMS hospital in Gadag town, ten kilometres away, which means bus fare, lost wages and uncertainty about costs. Irfan's father has diabetes and buys tablets from a Gadag pharmacy each month; Irfan sometimes sends five hundred rupees to help. Shahana's caesarean left them in debt and taught them that one large illness can break a household. They have an Ayushman card but have never used it and are not sure which hospitals accept it. Drinking water comes from a borough tap that runs for an hour in the morning; they boil it in summer. Irfan knows his cough will worsen with years but changing work is not easy.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Irfan is Muslim, part of Lakshmeshwar's small but old Muslim mohalla clustered around the Jama Masjid near the vegetable market. He prays five times most days, more faithfully during Ramzan, and walks to the mosque for Friday namaz. His family observes Eid, Muharram and Milad-un-Nabi; Shahana cooks biryani and sheer khurma and they visit relatives in Gadag and Ron. The mohalla has about sixty households, mostly weavers, tailors, small traders and workshop hands; everyone knows everyone and disputes are settled by elders over tea. Irfan's children play with both Muslim and Hindu children in the lane but he has noticed that high school friendships split along community lines. He respects the dargah at Shishunala Sharif in neighbouring Haveri district and visited it once on a friend's insistence; the shared Hindu-Muslim devotion there moved him. He avoids political arguments but feels a low hum of unease when he hears talk of Hubballi's Idgah dispute or communal trouble in Vijayapura. The madrasa next to the mosque runs evening Quran classes for children; Ayesha attended for a year but Shahana stopped sending her because homework clashed. Irfan's uncle is active in the mosque committee and sometimes speaks of Urdu schooling and wakf property issues. Irfan wants his children to know their faith but also to fit into the wider Kannada world; he sees no contradiction but knows others do. Lakshmeshwar's annual urs at a local dargah draws a small crowd and Hindu neighbours sometimes visit out of respect. He trusts the local imam and the mohalla network more than any government department.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Irfan has a ration card—white card, not BPL—and collects rice under Anna Bhagya from the fair-price shop near the bus stand; the rice is decent and saves them about four hundred rupees a month. He has heard of Gruha Lakshmi but Shahana does not receive it because she is not the household head on the ration card, a bureaucratic tangle they have not untangled. Ayesha benefits from Shakti when the school takes them on a rare excursion by NWKRTC bus, but day-to-day they walk. He has an Ayushman card issued two years ago but has never tested it. When Zara was born he went to the taluk office for a birth certificate; it took three visits and a fifty-rupee tip to the clerk. He has not encountered MGNREGA because he has steady if low-paid work. The winter session at Belagavi's Suvarna Soudha feels remote; he knows it happens and North Karnataka leaders speak there, but it has not changed his lane's broken drainage or the taluk hospital's doctor shortage. He views officials as people to avoid unless paperwork compels him, and even then he expects delays and rudeness. His uncle mutters about the Kittur Karnataka board that some demand, saying Kalyana Karnataka has Article 371(J) money while Gadag gets nothing special; Irfan is not sure of the details but he recognises the sense of neglect. He trusts his vote less each year but still goes to the booth, partly from habit and partly from his mother's memory—she told him it was the one power a poor man had.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Irfan worries most about Ayesha's schooling—will they afford PU fees, will marriage talk derail her, will Kannada medium truly open salaried jobs—and about Amir's wandering attention. He blames the decline of Lakshmeshwar's blanket trade on cheap machine-made goods and government indifference to handloom craft, though he knows global markets and tastes have shifted. He resents that the winter session in Belagavi makes headlines but his town's hospital has no full-time doctor and his children's school has no library. He wishes his wages were higher and his cough less persistent, and he wishes Shahana did not have to stitch blouses late into the night. He is proud to be from Lakshmeshwar, a town of old temples, the Someshwara stepwell and a layered history, but he feels the future is elsewhere—Hubballi, Bengaluru—and that people like him are left to manage. He wants his children, especially Ayesha, to escape the cycle of craft-trade uncertainty, to have the salaried security he never will. He does not expect much from government but he expects schools to function, doctors to attend and ration rice to arrive; when they do not, his frustration simmers quietly. He dislikes speeches about Kittur Karnataka pride when his lane has no proper drainage, but he also feels a tug of regional identity when leaders speak of neglect compared to Bengaluru. He wishes outsiders understood that Muslim families in towns like Lakshmeshwar are not uniform, that they worry about school fees and water supply and jobs just as Hindu neighbours do, and that Urdu is a language, not a barrier, though the world increasingly treats it as one.

personas.name: Zainab
personas.definition: Zainab is a composite portrait of a Muslim woman in Navalgund taluk, Dharwad district, who rolls beedis at home while managing household responsibilities and navigating the schooling aspirations of her children. She represents the experience of women balancing piecework income with family care in a town where Urdu medium schools serve the community but higher education requires difficult choices.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Zainab wakes before dawn for namaaz and begins her day rolling beedis at the small table in her two-room house near the Navalgund bus stand. She collects tobacco and tendu leaves from a contractor each Monday and returns filled bundles by Saturday, earning about forty to fifty rupees per thousand beedis, which translates to three to four thousand rupees in a good month when her fingers and eyes cooperate. The work is tedious and her thumbs ache by evening, but it allows her to stay home with her youngest child and contribute to household expenses. Her husband drives an auto-rickshaw on the Navalgund-Hubballi route, bringing in six to eight thousand rupees a month depending on diesel prices and passenger flow. Together they manage rent of two thousand five hundred, ration rice under Anna Bhagya, and careful spending on vegetables, kerosene and clothes. Zainab buys from the Thursday haat and saves on gas by cooking on a chulha when time permits. The joint income barely covers expenses, and any medical cost or school fee throws the month into arrears with the neighbourhood kirana shop.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Zainab lives with her husband, three children and her mother-in-law in a rented house in the Urdu-speaking mohalla of Navalgund. Her eldest daughter is fifteen and studies in Class 10 at the government Urdu medium high school, her son is twelve and in Class 7, and her youngest daughter is six and attending the anganwadi. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties, was widowed young and worked as a domestic helper for decades; she now suffers from joint pain and helps with cooking and childcare when she can. Zainab was married at seventeen, shortly after her own schooling ended in Class 8 when her family could not afford the fees and uniform for high school. Her husband is a steady man but the auto earnings are unpredictable, and he worries about competition from app-based cabs in Hubballi. Zainab makes most day-to-day decisions about food and children's needs, though larger expenses and schooling choices are discussed together. She hopes her daughters will study further than she did, but fears the cost and distance if they must go to Hubballi for PU college.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Zainab's eldest daughter attends the government Urdu medium high school in Navalgund, where she studies in Class 10 and prepares for her SSLC exams. The school is a ten-minute walk from home and there are no fees, though Zainab spends about fifteen hundred rupees a year on notebooks, pens, and the occasional tuition class for mathematics. Her daughter is a serious student and Zainab dreams of her becoming a teacher, but after SSLC the family will face a hard choice: Navalgund has only one PU college and it teaches in Kannada medium, which her daughter struggles with, while the Urdu-medium colleges are in Hubballi, requiring daily bus fare or hostel costs they cannot afford. The youngest girl goes to the anganwadi and will start Class 1 next year. Zainab attended school herself until Class 8 in a village near Gadag, learning to read Urdu and some Kannada, and she insists her children continue as long as possible. The free Shakti bus pass helps her daughter travel for exams or errands, and the midday meal keeps them in school, but Zainab knows that after SSLC the real costs and distances begin.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Zainab's mother-in-law has chronic knee pain and occasional breathlessness, visiting the government hospital in Navalgund for check-ups and tablets that sometimes run out before the next appointment. Zainab herself suffers from recurrent back pain from long hours hunched over the beedi work and poor eyesight that makes rolling harder each year; she has never had glasses fitted. Her youngest daughter was anaemic as a toddler, and the anganwadi worker advised eggs and greens, but eggs are costly and the family eats them only occasionally. When someone falls seriously ill they go to Hubballi, to KIMS or a private clinic, and the costs can run into thousands; two years ago her husband's accident required stitches and an X-ray that cost four thousand rupees, borrowed from relatives and still being repaid. The family is enrolled under Ayushman Bharat but navigating the hospital cashless process is confusing, and they often pay upfront and fail to claim reimbursement. Zainab boils neem leaves for fevers and uses home remedies her mother-in-law teaches her. She worries about her own health as she ages, knowing there is no pension or insurance if she cannot work, and that her daughters will have to bear the burden.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Zainab's family are Sunni Muslims and the rhythm of her week follows namaaz times, Friday visits to the masjid for her husband, and Ramzan fasting and Eid preparations that bring the mohalla together. The Urdu-speaking community in Navalgund is close-knit; neighbours lend small sums, share news of work or school admissions, and gather for weddings and condolence visits. Zainab's mother-in-law recalls the annual urus at Shishunala Sharif in nearby Shiggaon, where both Hindus and Muslims visit the dargah, and Zainab took her children there once. She values the respect the dargah commands across communities and wishes more people remembered that shared devotion. The Urdu medium school and madrasa are anchors of community life, though Zainab notes that some better-off families now send children to Kannada or English medium schools in Hubballi. She feels the double edge of being Muslim in a time of uncertain politics: proud of her faith and community solidarity, but wary of her children facing bias or being left behind if Urdu medium limits their opportunities. Her mother-in-law insists on modest dress and Quranic learning; Zainab herself wears a headscarf and prays daily, finding comfort in faith even when money is short.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Zainab's family has a ration card and receives Anna Bhagya rice each month, a staple she depends on. She receives Gruha Lakshmi payments, but the last two instalments were delayed and arrived together in August 2026, causing confusion about the schedule. Her daughter uses the Shakti free bus pass to travel to Hubballi for tuition once a fortnight, and Zainab sees it as a great help though the NWKRTC buses from Navalgund are often crowded. The family has not received direct crop compensation because they own no land, but the drought of 2023 and again in 2026 raised vegetable prices and hit the auto business as rural passengers made fewer trips. Zainab knows little about the Mahadayi water project or Almatti dam issues that dominate the newspapers her husband brings home, but she understands that Navalgund farmers are angry about delayed canal water and that this anger flows into every election. The winter session at Belagavi's Suvarna Soudha is a pride for North Karnataka, her husband says, but she wonders what it delivers for people like them. She has never visited a taluk office or dealt with Bhoomi or Seva Sindhu; her husband handles such matters. She trusts the anganwadi worker, who is kind and from the same mohalla, more than distant bureaucrats.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Zainab worries most about her children's future: whether her eldest daughter can continue to PU college and become a teacher, whether her son will stay in school or drift into unskilled work, and whether her youngest will have better chances than she did. She is proud that her daughter studies seriously and knows Urdu, Kannada and some English, but fears the Urdu medium will close doors in a job market that prizes Kannada or English. The delays in Gruha Lakshmi frustrate her because every month's budget is tight, and she resents hearing about corruption when basic services falter. She wishes Navalgund had better hospitals, an Urdu-medium PU college, and more beedi contractors so women could earn without travelling. Zainab admires the discipline of her mother-in-law's generation but sees the world changing fast: her daughter speaks of becoming independent, of work and choice, ideas that make Zainab both hopeful and anxious. She is proud of her faith and her community's resilience, and she wants outsiders to see Muslim families like hers as hardworking and rooted in Karnataka's soil, not as outsiders or threats. She dreams her children will not have to roll beedis or drive autos, that education will lift them, but every year the costs and distances remind her how hard that dream is to reach.

personas.name: Hameed
personas.definition: Hameed is a composite portrait of a Muslim chilli trader in Kundgol taluk, Dharwad district, who built his business from a single tempo into a small fleet of three lorries hauling produce to Hubballi APMC and beyond. He embodies the trading networks, multilingual ease, credit pressures and educational aspirations that shape middle-tier agricultural commerce in the black-soil cotton and chilli belt of Kitturu Karnataka.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Hameed owns three Tata 407 lorries and trades chilli, cotton and jowar between Kundgol, Hubballi APMC and occasionally Byadgi market. His day begins at four-thirty with Fajr prayers at the neighbourhood mosque, followed by phone calls to commission agents and farmers about the day's rates. By six he is at the Kundgol market yard, inspecting heaps of dried chilli and negotiating prices per quintal with smallholders who know him by name. He arranges loading, drafts invoices and dispatches one lorry to Hubballi by eight. The other two run fixed routes to Gadag and Haveri, returning by evening. His income swings wildly: in a good month he clears thirty to forty thousand rupees after diesel, driver wages, toll and APMC fees, but when chilli prices crash—as they did in March 2024, falling from twenty thousand to eight thousand per quintal—he barely covers costs. He has taken loans from two commission agents and a Canara Bank overdraft of three lakh rupees, which he services by juggling payments and delaying repairs. His phone never stops; he speaks Kannada with farmers, Urdu with relatives and a mix of both with his drivers, one Hindu and two Muslim.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Hameed lives in a rented two-room house with a small courtyard in Kundgol town, sharing the compound with two other tenant families. His wife Ayesha, thirty-eight, manages the household and cooks for the family of six: their three sons aged nineteen, sixteen and twelve, and a daughter aged fourteen. His eldest son completed PU in Kannada medium at the Government Junior College in Kundgol and now helps with the lorry business, learning accounts and market talk. The second son is in tenth standard at the same college, preparing for SSLC, and Hameed insists he continue to PU and perhaps attempt a BCom. His daughter studies in ninth at the Government High School and Hameed wants her to finish at least SSLC, though his wife worries about the cost of private PU college if the government one has no Urdu option. His youngest son is in seventh. Ayesha's day revolves around meals, the children's homework and managing the ration card and Gruha Lakshmi payments, which arrived late three times this year. Hameed's mother, seventy, lives in their native village near Gadag and he sends her two thousand rupees monthly. Gender roles are traditional: Ayesha does not work outside, but she controls household savings and decides on children's clothes and school fees.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: He is determined his children will finish at least PU. His eldest completed PU in arts stream with sixty-two per cent, good enough for a BCom seat, but Hameed needs him in the business now and promised he can study part-time later. The second son, in tenth, travels five kilometres by bus to Kundgol for school; the annual cost—uniforms, books, fees, tuition for maths and science—comes to around twelve thousand rupees. Hameed pays another six thousand yearly for private tuition because the government high school classes are overcrowded and the boy struggles with English. His daughter attends the same school; she is a strong student, but there is no girls' hostel nearby and Hameed has heard that the Urdu-medium stream at PU level in Kundgol is weak, so he may send her to a private Kannada-medium college in Hubballi if he can afford the fifteen thousand rupees per year. His youngest son studies at the Urdu-medium primary school in the market ward. Hameed worries that his sons will not find stable jobs without degrees, yet he also sees educated boys from the neighbourhood driving autos or working shop counters. He wants at least one son to study BCom or ITI so the family has a government or bank job to fall back on when market swings hurt.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Hameed suffers from acid reflux and high blood pressure, diagnosed two years ago at a private clinic in Kundgol after chest pain scared him into a check-up. The doctor prescribed daily tablets—Telma and a statin—which cost four hundred and fifty rupees a month, but Hameed skips them when cash is tight. He smokes five to six beedis a day, a habit he knows he should quit. His wife has chronic joint pain and anaemia; a blood test at the government PHC in Kundgol showed low haemoglobin, and the ANM gave her iron tablets, but she says they upset her stomach. The children are mostly healthy, though his daughter missed school for a week last monsoon with dengue-like fever; they took her to a private doctor in Hubballi who charged two thousand rupees for tests and drips. Hameed knows serious illness means a trip to KIMS Hubballi or SDM Hospital in Dharwad, an hour away, and that scares him because one hospitalisation could wipe out his savings. He is enrolled in Ayushman Bharat through his ration card, but he has never used it and is not sure which hospitals accept it. Drinking water in Kundgol comes from borewells and an open tank; in summer it smells faintly of mud and everyone boils it. Heat exhaustion hits the lorry drivers in April and May; Hameed keeps ORS sachets and a first-aid box in each vehicle.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Hameed is Muslim, part of a Dakhni Urdu-speaking community in Kundgol that has lived here for generations, originally as traders and weavers. He prays five times a day at the Jama Masjid near the market, a modest whitewashed building that also runs a small maktab for Quranic education in the evenings; his youngest son attends twice a week. Ramzan and Eid are the year's anchors: the family fasts, the mosque organises communal iftar, and Hameed distributes zakat to poorer families and labourers. Relations between Muslims and Lingayats in Kundgol are mostly cordial; Hameed's business depends on Hindu farmers and agents, and he attends their functions when invited, though he declines food during Ramzan. The dargah of Shishunala Sharif in nearby Shiggaon draws both Hindu and Muslim pilgrims, and Hameed visits once a year for the urs, taking his sons along. His wife is more observant than he is, covering her head in public and insisting their daughter do the same after puberty. Hameed supports Congress because he feels BJP's local leaders favour Lingayat traders and sometimes speak harshly about Muslims, though he never discusses politics openly. He trusts the imam and a few older traders in the community, and they informally mediate disputes and pool funds for weddings or medical emergencies. He has no link to any NGO or formal SHG.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Hameed interacts with government mostly through the APMC and the RTO. He renews his lorries' permits and pays road tax yearly at the Hubballi RTO, a process that always involves a tout and costs more than the official rate. He holds a BPL ration card—upgraded to Antyodaya during COVID—and collects five kilos of rice and two of sugar monthly from the fair-price shop in Kundgol; the rice quality is poor but free, so his wife mixes it with market rice. His family receives Gruha Lakshmi—two thousand rupees monthly deposited in Ayesha's account—but it has been delayed three times in the past six months, forcing them to borrow from neighbours. Hameed has never claimed crop insurance because he is a trader, not a farmer, though many of the farmers he deals with complain they receive only a fraction of promised compensation after drought or hail. The local corporator is a Lingayat; Hameed went to him once to complain about garbage piling near the market, and the man listened politely but nothing was done. Hameed knows the Deputy Commissioner only as a name. He believes government schools are adequate for primary but weak in high school, and that the real benefits—pensions, Ayushman, Jal Jeevan—reach only those with political or caste connections.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Hameed is proud he built his business from nothing, and proud that his children will study further than he did. He worries constantly about debt: the overdraft, the dues to commission agents, the cost of one major lorry repair, and what happens if chilli or cotton prices collapse again. He fears one bad season or accident could force him to sell a lorry. He is proud of Kundgol's place in the Dharwad belt, the legacy of Sawai Gandharva, and the respect accorded to Urdu and Kannada both, though he quietly resents that Urdu-medium PU options are disappearing and that his daughter may have to study in Kannada or pay private fees. He blames middlemen and hoarders for price crashes, and blames the state for ignoring North Karnataka traders while favouring Bengaluru. He sees the Kittur Karnataka board demand as fair—Kalyana Karnataka got Article 371(J) funds, so why not Kundgol?—but doubts it will happen. He trusts the mosque, the dargah and old trader friends more than any government office. He is frustrated that educated Muslim boys struggle to find jobs outside teaching or small business, suspecting bias he cannot prove. He wants his children to have choices he did not: stable income, respect, and freedom from the daily grind of market swings and debt calls.

Arranges loading, drafts invoices, dispatches one lorry to Hubballi APMC for the day's run.
Other two lorries return from Gadag and Haveri routes; phone never stops with market calls.
Home to family, tries to remember blood pressure tablets when cash allows, plans tomorrow's routes.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.headline: Three lorries hauling chilli, cotton and market swings
points: Owns three Tata 407 lorries trading chilli, cotton and jowar between Kundgol, Hubballi APMC and Byadgi market daily.
Income swings wildly: good months clear thirty to forty thousand, but March 2024 chilli crash barely covered costs.
Services three lakh overdraft from Canara Bank and loans from two commission agents by juggling payments and delaying repairs.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.headline: Six in two rooms, managing ration and dreams
points: Lives in rented two-room house in Kundgol compound with wife Ayesha and four children aged nineteen, sixteen, fourteen and twelve.
Eldest son completed PU and now helps with lorry business; second son in tenth preparing for SSLC.
Ayesha manages household, ration card and Gruha Lakshmi payments which arrived late three times this year; sends mother two thousand monthly.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.headline: Determined children finish PU despite cost and gaps
points: Second son's annual school cost runs twelve thousand; pays six thousand more for private tuition in overcrowded government classes.
Daughter is strong student but weak Urdu PU stream may force fifteen thousand yearly private Kannada college in Hubballi.
Wants one son to study BCom or ITI for stable government or bank job when market swings hurt the business.

points: Diagnosed with acid reflux and high blood pressure two years ago; daily tablets cost four hundred fifty rupees monthly but skips when tight.
Wife has chronic joint pain and anaemia; iron tablets from PHC upset her stomach; daughter had dengue-like fever costing two thousand.
Enrolled in Ayushman Bharat but never used it and unsure which hospitals accept it; fears one hospitalisation wipes savings.

topics.headline: Prayers five times, zakat and dargah visits anchor life
points: Prays five times daily at Jama Masjid near market; youngest son attends maktab for Quranic education twice weekly.
Ramzan and Eid are year's anchors; distributes zakat to poorer families and mosque organises communal iftar for the community.
Visits Shishunala Sharif dargah in Shiggaon yearly for urs with sons; relations with Hindu farmers mostly cordial, business depends on them.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.headline: RTO touts, delayed Gruha Lakshmi and ignored complaints
points: Renews lorry permits yearly at Hubballi RTO through touts costing more than official rate; interacts mostly through APMC.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.headline: Proud of three lorries, haunted by debt and bias
points: Proud built business from nothing but worries constantly about overdraft, agent dues and what happens if prices collapse again.
Quietly resents disappearing Urdu PU options and suspects bias keeps educated Muslim boys from jobs outside teaching or small business.
Supports Kittur Karnataka board demand as fair—Kalyana Karnataka got Article 371(J) funds, so why not Kundgol?—but doubts it will happen.

personas.name: Sushila
personas.definition: Sushila is a composite portrait of a woman balancing seasonal factory work and household management in a coastal taluk of Uttara Kannada, where Gulf remittances and local processing industries shape family decisions about education and migration. She represents households caught between the promise of Karavali's high literacy rates and the daily pull of wage work and limited local opportunity.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Sushila works at a cashew processing unit near Kumta town, shelling and grading kernels during the peak season from February through June. The work pays roughly one hundred and eighty to two hundred rupees per day, though payment often arrives weeks late and depends on the quantity processed rather than hours worked. Outside the season she takes up piecework sorting dried fish or weeding coconut plots for neighbours. Her husband Prakash works as a driver for a timber merchant in Sirsi, home only on Sundays. The household runs on his monthly salary of about twelve thousand rupees plus her seasonal earnings. Cashew dust irritates her throat and the factory shed has poor ventilation, but the work is close enough to reach by bus under the Shakti scheme, saving the fare. Prices for raw cashew nuts have climbed and the merchant complains about competition from Vietnamese imports, making every season uncertain. She keeps a kitchen garden of greens and drumstick behind the house, and neighbours share jackfruit and mangoes when the trees bear. Daily meals centre on rice, coconut chutney, fish curry when affordable, and dhal. Prakash's timber-merchant employer sometimes delays salary during the monsoon when logging stops.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Sushila lives with her two sons, aged nineteen and fourteen, and her mother-in-law, who is in her seventies and manages the cooking when Sushila is at the factory. Her husband Prakash stays in a shared room in Sirsi during the week. Her elder son Suresh completed his second PUC last year at the government college in Kumta and now works at a mobile-phone shop in town, earning about seven thousand rupees a month while he prepares for the police recruitment exam. Her younger son Pradeep is in ninth standard at the government high school. Suresh's income helps but he is restless, talking about joining his maternal uncle in a hotel kitchen in Mumbai or trying for Gulf work through an agent in Bhatkal. Sushila's mother-in-law, widowed thirty years ago under the old Aliyasantana property customs that gave Billava women some holding rights, owns the small house plot and a share in an adjoining coconut garden, though the trees are old and yield little. Sushila's own mother lives in her brother's household near Honnavar. Housework, fetching water from the public tap during summer shortages, and looking after her mother-in-law's medicines for blood pressure fall to Sushila when she is not at the factory. Pradeep sometimes complains that his friends' families are building new houses with Gulf money while they remain in the old tiled house.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Sushila studied only until seventh standard in the village school near her childhood home, leaving when her family needed her labour in the fields and during the fishing season. She reads Kannada slowly and cannot follow English at all. Suresh and Pradeep both attended the government Kannada-medium school in Kumta; Suresh passed his SSLC with a second class and his PUC with lower marks, enough to keep the door open for a constable post but not for engineering or degree college without paying for private coaching the family cannot afford. Pradeep is a better student, ranking in the top fifteen in his class, and his teachers say he should aim for PUC science stream. The school is three kilometres from home; Pradeep cycles or takes the morning bus. There is no tuition cost under government schooling but books, uniforms, the bicycle repair and the PUC college fee of about three thousand rupees a year stretch the household budget. Sushila wants Pradeep to finish PUC and find a government job or join a diploma course, but Suresh's example worries her—two years of college and still no permanent job. Her husband talks about putting Pradeep into a hotel-work apprenticeship after tenth if no decent exam result comes, saying the Udupi-hotel network has built more family security than degrees. She resists but knows the pull of immediate earnings. She wishes Kumta had a private English-medium school they could afford, seeing how the doctor's and merchant's children speak confidence her sons lack.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Sushila's throat trouble from cashew dust worsens each season; she treats it with home remedies and occasional visits to the government primary health centre in Kumta, where the doctor gives an inhaler she uses sparingly to make it last. Her mother-in-law takes tablets for high blood pressure and diabetes, collected free under the government scheme at the taluk hospital, though the queues are long and the daughter-in-law must accompany her. Prakash injured his back two years ago lifting timber and still feels pain during the monsoon; he went once to a private clinic in Sirsi and paid fifteen hundred rupees for an X-ray and tablets but has not returned for follow-up. The family is enrolled under Ayushman Bharat but has never used the hospitalisation cover; serious cases from Kumta go to Karwar district hospital or, if one can pay, to Manipal, which feels impossibly far and expensive. Pradeep had dengue fever during the monsoon last year and recovered at home with paracetamol and boiled neem water. There is fear of snakebite during the rains when the fields flood and of monkey fever in the forest-edge villages, though Kumta town itself has been spared recent outbreaks. Sushila has not seen a dentist despite a nagging pain in one molar. Her mother-in-law's eyesight is failing and neighbours say cataract surgery is free under a government camp, but the old woman refuses to travel to Karwar. Sushila herself feels tired much of the time, a tiredness she attributes to age and work rather than illness.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Sushila's family belongs to the Billava community, historically associated with toddy-tapping and coconut cultivation, and now spread across many occupations in coastal Karnataka. She feels pride in the community's Koti-Chennaya oral epic and in the social mobility Billavas have achieved in the past generation. The family worships at the local Durgaparameshwari temple and participates in the annual Jatre, where Bhuta Kola performances invoke the daivas through the night. Her mother-in-law insists on specific offerings before the household deity each morning. Sushila respects these practices but does not share the older woman's intensity. Neighbours are a mix of Billava, Havyaka Brahmin, Mogaveera fishing families and a few Beary Muslim households; relations are civil though each community keeps to its own marriage and ritual circles. She has two close friends from the cashew factory, one Billava and one Mogaveera, with whom she shares complaints about wages and in-laws. The local Billava Sangha occasionally organises meetings about reservation policies and community welfare schemes, and her husband attends when he is home. Caste identity is spoken of openly here in a way that surprises visitors from cities. Sushila knows the GSB and Bunt families who own the larger cashew and trading businesses but has no social contact beyond the employer-worker relationship. During election seasons the community's leaders mobilise Billava voters and candidates promise attention to toddy-tappers' issues and labour rights, though Sushila sees little change.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Her mother-in-law draws an old-age pension of six hundred rupees per month, collected from the post office. The household has a ration card and receives rice and kerosene, though the quantities have shrunk and the shop sometimes runs out. Sushila applied for a toilets-construction grant years ago under the Swachh Bharat scheme but the funds never arrived and the family built a makeshift latrine with their own savings. She travels free on government buses under the Shakti scheme, a benefit she uses almost daily during the work season and considers the most tangible government help she has received. The gram panchayat is dominated by families with money and land; she has never spoken at a meeting. She hears of MGNREGA work but the going rate of two hundred and eighty rupees per day feels barely more than the cashew factory pays, and the work is irregular and requires forms she does not understand. Pradeep received a bicycle under a school scheme two years ago, which the family appreciated. When the timber merchant delayed Prakash's salary, the family had no one in the labour department to complain to and simply waited. Sushila is vaguely aware of Ayushman Bharat and other health schemes but finds the paperwork and hospital procedures intimidating. She trusts the anganwadi worker who visits her mother-in-law, less so the revenue officials who appeared once asking about property records she could not produce.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Sushila worries most about Suresh leaving for Mumbai or the Gulf before securing a stable future, fearing he will fall into debt to an agent or waste years in irregular work as so many boys from Kumta have done. She is proud that both her sons are literate and that Pradeep still attends school regularly, something she could not do, but she fears the education will lead nowhere without money for further study or contacts for a government job. She wishes Uttara Kannada had the opportunities that Mangaluru and Udupi offer—a medical college, an airport, the kind of private companies that hire steady workers—and resents that every ladder out of Kumta requires her sons to leave home. She blames the merchants who delay wages and the agents who lure boys with false promises of Gulf riches, and she blames a government she feels takes her vote and gives little back beyond the bus fare. She is proud of her ability to manage the household on a thin budget and of her mother-in-law's strength, and she takes satisfaction in the small respect neighbours give her for keeping her sons in school longer than many. She does not think caste discrimination has held her family back as much as simple poverty and geography, though she knows Brahmin and Bunt families command easier credit and better connections. She wants Pradeep to stay in school and finish PUC, then find any secure job with a pension, even a clerk's post. She demands nothing grand, only stability, a government hospital in Kumta that works without sending patients to Karwar, and an end to the cashew factory's wage delays.

personas.name: Suma
personas.definition: Suma is a composite portrait of a Kuruba woman in Shiggaon taluk, Haveri district, who runs a small tailoring shop from her home while managing household and farm responsibilities. She represents families navigating drought, onion-price crashes, and the gap between government promises and the daily struggle to keep children in school.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Suma wakes before dawn to prepare breakfast and pack tiffin for her husband Basavaraj, who farms three acres of rainfed land half a kilometre from their home in Shiggaon town. After sending her two daughters to school, she opens the small tailoring shop attached to the front room of their house, where she stitches blouses, school uniforms and salwar sets on a pedal machine bought twelve years ago. On good days she earns Rs 200 to Rs 300, but orders drop sharply during the summer months and in years like 2023 and 2026 when the rains fail. Basavaraj grows onion, cotton and jowar; last season the onion price collapsed below Rs 10 per kilo and they could not recover the cost of seed and labour. The household earns perhaps Rs 80,000 in a good year from the farm and another Rs 40,000 from her tailoring, but drought years push them to borrow from the Shiggaon cooperative bank at eighteen per cent or from a private moneylender at two per cent per month. Suma also takes MGNREGA work when it is available, digging farm ponds for Rs 300 a day, though the guarantee of a hundred days is rarely met.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Suma lives with her husband Basavaraj, their daughters Kavya (fifteen, studying in Class 10 at the government high school) and Deepa (twelve, in Class 7), and Basavaraj's widowed mother, who is seventy and receives a Rs 1,000 monthly pension under the Sandhya Suraksha scheme. Suma married at eighteen, soon after finishing Class 10; her parents could not afford to send her further and the family needed one less mouth to feed. She had hoped to study tailoring formally, but learned by watching her aunt. Basavaraj finished PU first year and speaks often of the value of education, insisting both daughters will complete PU and perhaps study further. Kavya is bright and wants to become a nurse, but the family worries about the cost of a nursing course in Haveri or Dharwad—hostel, fees and travel could run to Rs 50,000 a year. Deepa is quieter and enjoys helping her grandmother cook jolada rotti and ennegaai. Suma manages all the cooking, cleaning, washing and caring for her mother-in-law, who has arthritis and cannot walk far. Basavaraj helps with the heavier housework when he is not in the fields, but neighbours expect Suma to do most of it, and she rarely leaves Shiggaon except for the annual Yellamma jatra at Saundatti or a family wedding.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Suma completed SSLC at the Shiggaon government girls' high school in 2004, scoring a second class, and her tailoring skill comes from informal apprenticeship rather than any ITI course. Kavya studies in the Kannada-medium government high school about a kilometre from home; she walks there with friends each morning and returns by two in the afternoon. The school charges no fees under the government scheme, and midday meals are provided, though Kavya says the sambar is often watery and the rice insufficient. Textbooks and uniforms are free, but the family spent Rs 3,000 this year on a geometry box, bags, notebooks, pens and a Rs 500 exam fee for a private coaching class Kavya attends twice a week to prepare for SSLC. Suma worries constantly about whether Kavya will pass—news that Haveri district topped the state in SSLC 2026 with 96.87 per cent brought pride, but also pressure. Suma wishes she had studied more and is determined that her daughters will not face the same limits, though the cost of college and the drought weigh on every conversation about the future.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Suma's mother-in-law suffers from arthritis in both knees and finds it painful to climb stairs or squat for cooking; she takes a painkiller from the Shiggaon government hospital when the pain is severe, but the doctors there have advised surgery at Haveri district hospital, which the family cannot afford. Suma herself has had anaemia since her second pregnancy and was advised to take iron tablets, but she forgets or cannot afford them regularly. She goes to the government hospital for fevers and minor ailments, but serious cases require a trip to Haveri town, twenty-five kilometres away, or even to Hubballi for specialists, which means a day's lost work and Rs 1,000 or more in travel, consultation and medicines. Kavya fainted once during her periods and was found to be anaemic; the school health check-up recommended iron supplements and better food, but Suma struggles to provide eggs or meat more than once a week. The family drinks water from a borewell that Basavaraj suspects has high fluoride—several neighbours have dental fluorosis and joint pain—but testing costs money and the alternative is buying water or boiling it, neither easy. During the summer months the well runs dry and they depend on tanker supply from the gram panchayat, which arrives irregularly. Suma worries about her daughters' health, about the cost of any serious illness, and about her own exhaustion, which she attributes to overwork and the relentless summer heat.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Suma's family belongs to the Kuruba community, a shepherding and farming caste that is listed as OBC in Karnataka; many Kurubas in Haveri district have small or marginal landholdings and depend on rain. The community reveres Kanaka Dasa, the sixteenth-century Haridasa saint, and the Kaginele Kanaka Guru Peetha near Haveri is an important centre of pride and pilgrimage. Suma visits the Peetha once a year with her family, and the mutt has run a free hostel for Kuruba children in Haveri town, though she did not know about it in time for Kavya. The family also goes to the annual Devaragudda Mailara jatra in Haveri district, where thousands gather and the karnika (oracle) delivers prophecies while in trance—Suma finds the atmosphere both frightening and reassuring. They celebrate Ugadi, Deepavali and Sankranti at home with jolada rotti, shenga chutney and jaggery. Suma's husband is devout and often speaks of the Lingayat-Kuruba social closeness, though he also resents that Lingayats dominate local politics and the cooperative society. Neighbours are mostly Kuruba, Lingayat Banajiga and a few Scheduled Caste families; everyone knows everyone and helps during weddings or emergencies, but caste distinctions remain strong and inter-caste marriages are rare. Suma trusts the mutt more than she trusts politicians, and she wishes the Peetha's schools and hostels were closer.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Suma's family has a ration card (BPL until two years ago, now revised to APL because of the land ownership, though their income has not improved), and they receive five kilos of rice per person per month under Anna Bhagya, which is crucial when cash is short. Suma receives Rs 2,000 per month under Gruha Lakshmi, though the payment has been delayed twice—once for two months in early 2026—and she has heard rumors that the scheme may be revised after the new Chief Minister took office in June 2026. She used the first few instalments to buy a steel cupboard and save a little for Kavya's coaching fees. Basavaraj has tried to register for MGNREGA work but complains that contractors skim wages and the full hundred days are never available; last year he got only thirty-seven days. The family was declared drought-affected in 2023, and they received Rs 4,000 as crop-loss compensation after a taluk officer inspected the fields, though Basavaraj says the loss was much greater. Suma travels to the taluk office in Shiggaon town for certificates or Bhoomi records, and she finds the officials polite but slow; a caste certificate for Kavya's school took four months. She has heard of Kalasa-Banduri and the demand for water from the Mahadayi river, and Basavaraj speaks bitterly about how Kittur Karnataka is ignored while Kalyana Karnataka got Article 371(J) funds and Bengaluru gets everything else.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: She worries most about money—whether the onion crop will fetch a decent price this year, whether the rains will come, whether Kavya will pass SSLC and what it will cost to send her to PU or nursing college. She worries that Deepa, who is quieter, will lose interest in school if the family faces another drought or if neighbours start talking about marriage. Suma blames the government for not protecting farmers from price crashes and for delaying the Mahadayi project, which she has heard could transform Haveri's water situation, but she does not understand why it is taking so long. She blames moneylenders and middlemen for squeezing farmers, and she blames herself for not having studied more or saved more. She is proud of her tailoring, proud that her daughters speak Kannada confidently and study without fear, and proud that her family has never taken a loan from a private moneylender at the worst rates, though they came close last year. She demands better crop prices, reliable water, timely MGNREGA wages, and a government that keeps its promise on Gruha Lakshmi and education costs. She resents that outsiders think North Karnataka is all about Belagavi's border dispute or Hubballi's growth, when most families like hers are simply trying to survive the next drought and keep their children in school.
