personas.name: Prakash
personas.definition: Prakash is a composite portrait of a Kuruba man in his mid-forties who supervises the ginning floor at a small private cotton mill in Byadgi town, Haveri district. He embodies the experience of industrial workers in the Haveri cotton belt who have navigated two decades of price volatility, mill closures and the squeeze between farmers' distress and mill owners' margins.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Prakash works the morning shift at a ginning mill on the Ranebennur road, arriving at six and leaving by three in the afternoon. He supervises eight workers who feed raw cotton into the gin stands, bale the lint and separate the seed for the oil press. During the October-to-February ginning season he earns around sixteen thousand rupees a month; off-season he takes on repair work, painting jobs and occasional MGNREGA labour to keep some income flowing. The mill has run only four months in the last year because cotton prices crashed to thirty-five hundred rupees per quintal in early 2024, leaving farmers and gin owners both squeezed. Prakash cycles four kilometres each way and carries lunch from home—jowar rotti and shenga chutney most days. He worries that the mill may not open next season if prices stay low and onion farmers switch away from cotton altogether.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Prakash lives in a rented two-room house in Byadgi's Kuruba colony with his wife Leelavati, who works as a domestic helper in three households, and their three children. His eldest daughter Kaveri, aged twenty-two, completed a BA through correspondence and now works as a shop assistant in Haveri town; she sends home two thousand rupees each month. His son Kiran is in second-year pre-university at the government college in Byadgi, studying commerce, and his younger daughter Anusha is in Class 9 at the Kannada-medium high school. Prakash's mother, now seventy, lives with his brother in their village near Hirekerur and receives the widow pension. Leelavati manages the household budget tightly, juggling ration-card rice under Anna Bhagya, Gruha Lakshmi instalments that sometimes arrive late, and loans from a self-help group and a private moneylender. Gender roles are traditional but Prakash insists both daughters study as far as his son does.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Prakash completed Class 7 in his village school before leaving to work on his father's farm and then as a mill hand. He regrets not finishing school and is determined that all three children complete at least pre-university. Kaveri's BA was hard-won—she studied at night after helping at home, and Prakash borrowed from a chit fund to pay the exam and convocation fees. Kiran travels by bus to the government college; the recent free bus pass for students has saved the family about six hundred rupees a month, a relief Prakash mentions often. Anusha attends the town high school, walking twenty minutes each way with classmates. Prakash hopes Kiran will pass the second PU exams and find an office job or join a bank, and that Anusha will finish SSLC and take up nursing or teacher training. He worries about college fees and the cost of competitive-exam coaching in Hubballi if Kiran aims for a government post.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Prakash suffers from chronic cough and occasional breathlessness, the result of inhaling cotton dust for two decades; he has never had a formal lung check but buys cough syrup from the town pharmacy when it worsens. Leelavati has anaemia and took iron tablets during her last pregnancy but stopped after a few months because they made her nauseous. The family goes to the government primary health centre in Byadgi for fevers and minor ailments, and once took Anusha to the taluk hospital in Haveri when she had dengue during the 2023 monsoon. Serious cases mean a referral to Haveri district hospital or even KIMS Hubballi, which costs travel, tests and lost wages. They have an Ayushman Bharat card but have not used the cashless facility yet. Prakash's mother has diabetes and his brother struggles to afford her monthly medicines. Heat during April and May is exhausting, and water supply in the colony is intermittent; the family stores water in drums and boils it during the monsoon to avoid diarrhoea.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Prakash is Kuruba, a community with a strong presence in Haveri district and pastoral and farming roots. He and his family worship at the Hanuman temple near the colony and visit the Kaginele Kanaka Guru Peetha during the annual fair; the peetha's demand for Scheduled Tribe status for Kurubas is a matter of pride and ongoing political talk in the colony. Prakash also attends the Devaragudda Mailara jatra in the district, where thousands gather and the karnika delivers prophecies. His wife is part of a neighbourhood self-help group that meets fortnightly and lends to members at modest interest; Leelavati values the group's savings discipline and mutual support more than any government scheme. Caste is not openly discussed every day, but Prakash is conscious of Lingayat mill owners and Jain traders holding economic power in Byadgi, while Kurubas, Dalits and Muslims form the labour force. Social ties are strongest within the colony, around the temple and at life-cycle events—weddings, naming ceremonies and funerals—where the community pools resources and labour.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He values the five guarantees in principle—Shakti helped his daughter travel to Haveri for her shop job, and Gruha Lakshmi instalments, though delayed, ease the monthly budget when they arrive. The thirty-second instalment came in August 2026, two months behind schedule, and Leelavati had to borrow to cover the gap. Prakash has worked a few days under MGNREGA but finds the seventy days insufficient and wage payment slow. He has never dealt directly with the taluk office beyond getting a caste certificate and ration card; for most government interactions he relies on a local agent who charges fifty or a hundred rupees. He hears talk at the mill and tea stalls about the demand for a Kittur Karnataka development board to match Kalyana Karnataka's Article 371(J) funds, and he agrees that Haveri and the region are overlooked compared with Bengaluru. The winter session at Belagavi's Suvarna Soudha feels ceremonial to him, not a source of real local power or investment.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Prakash worries most about income stability—whether the mill will operate next season, whether Kiran will find work after PU, and whether Anusha will marry before finishing her studies, as happened to two girls in their colony last year. He is proud that his children speak Kannada confidently, that Haveri's SSLC results rank near the top in the state, and that he has kept the family intact without migrating for sugarcane cutting, unlike some neighbours. He blames cotton and onion price crashes on middlemen, government neglect and global markets he does not fully understand, but he also faults local politicians for making promises at election time and vanishing afterward. He respects the Kaginele peetha's leaders and feels that the mutt-run hostels and free meals do more for Kuruba children than government schools alone. Prakash is frustrated that outsiders lump Haveri with either the Hubballi-Dharwad belt or the Kalyana Karnataka region, when it has its own cotton, chilli and onion economy and its own struggles. He demands stable crop prices, permanent jobs at the mill, better water supply in the colony and proper TB and lung-disease screening for mill workers. He wants his children to escape the mill floor and the cycle of off-season debt, and he pins that hope on education, government jobs and the occasional good harvest.

personas.name: Mushtaq
personas.definition: Mushtaq is a composite portrait of a Muslim wholesale fruit trader in Hosapete town, Ballari district, whose fortunes depend on the grape harvest from the irrigated Tungabhadra command and whose business connects him daily to the APMC market, lorry transporters and the stream of visitors to nearby Hampi. He represents the trading communities that anchor Hosapete's bazaar economy and the multilingual, multi-faith character of this town at the edge of Kalyana Karnataka and the ruins of the Vijayanagara Empire.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Mushtaq runs a wholesale fruit stall at Hosapete's APMC market, specialising in grapes brought in from farms along the Tungabhadra Left Bank Canal around Sindhanur and Manvi. His day begins at four in the morning when the trucks arrive; he grades the fruit, negotiates with commission agents and arranges onward transport to Bengaluru and Hyderabad. The income is good during the January-March grape season, bringing in perhaps thirty to forty thousand rupees a month when harvests are strong, but it swings sharply with yield and price. The rest of the year he trades pomegranates, bananas and whatever else moves, and earnings drop to half or less. He employs two assistants, usually young men from his mohalla, and owns a small Tata Ace for local pickups. The pressure is constant: perishable stock, tight credit from wholesalers in Bengaluru, and the diesel and labour costs that eat into margins. Hosapete's economy hums with the steel plant at nearby Toranagallu and Hampi tourism, so there is cash flow, but the fruit trade remains volatile and dependent on the canal water reaching the farms on time.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Mushtaq lives with his wife Fareeda, their three children and his widowed mother in a three-room house in a Muslim-majority lane near the Jama Masjid in Hosapete town. His wife manages the household, cooks, cares for his mother and helps their eldest daughter, now sixteen, prepare for her second-year PUC exams. Their second child, a son aged thirteen, is in eighth standard, and the youngest daughter is nine and in fourth standard. Fareeda wanted to take up tailoring work at home, but Mushtaq prefers she focus on the children's schooling, a decision they still debate. His mother, now in her seventies, is diabetic and needs regular medication. Gender roles in the household follow traditional lines: Fareeda does not work outside, Mushtaq controls the income and major decisions, and the girls are expected to help with cooking and cleaning after school. The family speaks Dakhni Urdu at home, Kannada in the market and a bit of Telugu with suppliers from across the border. Marriage is on the horizon for their eldest daughter, and Mushtaq is setting aside what he can for her wedding and dowry, a worry that keeps him awake at night.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Mushtaq studied up to seventh standard in an Urdu-medium school in Hosapete before leaving to help his father in the same fruit business. He regrets not finishing school and is determined his children will do better. His eldest daughter attends the government junior college in Hosapete for her PUC in the commerce stream; she travels there by auto, which costs about two hundred rupees a week. His son is in a Kannada-medium municipal school nearby, within walking distance, and the youngest daughter is in the same school. School fees are minimal, but the PUC coaching classes, textbooks and auto fare add up to several thousand rupees a term. Mushtaq wants his son to aim for a government job, perhaps in the railways or a clerk position, something with a steady salary and pension. For his daughters, he wants them to finish PUC and perhaps a BA, though he expects both will marry soon after; the eldest has already received a proposal from a family in Raichur. The children study in Kannada medium because that is what the better local schools offer, and Mushtaq believes it will give them more opportunities than Urdu medium, though his mother sometimes laments they cannot read the Quran as fluently as she did.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Health access in Hosapete is better than in the surrounding villages, with a government hospital, a few private clinics and a couple of decent pharmacies in the bazaar. Mushtaq's mother sees a private doctor for her diabetes, costing about five hundred rupees a visit plus another thousand a month for medicines; government doctors are free but the wait is long and she prefers the private clinic. His wife had a difficult delivery with their youngest daughter and needed a caesarean at a private nursing home, which put them fifteen thousand rupees in debt that took two years to clear. The children fall ill with fever and cough during the monsoon, treated at home with over-the-counter medicines and the occasional doctor visit. Mushtaq himself has chronic acidity, which he blames on irregular meals and the stress of the market, and he takes antacids daily. He has heard of the Ayushman Bharat scheme but has never applied for a card, unsure of the paperwork and assuming it would not cover his mother's ongoing diabetes treatment. Drinking water comes from a borewell in the lane, and everyone knows the water in parts of Hosapete and the canal belt can have fluoride, though Mushtaq has never had his family tested. The fear of serious illness, an accident or a major hospital bill is ever-present, and he has no health insurance.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Mushtaq's family belongs to the Dakhni-speaking Muslim community that has lived in Hosapete for generations, historically linked to trade and small business rather than farming. The mohalla where he lives is tight-knit, and Friday prayers at the Jama Masjid anchor the week. His mother is devout and insists the children learn Quranic recitation at the local madrasa, though Mushtaq is more relaxed, attending prayers on Fridays and Eid but not every day. Ties to the Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah in Kalaburagi are strong; the family makes the trip for the annual urs when they can afford it, and his mother has a framed picture of the dargah on the wall. Relations with Hindu neighbours and business partners are mostly cordial; the APMC market is mixed, and trust and credit flow across community lines in everyday trade. But Mushtaq is conscious of the political climate, the talk around the country about Muslims, and the occasional tension around Eid processions or Ganesh festival routes. He avoids political arguments, keeps his head down and focuses on business. Within the community, the mosque committee and local ulema wield influence, especially on questions of marriage, inheritance and religious schooling, and Mushtaq respects their authority even when he quietly disagrees.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Mushtaq's main dealings with government are through the APMC market, where he pays fees and relies on the market yard's infrastructure and the commission agents who mediate between farmers and traders. He has never attended a gram sabha or town municipal meeting and would not know how to raise an issue there. He applied once for a bank loan to expand his stall, but the paperwork and collateral demands defeated him, and he borrowed from a private moneylender instead. His family has ration cards, and they collect subsidised rice and kerosene from the fair-price shop, though the shop is often out of stock or closed at odd hours. He has heard of Gruha Jyothi and Gruha Lakshmi but does not fully understand how they work; his wife uses the Shakti free bus scheme occasionally to visit her parents in Raichur, which has saved them money. Mushtaq has little faith that government schemes reach people like him; he sees the schemes announced, the banners put up, but in practice it is the well-connected or those with influence who benefit. He blames neither the local officer nor the system in the abstract, but simply accepts that this is how things work.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Mushtaq worries most about price volatility in the grape market, the cost of his daughter's wedding, his mother's health and whether his son will find stable work in a government job or fall into the same precarious trading life. He is proud of Hosapete's location next to Hampi, the tourists who pass through and the steel-plant jobs that keep money circulating in the town, but he also sees the gap between the heritage tourism promoted by the government and the lack of investment in schools, hospitals and roads in the neighbourhoods where ordinary people like him live. He resents the stereotype, sometimes voiced by people from Bengaluru or coastal Karnataka, that this region is backward or not really Kannada; he speaks Kannada every day in the market, his children study in Kannada, and he is as much a Kannadiga as anyone, even if Urdu is his home language. He blames the long neglect under the Nizam and then by Karnataka governments for the region's difficulties, and he sees Article 371(J) as a recognition of that neglect, though he is not sure what it has delivered on the ground. He wants his children to have the education and security he never had, and he is willing to work brutal hours in the market to give them that chance. But he also knows that without connections, without someone in government or a steady salaried job, families like his remain one bad season or one medical emergency away from serious trouble. What he demands is simple: fair prices, reliable canal water for the farmers he depends on, decent schools and hospitals that work, and a government that treats Muslims as equal citizens rather than a political problem to be managed or mobilised at election time.

personas.name: Bhavani
personas.definition: Bhavani is a composite portrait of a Bhovi woman in her late thirties living in Hiriyur town, Chitradurga district, whose household relies on handloom weaving, dairy income and borewell-dependent agriculture in the semi-arid Bayaluseeme plains. She bridges the region's traditional weaving economy, its chronic water scarcity and the daily pressures of raising children on irregular cash flows.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Bhavani wakes at five to milk the two Amrita Mahal cross cows her husband bought three years ago with a district loan. She walks the milk to the Hiriyur town cooperative dairy collection point by six-thirty, earning roughly four thousand rupees a month when the cows are in milk, though this year the fodder cost climbed because groundwater dropped and green-feed became scarce. After breakfast she sits at the pit-loom in the rear room, weaving cotton dhoties and sarees on order from a Chitradurga town trader who supplies the yarn and pays per piece—twelve to fifteen rupees per metre, so a full saree takes two days and brings in around two hundred and fifty rupees. Her husband and his younger brother share the second loom and also do borewell-pump repairs in nearby villages for cash. The working day runs until eight in the evening with a break for lunch and the afternoon milk collection; the household earns roughly twelve to fifteen thousand rupees a month when both looms run and the cows give milk, but income drops sharply in summer when demand for cotton cloth falls and the cows go dry.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Bhavani lives with her husband, their three children, her mother-in-law and her husband's younger brother in a two-room stone house with a tiled weaving shed at the back. Her eldest daughter, aged sixteen, finished tenth standard last year at the Government High School in Hiriyur and now helps at the loom and with housework; Bhavani had hoped she would continue to PU College but the girl wanted to stay home, saying the college was too far and the fees too high. Her son, thirteen, is in eighth standard at the same school and says he wants to study engineering in Davanagere, though Bhavani worries about the cost. The youngest, a daughter aged nine, attends the Kannada-medium primary school near the weekly market. Her mother-in-law, now in her seventies, manages the kitchen and the small vegetable patch behind the house; her husband and brother-in-law share the farm work and weaving. Bhavani does all the cooking, cleaning, childcare and milk selling; her husband decides when to take loans or sell produce, though she controls the daily milk money.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Bhavani herself studied only until fifth standard—her parents pulled her out to help at home when her mother fell ill. She is determined that her children finish at least SSLC. Her son attends the Government High School, paying nothing for tuition under the state scheme but needing money for notebooks, the school bag, shoes and the annual sports-day fee, together around two thousand rupees a year; he also wants a smartphone for online classes, which the household cannot afford. Her younger daughter's primary school is free and closer, but Bhavani must still buy the uniform and pay for the mid-day meal contribution during festivals. The eldest daughter passed SSLC with a second class and was eligible for the government PU College seat, but the college is six kilometres away in the next town, the bus fare would cost fifteen hundred a month under the Shakti scheme's inter-district cap, and the girl said she felt uncomfortable travelling alone. Bhavani regrets the decision but believes it was the daughter's choice; she hopes the younger girl will be braver. The family dreams of the son becoming an engineer—Davanagere's Bapuji colleges are often mentioned—but they have no savings for fees or hostel costs.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Bhavani draws drinking water from the town's piped supply, which arrives every third day and tastes faintly bitter; the anganwadi worker once told her the underground water in Hiriyur has fluoride, though the tap scheme is supposed to treat it. Her mother-in-law has brown-stained teeth and joint pain, which the government hospital doctor said might be skeletal fluorosis, common in Chitradurga's borewell belt. Bhavani herself has chronic lower-back pain from sitting at the loom and carrying the milk cans, and occasional breathlessness, but she has never had time for a full check-up; the nearest government hospital is in Hiriyur town and the queue for the orthopaedic outpatient clinic can take half a day. Her youngest daughter was anaemic two years ago—the anganwadi gave iron syrup—but is better now. The household spends around five hundred rupees a month on outside medicines from the town pharmacy when anyone falls sick, because the government hospital often runs out of stock. Bhavani worries most about her mother-in-law's frailty and the cost of any serious illness; they have no health insurance, though they registered for Ayushman Bharat and are waiting for the card.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Bhavani's family belongs to the Bhovi community, traditionally stone-masons and lime-burners, though her husband's family shifted to handloom weaving two generations ago when the quarry work became irregular. The Bhovis in Hiriyur have their own neighbourhood near the old fort area, and the community association organises the annual jatre at the Bhovi Devasthana in the town, dedicated to a local guardian deity. Bhavani attends temple on Tuesdays and during Shivaratri, when the family makes a day trip to the Murugha Mutt in Chitradurga town; the mutt runs a free meal hall and a school that some Bhovi families send their children to, though Bhavani's children attend the government school. She speaks Kannada at home with a local accent distinct from the Telugu-border towns, and her mother-in-law still knows some old Bhovi work songs, though the younger generation does not sing them. Social ties within the Bhovi neighbourhood are strong—families lend each other money during weddings or medical emergencies—but there is little day-to-day interaction with the Vokkaliga or Lingayat families who dominate the town's trade and farm ownership.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Bhavani's household has a yellow ration card and collects five kilograms of rice and two of wheat each month from the fair-price shop, though the shop often opens late and the queue is long. They applied for an Ayushman Bharat card two years ago after a government camp in Hiriyur, but the card has not arrived; when her mother-in-law needed an X-ray last year they paid out of pocket. Her husband's younger brother got thirty days of MGNREGA stone-pitching work on the taluk road last summer, which brought in sixty-two hundred rupees, but the payment came four months late. The local gram panchayat is Vokkaliga-dominated and Bhavani feels the Bhovi colony's roads and drainage get less attention; she once went with a neighbourhood delegation to the taluk office over a blocked drain, and the officials listened politely but did nothing. She does not follow politics closely but knows the Murugha Mutt's backing matters in Chitradurga and that her community is classified as OBC, not SC, which her husband says costs them hostel seats.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Bhavani is proud of keeping the household and the loom running despite the water crisis, the fodder price rise and the irregular weaving income, but she worries constantly about money—whether the cows will stay in milk, whether the trader will cut the cloth price again, whether her son can afford college. She blames the borewell contractors for sinking pumps too deep and the government for delaying the Yettinahole scheme, though she is not sure the promised water will ever reach Hiriyur. She is frustrated that her eldest daughter did not continue schooling and fears the same will happen to the younger girl unless the PU College opens a hostel or the bus fare drops to nothing. What she wants most is a reliable town water supply without fluoride, stable weaving orders so the loom is not idle for months, and enough savings to send her son to Davanagere for a diploma course. She resents that Hiriyur supplies labour and stone to Bengaluru's construction sites but gets no piped Cauvery water or factory jobs in return, and she is tired of being told that handloom is a dying trade when every household she knows still weaves because there is no other work.

personas.name: Geetha
personas.definition: Geetha is a composite portrait of a powerloom weaver and homemaker in Honnali town, Davanagere district, navigating the decline of the region's handloom tradition while raising two school-age children and managing household expenses on fluctuating piece-rate income. She draws on the experiences of Padmashali weavers in Honnali and surrounding taluks who have shifted from traditional handlooms to powerlooms or migrated to Davanagere city's textile units, balancing pride in their craft heritage with the economic pressures of competition from Surat and Ichalkaranji synthetic fabrics.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Geetha works from home on a rented powerloom, weaving cotton and blended-fabric sarees and dhotis on order from a Honnali-based master weaver who supplies yarn and collects finished pieces twice a week. She earns between ₹6,000 and ₹9,000 a month depending on orders, down from steadier income a decade ago when Davanagere's mill-town legacy still supported local weaving. The loom occupies one room of their small rented house; she begins work at six in the morning after sending her children to school, breaks for cooking and household tasks, and resumes in the afternoon until seven or eight in the evening. Her husband drives an auto-rickshaw on the Honnali-Davanagere route, bringing in another ₹8,000-10,000 monthly, but diesel costs and vehicle repairs eat into earnings. Power cuts are less frequent now but still disrupt her weaving schedule. The master weaver's orders have shrunk as cheap synthetic sarees flood the market; Geetha worries the next lean season will force her to look for daily-wage work in Davanagere's garment units or as a domestic helper, leaving the loom idle.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Geetha lives with her husband and their two children: a daughter in Class 8 and a son in Class 5, both studying at the Honnali government Kannada-medium high school. Her husband's mother, widowed five years ago, lives in their ancestral village near Channagiri and visits during festival seasons; Geetha sends her ₹1,000-1,500 monthly for medicines. Geetha married at nineteen, shortly after completing her PUC, in an arranged match within the Padmashali community; her parents, small farmers near Jagalur, could not afford further education. Her daily routine revolves around the children's school timings, cooking two full meals, managing the loom and keeping the household accounts. Her daughter helps with cooking and younger-sibling care after school; Geetha insists she focus on studies and not learn weaving unless she chooses it after finishing school. Her husband's income is unpredictable, so Geetha controls most spending decisions, saving small amounts in a local chit fund when orders are good. Gender roles are traditional but negotiated: her husband expects meals on time, yet he also fetches vegetables from the market and helps the children with homework when she is at the loom late.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Geetha completed her PUC at a government college in Jagalur taluk but could not pursue a degree; her parents needed her earnings and arranged her marriage soon after. She is determined that both her children finish at least degree-level education. Her daughter, now in Class 8, is a steady student who wants to become a teacher; Geetha dreams of enrolling her in a private PU college in Davanagere if they can afford it, hoping the English-medium environment will open government-job or private-sector opportunities the Kannada-medium track rarely provides. Her son is less academically inclined but enjoys drawing; she has enrolled him in a weekend art class run by a local NGO at minimal cost. School fees are low—textbooks, uniforms and the midday meal are free—but extras add up: notebooks, pens, school-trip contributions, tuition for mathematics and science (₹500 per child per month), and the daughter's recently purchased mobile phone for online lessons during the pandemic, now used for schoolwork and entertainment. Geetha worries the daughter will face marriage pressure from relatives once she crosses sixteen, and she argues with her husband and mother-in-law to let the girl study further, pointing to friends' daughters who now hold bank or anganwadi jobs after degrees.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Geetha and her family rely on the Honnali government taluk hospital for routine care and the Ayushman Bharat card for major expenses; her mother-in-law's cataract surgery last year cost nothing out-of-pocket under the scheme, though the family had to pay for transport and attendant meals in Davanagere. Geetha suffers from chronic lower-back pain, which she attributes to long hours at the loom, and occasional wrist soreness; she takes over-the-counter painkillers from the local pharmacy and has never consulted a specialist. Her children are generally healthy, though her son had a prolonged fever two years ago that required a week's private-clinic treatment and antibiotics costing ₹3,000, draining their savings. Honnali's water supply comes from borewells and the Bhadra canal when it flows; Geetha boils drinking water during the monsoon, fearing contamination. She has heard of fluorosis in neighbouring Kolar and Chikkaballapur but believes Davanagere's water is safer. The anganwadi where she once took her children for growth monitoring has closed its local outpost; the nearest functional one is a kilometre away. Geetha worries about her daughter's iron levels—she looks pale and tires easily—but cannot afford regular doctor visits or the iron supplements the ASHA worker recommended.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Geetha belongs to the Padmashali weaver community, traditionally associated with handloom craft and historically classified under OBC. Her family observes festivals like Ugadi, Deepavali and Varamahalakshmi Vrata, and they visit the Honnali Anjaneya temple and the nearby Eshwara temple during Shivaratri. Her husband's family has loose ties to a local Veerashaiva-Lingayat mutt, though they are not initiated devotees; they attend the mutt's annual jathra and occasionally receive prasada and educational support from its outreach programmes. Geetha's social circle consists of a few neighbouring women—some weavers, others farmers' wives or anganwadi helpers—with whom she shares chit-fund membership, childcare advice and festival preparations. Caste remains a quiet but present force: Padmashali families prefer endogamous marriages, and Geetha's husband once mentioned that their daughter should marry within the community, though Geetha privately hopes education will give her daughter more choice. She feels proud of her weaving heritage but frustrated that the market no longer values it; she tells her children the Padmashali past was noble, but survival today requires degrees and salaries, not looms.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Geetha has an Ayushman Bharat card and a ration card; the family receives five kilograms of subsidised rice and two of wheat monthly, which helps but does not cover their needs. She enrolled for a loan under the Stree Shakti scheme three years ago to buy the powerloom but struggled with the paperwork and ultimately borrowed from a chit fund instead. Her husband uses the Shakti bus-pass benefit to travel to Davanagere for auto-rickshaw association meetings, which saves their household ₹100-150 weekly. Geetha has never attended a gram panchayat or town municipal council meeting but knows the local Congress councillor by face; her husband once approached him to fix a pothole on their street, which took six months. She blames both the state and central governments for failing to protect handloom weavers from synthetic-fabric dumping, though she is unclear on what policy could help. She believes government schools are improving—her children's teachers are more regular now than when she was a student—but worries that without private tuition, her children will fall behind in competitive exams.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Geetha is proud of her ability to weave sarees her grandmother would recognise and to juggle loom work, household tasks and children's schooling on a tight budget; she sees herself as carrying forward a centuries-old Padmashali craft tradition even as the market marginalises it. She worries most about the next lean season when weaving orders dry up, the daughter's future—whether they can afford PU college in Davanagere or whether relatives' marriage talk will derail her studies—and her son's weaker academic performance. She blames Surat and Ichalkaranji synthetic-saree manufacturers for killing local weaving, but also the master weavers who squeeze piece-rates, and the government for failing to enforce handloom protections or create steady work. She demands better schools in Honnali so families do not have to send children to Davanagere, more healthcare staff at the taluk hospital so she does not lose half a day waiting, and a support price or guaranteed orders for handloom weavers as farmers have for crops. She is sceptical that any government—Congress, BJP or JD(S)—will deliver, but the Gruha Lakshmi cash has made her feel, for the first time, that someone in power acknowledged women's unpaid work. She resents that Honnali and Davanagere's mill-town past brought prosperity to owners and traders but left weavers like her scrambling, and she is determined her children will escape the loom through education, even if that means the craft dies with her generation.

personas.name: Anand
personas.definition: Anand is a composite portrait of a coconut trader and small farmer from Honnali taluk, Davanagere district, navigating the uncertainties of borewell-dependent dryland farming and the volatile copra market in central Karnataka's open plains. He represents families balancing multiple income streams to manage debt and educate their children, while coping with groundwater depletion and fluctuating agricultural prices.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Anand owns four acres near Honnali town where he grows coconut, ragi and groundnut, supplemented by two borewells that have dropped from 80 to 240 feet in fifteen years. He wakes at five to irrigate before the power cut, then spends mornings at the Honnali weekly market buying coconut and copra from smaller farmers, which he resells to oil mills in Davangere city and Tiptur. The trading brings in roughly twelve to fifteen thousand rupees a month during good seasons, but competition is fierce and margins narrow. His own farm income is unpredictable: a good coconut harvest can earn sixty thousand rupees, but two successive dry years wiped out his groundnut crop and he borrowed one lakh at eighteen percent from a private financier to deepen one borewell. He hires labour only at harvest; his wife and unmarried daughter help with weeding and sorting. The household spends about eight thousand rupees monthly on groceries, school fees, electricity and loan interest, leaving little buffer. He worries the borewells will fail entirely and that his trading reputation depends on cash liquidity he barely maintains.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Anand lives in a tile-roofed house in Honnali town with his wife Pushpalatha, a homemaker who also manages the farm's daily labour and accounts, their married elder son who works as a salesman in Davangere city and visits monthly, their younger son in first-year degree college in Davangere, and their unmarried daughter who completed Class 12 last year and is waiting for nursing-course admission. His widowed mother, now seventy-two, lives with them and manages the kitchen. Pushpalatha keeps the household's ledger of market purchases, loan repayments and crop expenses; she insists the younger son stay in college despite the fees because she sees no future in farming for him. The elder son sends five thousand rupees home some months but his own household in Davangere is tight. Anand's daughter wanted to study nursing in Chitradurga but he preferred a local college to keep costs down; she is frustrated by the delay. Decisions about large expenses—college fees, a new pump, medical bills—are made jointly by Anand and his wife, though he controls the trading cash. Gender roles are traditional: women do not attend the market but Pushpalatha's bookkeeping gives her real influence.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Anand completed Class 10 in a Kannada-medium government high school in Honnali; his wife studied to Class 8. Their elder son finished a BCom from a private college in Davangere and wanted an MBA but could not afford it, so took the sales job. The younger son is in first-year BCom at Sri Taralabalu Jagadguru Institute of Technology in Davangere, paying sixteen thousand rupees annual fees plus eight thousand for hostel; Anand dipped into his coconut income and borrowed from a chit fund to cover the first year. Their daughter studied in the government PU college in Honnali and scored well enough for nursing but her CET rank was not high enough for a government seat; a private nursing college costs one lakh twenty thousand per year, which the family cannot manage, so she is waiting and helping at home. Anand is proud she finished PU but fears the delay will mean marriage instead of college.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Anand's family goes to the government taluk hospital in Honnali for fevers and minor complaints, and to Bapuji Hospital or JJM Medical College in Davangere city for anything serious; a road accident last year cost the family eighteen thousand rupees in private scans and surgery for his elder son, nearly emptying their savings. His mother has diabetes and high blood pressure managed with tablets from the taluk hospital's pharmacy, which are mostly free under Arogya Karnataka but sometimes out of stock. Anand himself has chronic knee pain from years of squatting to load coconut sacks and takes painkillers bought from a private shop. His wife complains of back pain and fatigue but rarely seeks treatment. The family drinks borewell water boiled and filtered; Anand has heard of fluorosis affecting Kolar and Chikkaballapur but believes Honnali's water is safer, though he has not had it tested. Heat exhaustion during summer market days is common. The younger son had typhoid two years ago, treated at a private clinic for five thousand rupees. Healthcare costs are a constant anxiety; Anand enrolled in Ayushman Bharat but has not yet used the card and is unsure how much it will cover.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Anand's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, historically a landholding caste in this region, and he is conscious of the social expectation to maintain respectability despite his debts. They are Hindu and observe Ugadi, Deepavali and Shivaratri; the family makes an annual pilgrimage to Devarayanadurga temple near Tumakuru, a day's journey that costs about three thousand rupees for the group. Anand is a nominal member of the Honnali Raitha Sangha farmers' association but attends only when there is talk of a price protest. His wife participates in a neighbourhood self-help group that rotates small savings; it lent her ten thousand rupees last year at lower interest than the private financier. His daughter's marriage will require a dowry and a large function; Anand dreads this expense but knows it is unavoidable, and he has started setting aside small sums in a chit fund. He respects the Murugha Mutt in Chitradurga for its schools and hospitals and has considered asking if they run a hostel for his daughter, though he has not followed through. Social ties in Honnali revolve around the market, the temple and family functions; reputation for fair dealing in the coconut trade matters greatly to him.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Anand holds a Bhoomi print-out of his land records and has used the Seva Sindhu portal once, with help from a cyber café, to apply for a caste certificate his son needed for college fee concession. He receives MGNREGA job-card updates on his phone but has never worked under the scheme; he sees it as for the landless. His wife draws two thousand rupees monthly child nutrition from the anganwadi for their grandson, though the anganwadi is in his elder son's Davangere neighbourhood, not Honnali. Anand received one drought-relief payment of four thousand rupees three years ago after a taluk declaration, but the process required multiple trips to the taluk office and he felt it barely covered his crop loss. He has heard of the Raitha Vidya Nidhi scheme for farmers' children but does not know if his younger son qualifies. His main interaction with government is through the electricity board—frequent cuts and unpredictable bills—and the ration shop, where he collects subsidised rice and kerosene monthly. He distrusts officials, expecting delays and bribes, and believes that larger farmers with political connections receive benefits first. He has no contact with his MLA except at election time.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Anand is proud that he has kept his children in school longer than his parents managed for him, and that he has built a trading business from scratch alongside farming, but he is haunted by debt and the fear that one more bad monsoon or medical emergency will break the family. He worries most about his daughter's future: the nursing course seems out of reach, marriage will be expensive, and he does not want her stuck at home indefinitely. He resents that coconut and copra prices swing wildly while input costs—diesel, fertiliser, borewell electricity—only rise, and he blames middlemen and oil-mill owners for squeezing farmers and small traders like him. He is frustrated that Honnali, despite being close to Davangere, lacks a good government degree college, forcing families to pay city fees. He believes the government favours big farmers and urban areas; Yettinahole and canal promises mean nothing here, he says, because Honnali has always relied on borewells and they are failing. He is angry at the private financier's interest rate but had no other option when the bank refused him a loan without collateral. He blames himself for not diversifying sooner, though he is unsure what else he could have done. He demands stable crop prices, cheaper education, reliable power for irrigation and a government that listens to small farmers, but he expects none of this will happen.

personas.name: Malathi
personas.definition: Malathi is a composite portrait of a woman working in the pepper and spice trade in the Malnad belt of Shivamogga district, drawing on the occupational patterns of families who moved from traditional areca cultivation into processing work. She represents households navigating the tension between agricultural heritage and wage labour, forest-fringe life and human-wildlife conflict, and the aspiration to give children urban-oriented schooling despite the geographic and economic constraints of Ghat-taluk residence.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Malathi works six-hour shifts five or six days a week at a small pepper-curing and sorting unit on the Hosanagara-Sagara road, grading dried pepper, packing spice orders and occasionally helping with cardamom when the season demands it. The unit is owned by a trader who buys from estates across Hosanagara and Tirthahalli taluks and sells to wholesalers in Mangaluru and Bengaluru. She earns around nine thousand rupees a month, paid weekly in cash, with no formal contract or provident fund. The work is indoors and less physically demanding than field labour, which matters because her knees have troubled her since a fall three years ago. Her husband, Ramesh, owns a small three-acre areca and coconut plot inherited from his father, but prices have been poor for two years and Yellow Leaf Disease has weakened several palms. He also drives an auto-rickshaw on the Hosanagara town route two or three days a week to cover household shortfalls. The combined family income hovers around twenty thousand rupees a month in good months, less when areca prices drop or pepper-unit orders slow. Expenses are high: school fees, provisions bought from the town ration shop and private vendors, medical costs and loan repayments to a local self-help group and a private moneylender. Fuel, fertiliser and pesticide for the areca plot drain whatever the land yields. Malathi starts her day at five-thirty, cooks breakfast and lunch, walks twenty minutes to catch a share-auto to the unit, works until two or three in the afternoon, returns home to cook dinner and helps her older daughter with homework. Weekends are for weeding the areca plot, washing clothes and attending the village temple. The rhythm is tight, money is always calculated to the week, and there is no savings cushion for an emergency.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Malathi lives with her husband Ramesh, their two daughters—fourteen-year-old Shruti and eleven-year-old Priya—and Ramesh's widowed mother, Sharada, who is sixty-eight and manages the household when Malathi is at work. Sharada cooks the midday meal, feeds the two chickens and one cow they keep, and watches the younger girl when school closes early. Malathi's own parents live in a village near Sringeri in Chikkamagaluru district; she visits them once or twice a year, usually during a festival or when someone is ill. Her marriage was arranged when she was nineteen, following Havyaka Brahmin custom, and she moved to Hosanagara taluk after the wedding. Ramesh is forty-one and comes from a family that once had a larger areca holding, but it was divided among three brothers twenty years ago. His two brothers have both left for Bengaluru—one works in a hardware shop, the other as a clerk—and rarely return except for major occasions. Gender roles are traditional: Malathi does all the cooking, cleaning and childcare, while Ramesh handles field work, auto-driving and interactions with traders and officials. Sharada expects both girls to marry into Havyaka families, though Malathi quietly hopes Shruti will finish a degree first. Decisions about spending, schooling and medical treatment are made by Ramesh after consultation with Malathi and his mother, but major choices—like whether to sell a portion of the land—rest with the men.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Malathi studied up to seventh standard at the government school in her natal village before her parents pulled her out to help at home and prepare for marriage; girls' secondary schooling was less common in Havyaka families in the 1990s, though that is slowly changing. Shruti, the elder daughter, is in ninth standard at the government high school in Hosanagara town, a forty-minute journey by bus each way. The school is better-equipped than the taluk's village schools, with a science lab and English-medium sections, but Shruti travels in a crowded KSRTC bus that is often late, and during the monsoon months from June to September the Sharavathi tributary near their village swells and the road becomes difficult. Priya, the younger daughter, is in sixth standard at the same school. The family pays around fifteen hundred rupees per term for books, uniforms and miscellaneous fees, plus the cost of daily bus fares under the Shakti scheme is now free for the girls, which has been a relief. Sharada grumbles that girls do not need so much education, but Malathi insists that Shruti should at least finish tenth standard and sit the SSLC exam; she dreams of Shruti becoming a teacher or a government clerk, something with a steady salary and respect. Ramesh agrees in principle but worries about the cost of PU college if Shruti passes tenth, and whether they can afford to send her to Hassan or Shivamogga town for further study. Priya is a weaker student and sometimes skips school claiming stomach aches; Malathi suspects she is anxious about English and mathematics, subjects the village primary school barely taught. The household's schooling hope is that one daughter will secure a government job and lift the family, but the fear is that Shruti will have to stop after tenth if money runs out or if a good marriage proposal comes early.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Malathi's knee pain, the result of a slip on wet mud three years ago, flares up during the monsoon and when she stands for long hours at the curing unit; she takes ibuprofen tablets bought from the Hosanagara town pharmacy and sometimes uses a turmeric-oil rub Sharada prepares. She has never seen an orthopaedic specialist; the nearest is in Shivamogga town, a two-hour journey, and the consultation and scans would cost thousands they do not have. Ramesh suffers from seasonal respiratory trouble, probably from pesticide exposure on the areca plot and auto-rickshaw exhaust; he uses an inhaler during bad months. Sharada has high blood pressure and diabetes, managed with tablets from the government taluk hospital, and she attends a monthly check-up though the wait is often three or four hours. The family uses the taluk hospital for fevers, minor injuries and antenatal check-ups, and the anganwadi nurse for the girls' immunisations when they were younger. For serious illness—like when Priya had dengue two years ago—they went to a private clinic in Hosanagara and borrowed five thousand rupees to cover the drips and tests. Malathi worries about Kyasanur Forest Disease because monkeys are common around the areca plot and several neighbours have fallen ill during the January-to-May peak season; the vaccination drive reached their village last year but Sharada refused the injection, calling it dangerous, and Malathi could not convince her. Snakebites and leopard scares are also real: a neighbour's cow was killed by a leopard last year and a boy from the next village died of a snakebite before he could reach hospital. Malathi ties a red thread and a black bead on Priya's schoolbag for protection, a habit Sharada insists on. Mental health is not named, but Malathi feels a constant low-level anxiety—about money, about Shruti's future, about the rains and the forest—and she prays at the village Sharadamba shrine every Thursday for peace of mind.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Malathi's family belongs to the Havyaka Brahmin community, traditionally areca cultivators and priests concentrated in the Malnad belt across Shivamogga, Chikkamagaluru and parts of Uttara Kannada. Havyaka families speak a distinct dialect of Kannada and maintain vegetarian households; Malathi's family observes all traditional rituals and festivals, with Sharada leading daily prayers to a small shrine of Sharadamba and Ganapati in the house. The family visits the Sringeri Sharada Peetham once or twice a year, a pilgrimage Sharada insists on, and Malathi feels a deep reverence for the temple and the Jagadguru. Within Hosanagara taluk the Havyaka community is a small minority; most neighbours are Vokkaliga, Kuruba, Gowda and Scheduled Caste families, and relations are polite but not close. Malathi's workplace at the pepper unit includes women from various communities and castes, and they share tea and talk during breaks, but socialising beyond work is rare. Sharada is stricter about caste rules than Malathi, refusing to eat food cooked by non-Brahmins and insisting the girls marry within the Havyaka fold. Malathi is more pragmatic, though she has not openly challenged her mother-in-law's views. The family does not participate in village panchayat politics, leaving that to Vokkaliga and Gowda households who dominate local leadership. Malathi's sense of community is layered: Havyaka Brahmin identity, Kannada-speaking Malnad identity and a vague notion of being from a "cultured" priestly lineage, all of which sit uneasily with the reality of wage labour and declining areca income. She takes pride in Kuvempu, the Jnanpith poet from nearby Kuppalli, whose house-museum she visited once on a school trip decades ago, and she tells Shruti that educated families like theirs must preserve Kannada and culture even when times are hard.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Malathi's household has a yellow ration card, which provides subsidised rice, wheat and kerosene, though the quantities have been less generous in recent years and the fair-price shop sometimes runs out of stock. Ramesh applied for a Kisan Credit Card but was refused because his three-acre holding is considered too small and informally split with his brothers, so he borrows from a self-help group linked to SKDRDP and from a private moneylender at higher interest. Malathi is a member of a women's self-help group that meets monthly in the village; she has taken two small loans over the years, one for Shruti's school fees and one to repair the roof after a storm. The group also organised a government training on organic farming last year, which Ramesh attended, though he has not adopted any of the methods. The family's main interaction with government is through the taluk hospital, the girls' school and the electricity board, whose power cuts during the monsoon can last hours. Ramesh once applied for compensation after a fallen tree blocked the road to their areca plot for two weeks, but the application was lost in the tahsildar's office and he gave up. She knows B.S. Yediyurappa's name because he is from Shivamogga and was chief minister, but she cannot name the current MLA. The 2018 state election and the 2019 national election brought campaign jeeps and promises of loan waivers, none of which materialised. The Kasturirangan Western Ghats notification has been a topic of worry since 2026: Ramesh attended a public meeting in Hosanagara where farmer leaders said the notification would prevent areca replanting and infrastructure, and he came home angry, calling it another way the government punishes Malnad while favouring Bengaluru. Malathi trusts little from government except the ration shop and the anganwadi nurse, and she believes getting ahead requires either a government job, which is nearly impossible without connections, or leaving the village entirely.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Malathi worries most about Shruti's future: whether the girl will pass her SSLC, whether they can afford to send her to PU college, and whether she will find a good husband who does not demand a large dowry. She fears that if Shruti stops schooling after tenth, she will end up like Malathi herself—married young, working for small wages, dependent on a husband's uncertain income. She is proud that Shruti is bright and disciplined, and she tells herself that education is the only ladder out of this life, but she also knows that money may force a different choice. Malathi worries about the areca plot: whether Yellow Leaf Disease will spread further, whether the rains will be good, whether Ramesh will be forced to sell the land to pay off the moneylender. She blames the government for not controlling areca prices and for ignoring Malnad farmers while spending crores on Bengaluru metro and IT parks. She blames the Forest Department for restricting access to minor forest produce and for failing to compensate quickly when elephants or leopards destroy crops or livestock; a neighbour waited two years for compensation after an elephant raid, and the amount was a fraction of the loss. She is ashamed that she works in a curing unit for daily wages, a job she thinks is beneath a Brahmin woman, but she does not voice this shame except in prayers. She demands that the government keep schools open during the monsoon, build a bridge over the river near the village so children do not miss classes, and guarantee areca prices through a minimum-support scheme like paddy. She wishes Malnad were not forgotten, that roads were better, that hospitals were closer, and that her daughters could study without fear of having to stop. She prays to Sharadamba every day for the strength to hold the household together and for Shruti to pass tenth standard with good marks.

personas.name: Dinesh
personas.definition: Dinesh is a composite portrait of a Vokkaliga pepper-curing unit supervisor living in Thirthahalli taluk, Shivamogga district, in the Malnad region. He represents families who bridge plantation and processing work, earning modest but regular incomes while facing the pressure of ghat-road disruptions, youth outmigration and the uncertainties of crop prices.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Dinesh works at a small pepper-curing unit on the edge of Thirthahalli town, where black pepper harvested from estates across the taluk arrives for drying, grading and packing. His day begins at seven in the morning, checking the boiling vats and drying racks, supervising three labourers who turn the berries on concrete floors under the sun. During peak season from December to February he works ten-hour days, coordinating lorry loads from estates in Hosanagara and Sringeri taluks and ensuring each batch meets the grade buyers in Mangaluru demand. His monthly salary is around fourteen thousand rupees, with a small bonus at year-end if the unit meets its target. Income is stable compared to daily farm labour but far below what estate owners earn. Monsoon months bring lighter loads and shorter hours; he uses that time to help his brother repair their family's small areca garden. Pepper prices swung wildly in recent years—peaks near six hundred rupees per kilogram followed by crashes to three hundred—and that volatility trickles down: when prices fall, the unit owner delays bonuses and talks of cutting shifts. Dinesh keeps an eye on Coffee Board bulletins and trader gossip, knowing his livelihood hinges on crop cycles he does not control.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Dinesh lives in a tile-roofed house in a Vokkaliga-majority neighbourhood a kilometre from the curing unit, sharing the compound with his wife Suma, their two children, his widowed mother and his unmarried younger brother. Suma works part-time as a tailor from home, stitching blouses and school uniforms for neighbours, adding three to four thousand rupees a month to the household budget. Their elder child, a daughter aged sixteen, is in second PUC at the government junior college in Thirthahalli town; their son, thirteen, attends eighth standard at the nearby high school. Dinesh's mother, now seventy, manages the kitchen and the small vegetable patch behind the house. His brother drives an auto-rickshaw on the Thirthahalli-Sringeri route and contributes to household expenses. Dinesh's father died eight years ago, leaving a half-acre areca garden that the brothers now maintain together, hiring labour for the annual harvest. Household decisions—what to plant, whether to repair the roof, how much to spend on the daughter's college fees—are made collectively over evening tea. Suma's earnings give her a voice in those discussions, though Dinesh's salary remains the anchor. Gender roles are conventional: Suma cooks, cleans and sews, Dinesh handles outside work and dealings with the unit owner, but the line blurs when harvest or festival demands call everyone into the garden.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Dinesh completed his SSLC in 1998 at the government high school in Thirthahalli, then worked for two years before attempting first PUC; he dropped out after failing twice, unable to manage studies alongside wage work his family needed. He learned pepper-curing on the job, starting as a labourer and rising to supervisor over fifteen years. His children's schooling is the household's clearest aspiration. His daughter travels three kilometres by KSRTC bus to the junior college every morning, studying the science stream with hopes of a nursing diploma or a BSc; the family spends around two thousand rupees per month on her college fees, textbooks and bus fare under the Shakti free-ride scheme, which helps but does not cover private tuition she takes for physics and chemistry. His son's school is closer, fees are nominal, but Dinesh worries about the boy's attention—he is more interested in his uncle's auto than in homework. The family hopes the daughter will finish PUC, secure a seat in a nursing college in Shivamogga or Manipal, and earn a steady job. Dinesh knows that path requires money they barely have; a government nursing seat costs upwards of fifty thousand rupees for three years, and private seats are out of reach. He has no savings earmarked for it yet.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Dinesh's health is generally sound, though he has begun to feel joint pain in his knees from years of standing on concrete floors, and a persistent cough from inhaling pepper dust during peak-season boiling and drying. He avoids doctors unless the pain becomes unbearable; a visit to the government taluk hospital in Thirthahalli costs him a lost day's wages. His mother has diabetes and high blood pressure, managed with tablets from the primary health centre, but the family spent eight thousand rupees last year when she needed an ECG and specialist consultation at McGann Hospital in Shivamogga town, a two-hour bus ride away. His daughter had dengue two monsoons ago, requiring a week's hospitalisation at a private clinic in Thirthahalli; the bill came to eighteen thousand rupees, borrowed from a self-help-group contact of Suma's and still being repaid. The household's main health anxieties are twofold: the cost of any serious illness that the government hospital cannot handle, and the seasonal risk of waterborne disease in the monsoon when the well water turns cloudy. Dinesh knows families in forest-fringe villages near Sringeri who lost members to Kyasanur Forest Disease and snakebite, but Thirthahalli town feels removed from that; still, every January when KFD cases appear in the newspapers, his mother mutters prayers. No one in the household is covered by health insurance; Dinesh applied for Ayushman Bharat but his card has not arrived. Suma's tailoring gives her chronic neck and eye strain; she refuses to spend money on spectacles.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Dinesh's family is Vokkaliga, the dominant landowning community across much of Hassan and southern Shivamogga, though Thirthahalli's population also includes Havyaka Brahmins tied to the areca economy, Kurubas, Scheduled Castes, a small Muslim trading community and migrant labourers from north Karnataka and Odisha who work the estates. Dinesh attends the Rama temple near the taluk office for major festivals—Ugadi, Dasara—and his mother insists on a daily lamp at the household shrine. The family observes Sankranti with sugarcane and sesame sweets, and his mother makes a pilgrimage to Sringeri Sharada Peetham every two years. Community ties are dense: Dinesh's neighbours are mostly Vokkaliga families he has known since childhood, and mutual aid—borrowing rice, lending a vehicle for a wedding, helping with harvest labour—is routine. Suma's self-help group, linked to a local NGO and SKDRDP credit, meets twice a month; it is as much a social institution as a financial one, a space where women discuss children's schooling and arbitrate neighbourhood disputes. Caste surfaces in marriage alliances and in the unspoken preference for Vokkaliga tenants when his brother considers renting out a room, but day-to-day interactions at the curing unit, in the market and on the bus are functionally caste-blind. Dinesh is proud of Kuvempu's Thirthahalli connection and of the Keladi Nayaka heritage taught in school, though he admits he has never visited the Keladi museum.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He accessed the Vidya Nidhi scholarship scheme to help cover his daughter's first-year PUC fees but found the disbursement delayed by four months, forcing him to borrow short-term. Suma's self-help group helped her secure a small loan to buy a sewing machine, and Dinesh credits SKDRDP for being more reliable than the taluk panchayat office, where clerks demand repeat visits for simple certificates. The household does not qualify for a BPL card—Dinesh's salary pushes them just above the line—so they miss ration-shop subsidies and are ineligible for some housing and health schemes. Dinesh's most direct government interaction is the ESI dispensary at the curing unit, which provides basic medicines but nothing more. He has never attended a gram sabha, seeing it as the domain of landed farmers, but he joined a small roadside protest last year when the Thirthahalli-Sringeri road remained unrepaired through the monsoon, blocking pepper and coffee lorries for weeks. He expects little from officials unless pressure is applied collectively. The September 2026 legislature resolution on the Kasturirangan ESA, which he read about in Prajavani, reassured him that farm and plantation land would be protected, but he remains wary of any notification from Bengaluru that could redraw boundaries or restrict his brother's areca garden.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Dinesh is proud to live in Thirthahalli, the taluk that gave Karnataka Kuvempu, and he takes quiet satisfaction in the greenness of Malnad, the reliability of the monsoon and the quality of the pepper and coffee that pass through his hands. But that pride coexists with a constant, low-grade anxiety about money and the future. His daughter's PUC fees and the dream of a nursing seat loom large; he calculates and recalculates what he can save, knowing it will not be enough. He resents the way Bengaluru and the coast get highways, airports and medical colleges while Malnad roads wash out every monsoon and the nearest decent hospital is two hours away. The Kasturirangan ESA notification, though softened by the September resolution, still feels like a threat—one more rule from the city that ignores how families like his make a living. At the same time, he blames estate owners and traders for squeezing labour and keeping wages low while pepper and coffee prices soar. He demands better roads, local colleges, job schemes for youth and reliable health clinics. He wants his children to have the choices he did not, and he fears they will leave the moment they do.

personas.name: Raghav
personas.definition: Raghav is a composite portrait of a skilled industrial worker navigating the coastal economy where processing exports and service-sector growth shape household opportunity. He embodies the pressures facing households dependent on seasonal factory wages in a district known for high literacy yet where migration, private-school competition and economic volatility alter what families can afford to plan for their children.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Raghav supervises the second shift—afternoon through late evening—at a medium-sized cashew-processing unit on the edge of Udupi town, one of a cluster that feeds the Mangaluru export hub. His day begins around noon: checking the roasting drums, ensuring the women on the peeling line meet tonnage targets, troubleshooting machinery breakdowns that can idle fifty workers at once. The unit processes raw cashew from Kerala and local estates; peak season runs October through March, then work thins for four months. He earns about eighteen thousand rupees a month during the season, dropping to twelve when orders slow, plus a modest Diwali bonus if the export price holds. His employer is better than most—wages arrive on time, the factory has fire exits—but dust and heat are constants, and the peeling women, many migrants from north Karnataka, work for daily rates he knows are low. Raghav walks or rides a scooter the three kilometres from home; fuel and vehicle repair are monthly headaches. The job is stable by Udupi's processing-sector standards, but cashew prices swing with global demand and currency rates, so layoffs and short-time are always possible. He worries the younger generation sees only IT jobs in Manipal or Bengaluru and scorns shop-floor work.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Raghav lives with his wife Jyothi, their two children—a daughter in Class 9 and a son in Class 6—and his widowed mother in a small rented house in one of the older residential lanes near the Udupi market. Jyothi worked in a garment unit years ago but left after their son was born; she now stitches blouses at home for a neighbourhood boutique, earning three to four thousand rupees a month. His mother, in her late sixties, manages the cooking and watches the children after school, a presence Raghav depends on entirely because his shift ends at ten-thirty at night. His elder brother migrated to Mumbai two decades ago and works in a hotel; remittances have dwindled as his brother's own children's expenses climbed, so Raghav shoulders most of the household budget. Decisions about schooling, especially whether their daughter will continue to PU college and beyond, are made jointly by Raghav and Jyothi, though his mother's voice—rooted in older expectations about marriage timing—carries weight. Gender roles are traditional: Jyothi manages money, food and the children's homework; Raghav handles rent, school fees and any encounter with government offices. The house has two rooms, a narrow kitchen and an attached toilet; privacy is scarce and tensions over study space and screen time common.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Raghav completed his SSLC at a Kannada-medium government high school in a taluk town and tried first-year PU but dropped out when his father fell ill and income was needed; he has always regretted not finishing. His daughter attends a private English-medium school near the town centre—fees are about twenty-five thousand a year with books and uniform, a quarter of his annual earnings—while his son is in a less expensive Kannada-medium aided school, a compromise driven by cost. The daughter is a steady student; Raghav and Jyothi hope she will reach degree level and perhaps teacher training, though anxiety about PU college fees and hostel costs if she must study away looms large. Udupi town has many private schools, some backed by trusts with reputations stretching back generations; the government school nearby is poorly enrolled, its playground shared with a bus stand. Tuition is assumed necessary from Class 8 onward—another three thousand rupees a month the household can barely meet. His daughter has asked to study science in PU, which would require coaching Raghav knows he cannot afford without borrowing.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Health access in Udupi town is good on paper—a government taluk hospital, numerous private clinics and Manipal's big hospitals twenty minutes away by bus—but cost is the barrier. Raghav's mother has diabetes and high blood pressure; her monthly medication, even from a government hospital's pharmacy, costs about eight hundred rupees, and when supplies run out they buy from private chemists at double. A serious illness means referral to Manipal or Mangaluru, and while the household holds an Ayushman Bharat card, navigating the cashless system and securing a bed in empanelled hospitals has proven confusing and sometimes requires out-of-pocket deposits anyway. Jyothi suffered a complicated delivery with their son and needed a Caesarean at a private maternity home; they are still paying off that loan in small instalments to a relative. Raghav's work environment—heat, dust, noise—leaves him with a persistent cough he has never had properly investigated; factory health checks are cursory. The children are generally healthy, vaccinated through government drives at school, though dental care is unaffordable unless pain becomes unbearable. Household water comes from a municipal tap, safe enough, though summer shortages mean buying tanker water some years. Mental-health vocabulary is absent; stress and exhaustion are borne silently. The cashew factory has no health insurance scheme for supervisors, and accident or injury would devastate the family budget immediately.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Raghav's family is Hindu, loosely tied to a neighbourhood temple dedicated to a local deity where his mother goes for monthly pujas; there is no strong caste-organisation membership or ritual leadership role. Udupi town's public culture is visibly diverse—Jain basadis, the Krishna Matha complex, churches, mosques—but daily socialising remains within broad religious lines. Raghav has Muslim and Christian co-workers at the factory; relations are cordial, professional, with no memory of personal friction, though he is aware that communal rhetoric surfaces around elections and sometimes at college campuses. He does not participate in any Bhuta Kola or Yakshagana events personally, though he respects them as important local tradition and took his children once to a Yakshagana performance at Kateel. Social ties are anchored in the neighbourhood lane—borrowing, shared wedding invitations, children's friendships—and in the loose network of factory colleagues. His mother's generation speaks of communal harmony as Udupi's strength, yet Raghav has heard grumbles among co-workers after moral-policing incidents reported in Udayavani about couples harassed near the beach or college students targeted, discomfort that it tarnishes the town's image. The family has no land, no CAMPCO membership, no Gulf relatives—so the kinship safety nets that cushion other Udupi households are missing. Community is functional, not deep; support is neighbour-to-neighbour, case-by-case.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Raghav's encounters with government are mostly bureaucratic frustrations. Obtaining his mother's diabetes medication requires monthly queues at the taluk hospital pharmacy, where stock-outs are common and counters open late. The family's ration card is functional—they draw subsidised rice and kerosene—but Aadhaar-linking glitches have caused payment delays twice, requiring hours at the taluk office to resolve. His children's school certificates and his own SSLC documents needed for a bank-loan application took weeks and small bribes to extract from the education-department record room. He has never attended a gram sabha or municipal ward meeting; politics feels distant, something decided by larger players. The Shakti free-bus scheme has been a real gain for Jyothi and his daughter, cutting travel cost for tuition and hospital visits. He has heard of Ayushman Bharat but finds the enrollment process and hospital empanelment opaque. No one in the household receives a pension or MGNREGA wages; the labour-department helpline for factory-worker grievances exists in theory but he would never risk his supervisor post by filing a complaint. Local municipal services—garbage collection, street lights—are acceptable in his lane, worse in the poorer migrant-labour colonies near the factory.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Raghav is proud that his children are studying in better schools than he did, and proud of Udupi's reputation—temples, Manipal's colleges, the cleanliness compared to other towns he has visited. But pride is shot through with anxiety: will his daughter's education lead to a job, or only to marriage and a demand for dowry he cannot meet? He worries about his own job security as younger men are willing to work for less, and worries that mechanisation or a bad export season could make him redundant. He blames no one villain but feels the system is rigged for those who already have—land, Gulf money, connections to get a government job. He respects education but resents its price, and resents that private schools treat parents like customers while government schools are seen as dumping grounds. He is angered by news of corruption and by the sight of political leaders' convoys while his lane's drainage remains broken, yet he does not believe any party will truly change things for a family like his. What he wants is stability—his job to continue, his daughter to finish PU without the family taking ruinous loans, his son to find some decent work, his mother's health to hold. He does not expect government help beyond ration and bus fare, but demands it function without humiliation: medicines in stock, certificates issued on time, school teachers who teach. He fears climate-linked disruption—floods have worsened in recent years, and one season the factory was waterlogged for a week—and fears the gap between his household and the Manipal-Mangaluru prosperity he sees around him will only widen.
