personas.name: Raghu
personas.definition: Raghu is a composite portrait of a private bus driver navigating the Puttur-Mangaluru route in Dakshina Kannada district, balancing household expenses against the pressures of an intensely competitive stage-carriage market. He embodies the economic realities of a working family in the coastal belt where literacy is high but schooling expenses, occupational uncertainty and Gulf-migration patterns reshape children's educational trajectories.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Raghu drives a private stage-carriage bus on the Puttur-Mangaluru route six days a week, beginning his shift at four-thirty in the morning and finishing after eight in the evening. He earns around sixteen thousand rupees monthly as salary plus a small share of the daily collection, which fluctuates with passenger numbers and petrol prices. The Shakti free-bus scheme for women has cut his operator's revenue sharply since it began, forcing management to run fewer trips and demand faster turnarounds. Raghu eats breakfast at a roadside hotel in Kabaka, packs lunch from home and takes his evening meal at a friend's tea-shop near the Pumpwell junction in Mangaluru. His knees ache from the clutch, his eyes burn from the glare off the NH-66 tarmac and he has developed chronic acid reflux, treated with over-the-counter antacids he buys at the petrol-bunk pharmacy. He holds a commercial driving licence renewed every three years and has worked this route for seventeen years, first as a conductor, then passing his heavy-vehicle test in 2012. Debt from a failed arecanut-plantation venture a decade ago still constrains the household budget.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Raghu lives with his wife Sharada, their two sons aged nineteen and fifteen, and his widowed mother in a modest tiled house on the edge of Puttur town, within walking distance of the bus stand. Sharada works part-time as an assistant in a private Kannada-medium primary school, earning about four thousand rupees monthly, which covers groceries and the younger son's tuition fees. Their elder son Kiran completed his second-year pre-university at a government college in Puttur but left in mid-year to take up work at a Gulf-recruitment agency in Mangaluru, preparing documents and translating for Beary-speaking applicants; the family hopes he will eventually secure his own Gulf posting through the contacts he is building. The younger boy Tejas studies in Class 10 at a Kannada-medium government high school and is a good student, regularly scoring above seventy percent, but the family worries about affording private pre-university tuition if he passes his SSLC this year. Raghu's mother, now seventy-one, manages the household kitchen and receives a small widow's pension. Sharada's earnings, though modest, give her a say in decisions about the boys' futures, and she insists Tejas should finish his studies before thinking of work.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Raghu himself studied only up to Class 7 in a village school near Sullia taluk before his father's ill-health forced him to begin working as a conductor at seventeen. Sharada completed her SSLC and worked in a garment unit before marriage, and her schooling opened the door to her current school job. Kiran attended the same government high school where Tejas now studies, scoring sixty-eight percent in his SSLC and gaining admission to the commerce stream at the government pre-university college; the family paid nothing for his high-school years apart from textbooks and uniform, but college brought expenses for bus fare, notebooks and private coaching in accountancy, totalling roughly three thousand rupees a term. When Kiran left college mid-way, Raghu was disappointed but accepted it as practical: the recruitment-agency job pays eight thousand rupees monthly now and promises a Gulf opening within two years, and the household cannot afford to keep an earning-age son dependent. Tejas wants to study science and become a lab technician, but private pre-university colleges charge fifteen to twenty thousand rupees yearly and government seats are fiercely competitive; the family has not yet decided whether they can afford the full two years or whether Tejas too will need to find work after his SSLC.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Raghu's chronic reflux and knee pain, left untreated apart from painkillers, limit his ability to work past fifty, a worry he does not voice openly. He attends the government community health centre in Puttur for minor ailments but travelled to a private clinic in Mangaluru last year when severe abdominal pain frightened the family; the consultation, ultrasound and medicines cost nearly four thousand rupees, wiped out by a loan from his bus-owner. Sharada developed anaemia two years ago and takes iron tablets supplied free at her school's health camp, organised under a district nutrition programme. Raghu's mother has mild diabetes, managed with subsidised Metformin from the Jan Aushadhi pharmacy and careful diet; a cataract is forming in her right eye but surgery will wait until the household can afford the five thousand rupees the government hospital in Mangaluru will charge for lens and post-operative care under Ayushman Bharat. The family is enrolled under the Ayushman Bharat-Arogya Karnataka scheme, which would cover hospitalisation, but Raghu fears losing workdays more than the cost itself. Tejas had dengue during the monsoon two years ago, treated at home with paracetamol and oral rehydration, and recovered without hospital admission. No one in the household drinks heavily, but Raghu smokes four or five beedis daily, a habit Sharada criticises quietly.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: The family belongs to the Billava community, historically associated with toddy-tapping but now widely present in transport, small trade and labour across Dakshina Kannada. Raghu's household does not tap toddy, and he describes himself simply as a driver, but he remains proud of the community's Koti-Chennaya epic and its message of defiance against injustice. The family observes Deepavali, Ugadi and Dasara, and Sharada participates in a neighbourhood women's group organised by SKDRDP, Dharmasthala's self-help-group wing, saving fifty rupees weekly toward emergency expenses. They visit the Kudupu Sri Anantha Padmanabha Temple on important occasions and attended a Bhuta Kola performance at a relative's compound near Uppinangady two years ago, an all-night event Raghu remembers vividly for the possessed dancer's leaps and the beat of the drums. Raghu's late father had taken him as a child to the Kukke Subrahmanya Temple, a memory he holds dear. The family speaks Tulu at home, Kannada in school and work, and a little Beary-influenced Dakshina Kannada Kannada when dealing with Muslim traders in Mangaluru. Caste does not dominate daily conversation, but Raghu is aware that Bunts and Brahmins still hold most land and that his own family's economic mobility depends on wages, not property.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He has little direct contact with the gram panchayat, as his house lies on the town's edge under the Town Municipal Council's jurisdiction, but Sharada's school receives government mid-day-meal supplies and textbooks, which she says arrive mostly on time. Raghu applied for a Below Poverty Line card three years ago but was refused; the family now holds a yellow ration card and buys subsidised rice and kerosene monthly. He has never used MGNREGA, as his driving work precludes the hundred-day rural-labour guarantee. The household electricity bill under the Gruha Jyoti scheme is now zero up to two hundred units, a significant saving. Raghu deeply resents the new toll plaza on the Mangaluru highway, which forces his operator to pay daily and cuts further into revenue. He believes local MLAs care only about Mangaluru city and ignore Puttur's crumbling bus-stand and potholed approach roads. When the KSRTC raised its fares two years ago, he joined a one-day private-operators' strike, the only political action he has taken beyond voting.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Raghu is proud that his district ranks first in Karnataka for literacy and that both his sons can read and write fluently, something his own father could not do. He worries most about his livelihood: will private buses survive against free government transport, and what work will he find when his knees give out? He resents the Shakti scheme not because he opposes helping women but because it was introduced without compensating private operators, and he sees it as a political gimmick rather than genuine care. He blames the central government's fuel taxes for petrol crossing one hundred rupees per litre and the state government for failing to defend small transport workers. Raghu wants Tejas to study further and escape manual work, but he is resigned to the possibility that financial reality will cut that dream short, just as it did for Kiran. He admires Gulf-returned families who build concrete houses and start businesses, and he sees Kiran's recruitment-agency job as the family's one plausible path toward that prosperity. He fears illness and accident more than unemployment, knowing a single hospital stay could erase years of savings. He is uncomfortable with the communal rhetoric he hears from some passengers and colleagues but keeps his opinions to himself, believing politics and religion are best left unspoken on a bus. He is proud of Dakshina Kannada's Yakshagana and Bhuta Kola traditions and dislikes being told by outsiders that his region is defined only by moral policing and tension.

personas.name: Jayanth
personas.definition: Jayanth is a composite portrait of a Kodava pepper-nursery and homestay owner in his early forties, navigating the coffee and spice economy of Somwarpet taluk with pride in his heritage and anxiety over succession and market swings. He stands at the intersection of Kodagu's traditional plantation life and its newer tourism economy, balancing family land, hired migrant labour, government neglect of compensation and roads, and the question of whether his children will return.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Jayanth owns a fifteen-acre family estate inherited through the patrilineal okka system, planted with coffee, pepper, cardamom and a few areca palms, supplemented by a three-room homestay he and his wife opened in 2017. The coffee harvest runs November through February, when he employs six seasonal workers from Assam and Odisha, paying them around ₹450 per day plus meals and shed housing. Pepper vines climb the silver-oak shade trees, and he maintains a small nursery selling rooted pepper cuttings to neighbouring estates, earning ₹25,000–₹30,000 in a good monsoon year. The homestay brings in another ₹60,000–₹80,000 annually from trekking tourists and Bengaluru families, though bookings dropped sharply during the 2018 floods and again during the pandemic. His wife manages the cooking and laundry; he drives guests to Igguthappa temple or the Abbey Falls viewpoint in his aging Bolero. Income swings with the Coffee Board's post-blossom estimate and the pepper price, which crashed below ₹300/kg in 2023 before recovering slightly. He worries the Kasturirangan notification will freeze any expansion or building, a fear sharpened by the September 2026 all-party resolution he read about in Udayavani but whose legal force he does not trust.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Jayanth lives in the family ainmane, a tile-roofed ancestral home his grandfather built, with his wife Kaveri, his mother, his son Aditya (twenty, studying hotel management in Mysuru), and his daughter Nandini (seventeen, in second PUC at a private college in Madikeri). His father passed away in 2015. Kaveri, also Kodava, married into the okka twenty-two years ago in a traditional wedding without a Brahmin priest, the couple circling the sacred lamp while clan elders blessed them. She keeps the household accounts, manages the homestay bookings via a travel aggregator app, and cooks pandi curry and kadambuttu for guests. Jayanth's mother, now seventy, helps with the kitchen garden and the annual Puthari harvest festival, when the family offers the first rice to the clan deity. Gender roles in the household follow a practical division: Kaveri's labour is recognised but unpaid, while Jayanth holds title to the land and deals with banks and labour contractors. He hopes Aditya will return and take over the estate and homestay, but his son speaks of hotel jobs in Bengaluru or Dubai, and Nandini wants to study nursing in Manipal, mirroring the outmigration trend he sees among cousins and neighbours.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Jayanth studied up to second PUC at the government college in Somwarpet, then dropped out to help his father on the estate when coffee prices were good and labour was cheaper. He regrets not finishing, though he reads Kannada newspapers daily and has taught himself basic bookkeeping and homestay marketing. Aditya attended the Kodava Vidyalaya boarding school in Gonikoppa through Class 10, then moved to a private PU college in Mysuru; fees, hostel and food cost the family around ₹1.2 lakh per year, financed partly by a Canara Bank education loan. Nandini commutes daily to Madikeri, a forty-minute drive on a road that turns treacherous in the monsoon; the family pays ₹35,000 per year in college fees. Both children studied in Kannada medium through Class 10, then switched to English for PU science, a transition Nandini found difficult. Jayanth is proud that both are on track to join professions his father never imagined—hotel management, nursing—but he worries they see the estate as a fallback, not a future. The 2018 floods closed schools for three weeks and damaged the Somwarpet college building; classes resumed in a repaired block, but the memory of that disruption lingers. He wants his children to have choices, yet he knows that if neither returns, the estate may be leased or sold, breaking a lineage his okka has held for four generations.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Jayanth's family relies on the government Primary Health Centre in Somwarpet for fevers and minor injuries, but serious cases mean a two-hour drive to Madikeri's district hospital or, increasingly, to Mysuru's larger hospitals. His mother has diabetes and high blood pressure, managed with monthly doctor visits and daily tablets that cost around ₹800 per month. The estate's location near the Pushpagiri Wildlife Sanctuary means constant vigilance for leptospirosis during the rains—Jayanth ensures workers wear boots in the fields and boils all drinking water. One of his Assamese workers fell sick with high fever and body ache in 2022; the PHC diagnosed leptospirosis and referred him to Madikeri, where he recovered after a week of intravenous antibiotics. Jayanth paid for the hospital stay, knowing that without it the man would have left mid-harvest and word would spread, making future hiring harder. Snakebite is a real risk; a neighbour's daughter was bitten by a pit viper two years ago and reached Madikeri just in time for antivenom. Pesticide exposure from spraying coffee and pepper is a low-level worry—Jayanth has started using organic fungicides after a Coorg Planters' Association workshop, but many neighbours still use cheaper chemical options. The family has health insurance under a private scheme that costs ₹18,000 annually, covering hospitalisation but not outpatient medicines, which add up.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Jayanth's identity is rooted in his Kodava okka, the patrilineal clan that traces its ainmane to this land and links him to cousins across Somwarpet and Virajpet. The okka meets for Puthari, the harvest festival in December, when the family offers new rice and celebrates with pandi curry, and for Kail Podh in September, when the men clean and worship the family's licensed firearms—a tradition Jayanth upholds with pride, though he rarely hunts. He speaks Kodava Takk at home and with clan elders, switching to Kannada for business and with his children, who understand Takk but reply in Kannada or English. The family visits the Igguthappa temple in Kakkabe for major festivals and has taken part in the Kodava Family Hockey Tournament, though Jayanth himself no longer plays. He is aware of the Kodava National Council's language-recognition and autonomy demands and broadly supports them, feeling that Kodagu's distinct culture is misunderstood or dismissed by Bengaluru bureaucrats. Relations with the Tibetan settlement families near Bylakuppe are cordial but distant—some buy coffee from him, and he has hired Tibetan workers in the past. The local Gowda and migrant-labour families live separately; Jayanth employs them but socialises mainly within Kodava circles. He attends Kaveri Sankramana at Bhagamandala when he can, joining the throng that gathers where the river is said to rise.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Jayanth's encounters with government are marked by frustration and mistrust. After an elephant destroyed part of his pepper crop and damaged a shed in 2020, he filed for Forest Department compensation; the claim took eighteen months to process, and he received ₹35,000 against an estimated loss of ₹80,000. The delay and partial payout feed his belief that the state neglects Kodagu's farmer-wildlife conflict while prioritising conservation. The Taluk Panchayat has funded a culvert repair near his estate and a water pipeline extension, but the main Somwarpet-Madikeri road remains pocked with potholes that worsen every monsoon, a standing grievance. Jayanth has heard of Jal Jeevan Mission tap-water schemes but his household has a borewell and does not depend on piped supply. He availed a small NABARD loan in 2015 for drip irrigation, which he repaid on time. The Kasturirangan Western Ghats ESA notification terrifies him; he attended a Coorg Planters' Association meeting in 2024 where the consensus was that the notification would freeze land use and kill livelihoods. The September 2026 all-party resolution gave him brief hope, but he doubts Bengaluru or Delhi will listen. His view of government is transactional: he pays property tax, files GST returns for the homestay, and expects roads, hospitals and fair compensation in return. When those fail, he falls back on the okka and neighbours.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Jayanth is proud to be Kodava and to own land his forebears cleared and planted, yet he is haunted by the possibility that neither of his children will carry it forward. He blames the lack of a railway line in Kodagu, the crumbling roads and the government's indifference to plantation farmers' struggles. The 2018 floods shook him; his family was safe, but friends in Makkandur lost homes, and the relief effort felt slow and chaotic. He worries that another such disaster will come, and that this time the state will be even less prepared. The Kasturirangan notification looms as an existential threat: he imagines officials arriving to tell him he cannot expand his homestay or replant a hillside patch, land his family has held for generations suddenly declared off-limits. He is angry that conservationists in Bengaluru or Delhi, who have never faced an elephant in the dark or lost a season's pepper to disease, can dictate his livelihood. At the same time, he takes quiet pride in Kodagu's forests, wildlife and the coffee heritage that draws tourists from across India. He hopes for a government that will defend farmers' rights, compensate losses promptly and build the roads and railway Kodagu has long deserved, but he has learned not to expect it. His deepest fear is that in twenty years the estate will be silent, sold to an outsider or leased to a corporate operator, the ainmane empty, and the Kodava Takk his mother speaks fading into memory.

personas.name: Shanta
personas.definition: Shanta is a composite portrait of a woman in her late thirties working in one of Nanjangud's silk-reeling units, navigating the demands of factory work, household care and farming in a taluk known for its sugarcane, paddy and temple festivals. She represents the generation of women in Mysuru's rural-industrial belt who balance wage labour with unpaid family responsibilities, education aspirations for their children and the pressures of Cauvery-dependent irrigation.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Shanta works six-day weeks at a privately owned silk-reeling unit on the edge of Nanjangud town, where she stands at a reeling basin from eight in the morning until five in the evening, drawing raw silk thread from boiled cocoons. Her hands are perpetually damp, her fingers calloused from the hot water and the repetitive motion of guiding the fine filament onto wooden reels. She earns around nine thousand rupees a month, paid fortnightly, with no written contract and unpaid leave deducted without question. The unit employs forty women, most from nearby villages, and the supervisor docks pay if the thread breaks too often or the weight falls short. Cocoon prices fluctuate with the season and the Chinese import market, so when the unit's orders slow she is sent home for a week at a stretch with no income. Her husband Nanjappa farms their three acres of mulberry and paddy, selling cocoons to the Ramanagara market or local traders and relying on canal water from the KRS system; in a deficient monsoon the second paddy crop fails and they borrow from the cooperative. Shanta rises at five to cook, feeds the household, walks twenty minutes to catch the seven o'clock KSRTC bus under the Shakti scheme, and returns by half past six to cook again, wash and help her daughter with homework under a single bulb.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Shanta lives in a two-room house with a tile roof and a small veranda in a hamlet three kilometres from Nanjangud town, sharing the compound with Nanjappa's widowed mother and his unmarried younger brother who drives an auto-rickshaw in town. Shanta was married at nineteen, shortly after completing second PU in Nanjangud; her parents, small farmers in a neighbouring village, arranged the match through a Vokkaliga network and paid a modest dowry of jewellery and cash. She has two children: a daughter Preethi, fourteen, studying in ninth standard at the government high school in the village, and a son Suraj, eleven, in sixth standard at the same school. Preethi is bright and wants to study science in PU, but Shanta worries about the cost of private college in Mysuru and whether the girl will be safe commuting daily. Suraj is less interested in books and helps his father in the field after school, learning to judge cocoon quality and operate the pump. Shanta's mother-in-law manages the kitchen garden and the two goats, grumbles about Shanta's long hours away from home, and expects her daughter-in-law to lead all the cooking for festivals and family functions. Nanjappa is supportive but leaves the children's schooling entirely to Shanta, saying he finished only seventh standard and cannot help with English or science. The household's income—Shanta's wages, Nanjappa's crop sales, his brother's auto earnings and occasional MGNREGA days—varies sharply with the monsoon and the silk market, and they have an outstanding loan of sixty thousand rupees from a microfinance SHG for a borewell that yielded brackish water.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Shanta herself studied in the Kannada-medium government school in her natal village and completed second PU at a government college in Nanjangud, stopping because her parents could not afford the fees and hostel costs for a degree and because marriage was the expected next step. She can read Kannada newspapers and do household accounts, and she wishes she had continued to become a teacher. Her daughter Preethi attends the government high school a kilometre from home, travelling by bicycle now that the Shakti scheme has freed up money for the purchase; before that she walked with classmates, and in the monsoon the mud path made her late or absent. Preethi studies well, scoring above seventy percent in the eighth-standard exams, and she wants to take science in PU and become a lab technician or nurse. Shanta dreams of sending her to a private PU college in Mysuru or Nanjangud where English instruction and better teachers might open a government job, but the fees are fifteen thousand a year and the bus fare, even under Shakti, means two hours of travel each day; Shanta worries about her safety and whether the girl will be teased or fall behind in English. Suraj is in sixth standard, a restless boy who prefers the field to the classroom and whose marks hover around fifty percent. The school has two toilets but no science lab, and the English teacher has been on long leave for six months. Shanta attends parent meetings when she can get leave from the unit, and she has joined the School Development and Monitoring Committee, pushing for a drinking-water filter and repair of the cracked classroom roof.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Shanta suffers from chronic lower-back pain and tingling in her wrists, which she attributes to standing all day at the reeling basin and the repetitive strain of guiding thread. The unit has no seating, no fans in summer and poor ventilation, and the air smells of boiled cocoons. She takes paracetamol from the village Janaushadhi shop when the pain is sharp, but she has never consulted a doctor because the nearest PHC is four kilometres away, open only in the mornings, and the doctor is often absent. For her mother-in-law's diabetes and her son's childhood vaccinations the family travels to the Nanjangud community health centre or, in emergencies, to Mysuru's KR Hospital, twenty-five kilometres away. Shanta had both her children delivered at the PHC with the help of an ASHA worker, and she received the Janani Suraksha cash benefit each time, but her second delivery was complicated and she was referred to Mysuru by ambulance in the night. She worries about her daughter reaching puberty and the need for pads, nutrition and information; the school has no health counsellor and the anganwadi in the hamlet closed years ago for lack of a worker. Nanjappa drinks occasionally, more heavily when the crop fails or cocoon prices fall, and twice he has come home drunk and angry, though he has never struck her. Shanta's own mother died young of an undiagnosed illness, and she fears the same, knowing that women in her family and community rarely seek care until it is too late. The microfinance SHG she belongs to organised a health camp last year where she learned her haemoglobin was low, but the iron tablets the ASHA gave her ran out and she has not asked for more.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Shanta's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, the dominant cultivating caste in the Nanjangud taluk and across Mysuru district, and they observe its marriage and festival customs, drawing social and economic support from a dense network of kin and caste fellows. Her husband's family has farmed the same land for three generations, and her father-in-law, before he died, was a member of the village Vokkaliga sangha that mediated disputes and organised the annual temple fair. Shanta's own father is a small farmer from a Vokkaliga hamlet five kilometres away, and her brother works in a sugar mill in Mandya; visits between the two families happen on festival days and for life-cycle ceremonies. The family worships at the Srikanteshwara Temple in Nanjangud during the annual car festival in March, joining thousands of pilgrims for the event, and they make an annual offering of jaggery and coconut at the small Kalamma temple in their hamlet. Shanta fasts on Varalakshmi Vratam and Gowri festival days, decorating the threshold with rangoli and praying for the wellbeing of her children and husband. Her mother-in-law is more devout and insists on stricter ritual observance, criticising Shanta for missing the evening lamp and for working outside the home. Shanta's SHG, run under NABARD's linkage programme, has ten women from the village, mostly Vokkaliga but including two SC women; they meet fortnightly, save small sums and borrow for school fees, medical bills and farm inputs. The group is her main space for conversation outside the household, though caste and economic differences are rarely discussed openly. She has heard of the Adichunchanagiri Mutt's scholarship schemes for Vokkaliga students but does not know how to apply, and the family has never visited the mutt.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Shanta's family holds a yellow ration card and collects ten kilograms of rice a month under Anna Bhagya from the fair-price shop in the village, though the shop is often closed and the rice is sometimes mixed with stones. Her husband has a Bhoomi land record and a Raitha Sangha membership card, but he does not attend the sangha meetings regularly and dismissed the last Cauvery-release agitation as a distraction. Shanta has an Aadhaar card, a voter ID and a bank account that her SHG insists on, and her wages are paid in cash fortnightly without a payslip; she has never been offered ESIC or any labour welfare. She travels free on KSRTC buses under the Shakti scheme, which has saved her nearly two thousand rupees a month and made it possible to work in town; before Shakti she often walked to save the fare. She has heard of the Gruha Jyothi electricity subsidy and assumes her household benefits, though she does not see the bills; water comes from a borewell they dug with an SHG loan, and the village tap connections are dry most of the year. She attended a gram sabha once when the SDMC election was held, but the men did most of the talking and she left early to cook. The anganwadi in the hamlet has been shut for three years and the panchayat has done nothing; the ASHA worker visits occasionally but has no medicines or supplies. Shanta knows nothing of the Aspirational District programme or MGNREGA entitlements beyond the few days her husband sometimes works on road repair. She distrusts officials and believes that schemes are for people with connections, not families like hers.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Shanta worries most about her daughter's future: will she be allowed to study beyond tenth standard, will the family afford PU college, will she be safe travelling to Mysuru, and will she end up married at eighteen and working in a silk unit like her mother? She is proud that Preethi studies well and dreams of a government job for her, something with a salary, respect and security, but she knows that without English-medium schooling and without money for coaching the dream is fragile. She resents the silk unit's casual cruelty—the docked pay, the absence of leave, the supervisor's gendered scolding—but she needs the income and believes there is no alternative. She blames no one in particular for the state of the village school or the closed anganwadi, only a vague sense that the government is for towns and cities, not for people like her. She is grateful for Shakti and believes the Congress government has done something real for women, though she wishes there were doctors at the PHC and that the electricity were more reliable. She does not follow state politics closely and has only a dim sense of the Cauvery dispute, knowing that canal water is life but not understanding the legal or inter-state details. She takes pride in the Srikanteshwara Temple festival and in Mysuru's Dasara, which she has attended twice, seeing them as markers of a dignified local tradition. She believes that girls should be educated as far as money and safety allow, that sons should respect their mothers, and that hard work will be rewarded if luck is kind, though her own experience leaves her uncertain.

personas.name: Ashok
personas.definition: Ashok is a composite portrait of a Lingayat small-business owner in Mysuru city, drawing together the lived experience of traders and practitioners in the city's established Ayurveda and herbal-products sector. His daily routines, family concerns and civic outlook reflect the perspective of a shopkeeper navigating Mysuru's heritage-tourism economy, managing the balance between traditional medicine's prestige and the pressures of modern retail competition.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Ashok runs a small Ayurveda shop on Sayyaji Rao Road, near the Devaraja Market, selling herbal medicines, oils, powders and consultations for common ailments. He opens at nine each morning, spending the first hour restocking shelves with stock from KSIC depots and local suppliers, then receives a steady stream of customers—elderly regulars seeking arthritis balms, mothers buying kashayams for children's colds, and occasional tourists drawn by Mysuru's sandalwood reputation. He earns between fifteen and twenty-two thousand rupees most months, depending on the Dasara season when footfall surges, though online pharmacies and big-chain stores have begun pulling away younger customers. Afternoons are quieter; he uses the lull to update his GST records on a worn laptop, to call suppliers in Bengaluru, and to advise walk-ins on formulations his father taught him. By six he pulls down the shutters, tallies the day's cash and digital payments, and walks home through the evening market crowds. The work is steady but income growth has stalled; he worries that his sons see the shop as old-fashioned and that rent and stock costs eat into margins each year.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Ashok lives with his wife, Renuka, their two sons—seventeen and fourteen—and his widowed mother in a two-bedroom flat in Vijayanagara, a fifteen-minute scooter ride from the shop. Renuka, trained as a teacher, has not worked outside the home since their elder son was born; she manages the household, cooks, oversees homework and cares for Ashok's mother, who has diabetes and arthritis. Their elder son is in second-year pre-university at a private PU college, preparing for engineering entrance exams; the younger attends a Kannada-medium aided high school nearby. Ashok's father passed away eight years ago, leaving him the shop and its goodwill; his younger brother moved to Bengaluru for a software job and rarely visits. Gender roles in the household are traditional: Ashok handles all financial decisions and shop matters, while Renuka's domain is domestic—though she increasingly questions why their sons do not help with chores. Marriage was arranged by their families; Renuka's father, also a small trader, judged Ashok steady and respectable. The family observes Lingayat customs, wearing vibhuti, visiting the Suttur Mutt during festivals, and contributing to its dasoha meals and school-hostel endowments.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Ashok completed his schooling in Mysuru's government Kannada-medium schools and one year of B.Com at Maharaja's College before his father's illness forced him to take over the shop at twenty-one; he regrets not finishing his degree. His elder son studies at a private PU college charging thirty-five thousand rupees a year; Ashok hopes he will pass the CET and secure an engineering seat, ideally in Mysuru or Bengaluru, though he worries about the cost of private-college fees if the government-quota rank does not come through. The younger son attends a Kannada-medium aided school, performing adequately but showing more interest in cricket than studies. Ashok pays for both sons to attend weekend coaching classes—mathematics and science for the elder, general tuition for the younger—adding another twelve thousand rupees annually. The family debates switching the younger boy to an English-medium school, but Ashok resists the expense and believes Kannada medium builds stronger roots. Renuka wants the boys to study further than their father did, to have salaried stability; Ashok agrees but also hopes one son might take over the shop, blending Ayurveda knowledge with modern marketing. He sees education as the route to security, yet feels his own incomplete degree left him capable enough to run the business his father built.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Ashok's mother attends the K.R. Hospital outpatient diabetes clinic monthly, receiving subsidised insulin and tablets; waits are long, but the care is adequate and cheap. She also suffers from knee arthritis; Ashok treats her with oils and kashayams from his own shop, and occasionally they consult a private Ayurvedic vaidya when her pain worsens. Renuka had a hysterectomy three years ago at a private hospital, costing ninety thousand rupees after insurance; they took a loan from a chit fund to cover the gap. Ashok himself is in fair health—mildly overweight, with occasional acidity—but has not had a full check-up in years; he relies on his own herbal remedies and dismisses the idea of preventive scans as unnecessary expense. The boys are healthy, though the elder suffers exam-season stress and headaches. The family trusts K.R. Hospital and JSS Hospital for serious illness, Ayurvedic treatment for chronic and minor complaints, and private clinics for speed when needed. Ashok worries about the cost of any major health event, knowing his savings are modest and that hospital bills can wipe out years of earnings. His mother's diabetes is managed but not cured; he accepts it as an aging inevitability and focuses on keeping her comfortable.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Ashok's family are practising Lingayats; they wear the ishtalinga, observe veerashaiva customs, and reject caste hierarchy in principle while acknowledging its social weight in practice. They visit the Suttur Mutt during major festivals, contribute to its dasoha free-meal programmes, and sent Ashok's younger brother to a Suttur-affiliated hostel for his high-school years. Ashok respects the Mutt's educational and welfare work and sees it as a unifying institution for Lingayats across Mysuru and Mandya. He also visits the Chamundeshwari Temple during Dasara, participating in the city's shared ritual calendar even though it is not strictly a Lingayat shrine; he sees no contradiction, treating it as part of Mysuru's collective identity. His social circle includes other small traders—some Lingayat, some Vokkaliga, a few Muslim—whom he meets at the market, the trade association and occasional community dinners. Renuka's closest ties are with neighbours and relatives; she attends women's bhajan groups and helps organise Suttur Mutt collection drives in their locality. Ashok values the Lingayat tradition of simplicity and service, but he also navigates Mysuru's broader social fabric pragmatically, maintaining good relations across communities because his shop depends on all customers.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Ashok holds a ration card and his family receives subsidised rice and kerosene, though the PDS shop's irregular hours frustrate him; he buys most provisions from the open market. He opened a Jan Dhan account years ago but uses it rarely, preferring his savings account at Canara Bank. He has not directly benefited from the five guarantees—his household has no woman bus commuter, the electricity subsidy is marginal, and his income sits above the Gruha Jyoti threshold—but he acknowledges that poorer customers mention Shakti and Anna Bhagya as helpful. His shop is registered for GST; he finds the monthly filing cumbersome and pays a small accountant to manage it. He is not a party member but follows politics through Kannada newspapers and evening television news. His encounters with the Mysuru City Corporation are limited to property-tax payment and occasional complaints about road potholes and waste collection; he finds the officials distant and unresponsive. He wishes the government would do more to support small traders against online and chain-store competition, perhaps through lower taxes or dedicated market zones, but he has little faith that his voice reaches decision-makers.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Ashok is proud of Mysuru—the Dasara pageantry, the palace illumination, the city's reputation for order and heritage—and he contrasts it favourably with Bengaluru's chaos and traffic, though he envies Bengaluru's economic dynamism. He worries most about his sons' futures: whether they will secure good college seats, whether they will find stable jobs, and whether they will stay in Mysuru or be pulled to Bengaluru or abroad, leaving him alone in old age. He blames online retail and big pharmacy chains for squeezing small shops like his, and he resents that the government offers them no protection; he feels traditional knowledge and local enterprise are being discarded in the rush toward modern convenience. He is frustrated by the city's slow infrastructure upgrades—potholes, unreliable water supply in some wards, the absence of metro connectivity—and he believes Mysuru is neglected compared with the state's focus on Bengaluru. He respects the Suttur Mutt and the Lingayat community's educational efforts, and he sees his own modest success as the fruit of his father's hard work and his own discipline. He wishes his sons valued the Ayurveda shop as a viable livelihood, not merely a fallback, and he hopes they will remember their roots even if they move away. He demands better support for small businesses, cleaner governance, and recognition that cities like Mysuru deserve as much investment as the capital.

personas.name: Lakshamma
personas.definition: Lakshamma is a composite portrait of a Soliga woman juggling flower vending and farm labour in Yelandur taluk, Chamarajanagara district, navigating seasonal work, tribal identity and the challenges of raising children in a remote, drought-prone landscape. She represents many in Chamarajanagara's tribal hamlets who straddle forest-linked livelihoods, wage work and persistent questions of land rights, school access and health reach.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Lakshamma rises before dawn most days to walk three kilometres to the weekly market in Yelandur town, carrying a basket of jasmine and marigold she buys from a local grower near Kollegal. She sells flowers to temple-goers and wedding planners, earning between three hundred and six hundred rupees on a good market day. Outside market days she works as a daily-wage farmhand weeding ragi and cotton fields, paid one hundred and eighty to two hundred rupees for seven hours under the sun. The work is irregular—Yelandur's rainfed agriculture offers fewer days than the canal-fed tracts near Mysuru, and drought declarations mean even fewer. Her husband migrates seasonally to coffee estates in Kodagu and Chikkamagaluru, sending home two to three thousand rupees a month when work is available. The household's income is precarious: flower sales fluctuate with festivals and weddings, farm wages dry up between sowing and harvest, and her husband's remittances are unpredictable. They own a small plot of dry land near the forest fringe, but lack a clear patta and have been unable to access bank credit. Economic pressure is constant; every illness or school expense forces a reckoning.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Lakshamma lives with her husband, three children—two daughters aged fifteen and twelve, and a son aged nine—and her aging mother-in-law in a thatched house on the edge of their hamlet, twenty minutes' walk from the paved road. Her husband is away for eight months of the year; she shoulders most daily decisions, from rationing rice to managing the children's schooling. Her elder daughter helps with cooking, fetching water from the hand pump and caring for her grandmother, whose arthritis has worsened. The family's Soliga identity shapes their social ties—most neighbors are kin or clan members, and they observe Male Mahadeshwara worship and forest-linked festivals. Gender roles are traditional but flexible by necessity: Lakshamma manages money, negotiates with flower buyers and deals with the anganwadi and school, tasks her mother-in-law says were once men's domain. Marriage happened early for her—she was sixteen—and she worries her elder daughter will face the same pressure, despite her own determination to keep the girl in school. The household is close-knit but stretched; caregiving, earning and managing fall mostly on her.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Lakshamma herself attended school only until Class 5; the nearest higher primary was too far, and her parents needed her labour. Her two daughters study at the government Kannada-medium school in the hamlet—the elder in Class 10, the younger in Class 7—and her son is in Class 4. The school runs until Class 10 but has only three teachers for over eighty children across all grades, and the headmaster post has been vacant for two years. Her elder daughter travels five kilometres by KSRTC bus under the Shakti scheme to attend bridge classes in Yelandur town, preparing for the SSLC exam; the free travel has been a relief, but the girl still misses days when household work piles up or the bus breaks down. Lakshamma dreams her daughters will finish SSLC and perhaps join a nursing course or government job, escaping the wage-labour cycle. The school provides midday meals and uniforms, but notebooks, pens and exam fees stretch the household budget. Her son is bright, but she worries his teachers don't push him. The Adichunchanagiri Mutt runs a residential school for tribal children in Chamarajanagara town, and neighbors have urged her to send her younger daughter there, but she is reluctant to part with her. Education is both hope and a daily struggle.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: The nearest primary health centre is in Yelandur town, an hour's walk or a fifteen-rupee auto ride away. Lakshamma's mother-in-law suffers from joint pain and high blood pressure, but the PHC rarely has the BP medication in stock, forcing them to buy it at a private pharmacy in town for a hundred and twenty rupees a strip. Lakshamma herself has chronic anaemia—diagnosed during a health camp two years ago—but she rarely takes the iron tablets because they upset her stomach and she can't afford to lose a day's work. Her children have been vaccinated at the anganwadi, but her son had a bout of fever and diarrhoea last monsoon that required two days at the Chamarajanagara district hospital, costing the family nearly three thousand rupees in transport, tests and medicines. Malnutrition and anaemia are common among children in the hamlet; the anganwadi worker distributes take-home rations, but the quantities are small. Access to safe drinking water is a worry—the hand pump sometimes runs dry, and during summer they fetch water from a borewell a kilometre away. Healthcare means lost wages, travel costs and uncertain outcomes; serious illness is a family crisis.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Lakshamma's Soliga identity is central to her life. The hamlet's social fabric is woven from kinship, shared labour and forest ties—families gather honey and tamarind from the forest fringe, though the BRT tiger reserve buffer restrictions have tightened access in recent years. The community observes Male Mahadeshwara Swamy's festival at MM Hills with an annual pilgrimage, and Lakshamma saves for months to make the journey with her children. The Soliga language is spoken at home and among neighbors, though her children learn Kannada at school and are beginning to shift. The hamlet has no formal caste hierarchy, but interactions with non-Soliga landlords and flower buyers often carry an undertone of condescension. Lakshamma participates in a women's self-help group organized by an NGO working with tribal communities; it meets monthly and has helped her save small sums, though she has not yet taken a loan. Trust and reciprocity within the hamlet are strong; outside it, she navigates a world where her tribal identity often means being overlooked or spoken down to.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Lakshamma's household receives ten kilograms of rice per person per month under Anna Bhagya, collected from the ration shop in Yelandur town; the shopkeeper sometimes shortchanges the weight, but complaining feels risky. She has a voter ID and votes in every election—her hamlet is a polling booth—but she feels politicians visit only during campaigns and forget them afterward. Her husband worked under MGNREGA for forty days last year, earning a little over seven thousand rupees, but the work dried up and payment was delayed. The family has applied for a land patta under the Forest Rights Act, with help from the NGO, but the application has been pending for three years without explanation. The anganwadi worker is helpful but overstretched, covering three hamlets. Lakshamma has heard of the Aspirational District program for Chamarajanagara and seen district officials visit the school during a health camp, but no tangible change has followed. The local gram panchayat member is from a non-Soliga community and rarely consults the hamlet. She sees government schemes as essential—ration, Shakti, school meals—but their reach is patchy, their implementation indifferent, and the tribal community's voice weak. Politics feels distant; survival is immediate.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Lakshamma worries most about her daughters' futures—whether they will finish school, avoid early marriage and find work that offers dignity and security. She is proud of her Soliga heritage and Male Mahadeshwara worship, but she also resents that her community is seen as backward or in need of rescue rather than respect. She blames the forest department for restricting access to honey and minor forest produce that once supplemented income, and she blames the education and health systems for being absent when most needed. She wishes her husband could find steady work closer to home so the family wouldn't be split for months on end. She takes pride in managing the household alone, in sending her children to school and in saving a few hundred rupees each month in the SHG, small victories against relentless pressure. She demands better teachers, a PHC with reliable medicine stocks, land rights that are honored, not just promised, and recognition that tribal families like hers are not charity cases but citizens. Her worldview is grounded in the daily calculus of survival, the fierce love for her children, and a quiet, persistent anger that Chamarajanagara, and Yelandur especially, are always last in line.

personas.name: Mahesh
personas.definition: Mahesh is a composite portrait of a Kuruba auto-rickshaw driver and small farmer in Kollegal town, Chamarajanagara district, navigating seasonal drought, irregular fares and the costs of sending three children to school. He is drawn from the lived experience of families in this border taluk who balance urban gig work with rainfed farming and hope their children will escape both.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Mahesh owns a thirteen-year-old auto-rickshaw and operates on the Kollegal town stand, ferrying passengers to the taluk hospital, the bus station, nearby villages and occasionally across the Tamil Nadu border to Bargur or Dhimbam. His daily income varies sharply: a good day brings seven hundred rupees, a lean one barely two hundred, with fuel, maintenance and the monthly loan instalment eating into every trip. He also cultivates three acres of dryland on his wife's family's holding, two kilometres outside Kollegal, where he grows ragi and cotton under uncertain rainfall. Ploughing, weeding and harvest pull him away from the auto stand for weeks at a time, forcing him to skip days or leave the vehicle idle while his eldest son, who left PU college after first year, sometimes takes short trips. The cotton crop failed last year after a delayed monsoon, leaving him with a thirteen-thousand-rupee loss and an outstanding pesticide bill. Auto work offers cash flow but no security: fares drop in the monsoon, maintenance costs spike on potholed roads, and competition from app-based bike taxis has begun to cut into his regulars. He wakes at five, checks the farm if it is the season, reaches the stand by seven and works until eight or nine at night, returning home bone-tired to a meal of ragi mudde his wife keeps warm.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Mahesh lives with his wife, three children and his widowed mother in a small house they built twelve years ago on a site his wife inherited at the edge of Kollegal. His wife, forty-two, works as a domestic help in three households in the town, earning four thousand rupees a month; she also manages the farm labour they hire at peak times and cooks, cleans and cares for his seventy-year-old mother, who has diabetes and poor eyesight. Their eldest son, twenty-two, dropped out of first-year PU commerce to help on the farm and occasionally drives the auto; Mahesh had hoped he would finish and find a government job, but the boy saw no point and now talks of migrating to Bengaluru for factory work. Their daughter, eighteen, passed SSLC last year and is in second PU science at the government college in Kollegal; she is bright, wants to study nursing, and Mahesh is determined she will not marry before finishing, though relatives have begun to ask. Their youngest son, fourteen, is in ninth standard at the town high school and shows interest in mechanics. Mahesh's wife makes most day-to-day decisions about the children's schooling and health; he defers to her on household spending but insists on the final word about land and the auto. Gender roles are clear: she manages the inside, he the outside, though the lines blur when cash runs short and both scramble to cover fees or medical bills. His mother's insulin and eye drops cost fifteen hundred a month, a strain they carry without complaint.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Mahesh himself studied only up to seventh standard in a village school before his father pulled him out to work; he regrets it and is fierce that his children will study further. His daughter attends the Government PU College in Kollegal, where the Shakti scheme and a bicycle have made daily travel possible; fees are low, but books, uniforms and the biology practical kit cost money, and private tuition for the CET exam will be another expense he has not yet figured out how to meet. His youngest son goes to the government high school in town, within walking distance, and pays no fees under the guarantee schemes; still, Mahesh spends roughly two thousand rupees a term on notebooks, shoes and the odd teacher's demand for photocopies or charts. Mahesh had dreamed of an office job for him, but the dream died and he does not speak of it now. His daughter's nursing ambition fills that void; if she clears CET, he will mortgage the farm to pay for a private nursing college if no government seat comes. The schools are there, but the jobs the degrees promise feel distant and uncertain, and he wonders if his sacrifice will be enough.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Mahesh's mother's diabetes is the household's chronic worry: her fasting sugar runs high, the government hospital in Kollegal dispenses insulin and metformin free under Arogya Karnataka, but the strips for her glucometer, her diet and the quarterly specialist check-up in Mysuru cost time and money they juggle month to month. Last year she had a hypoglycaemic episode at home and Mahesh rushed her to the taluk hospital; the doctor stabilised her and scolded him for irregular monitoring, a rebuke he felt keenly. His own health he ignores: his knees ache from clutch-work, his back hurts, he has a persistent cough he attributes to dust and exhaust, but he has not seen a doctor in three years because he cannot afford to stop earning. His wife suffers from anaemia—she was prescribed iron tablets at the anganwadi during a check-up for his mother—but takes them irregularly and says she is too busy to rest. The children have been mostly healthy, though his daughter had dengue two years ago and the week in a private Kollegal clinic cost twenty-two thousand rupees, borrowed from a relative and still being repaid. They rely on the government hospital for fevers and injuries, but serious illness means private care, debt and fear. The free-medicine scheme helps, but stocks run out and the pharmacy then quotes prices that sting. Mahesh's main health fear is an accident or major illness that would stop him working; he has no insurance, and a month without income would topple the family. He drinks occasionally, more when the crop fails or fares are lean, and his wife worries but says nothing.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Mahesh is Kuruba, a shepherding community with a presence across Mysuru and Chamarajanagara, though his family left herding two generations ago for farming and town work. He participates in Kuruba Sangha meetings in Kollegal, where men discuss caste-certificate issues, scholarship access for ST/OBC children and, occasionally, politics; he feels pride when the chief minister's Kuruba background is mentioned, though he is sceptical that it has brought tangible benefit to families like his. His wife is also Kuruba, from a village near Yelandur; the marriage was arranged by their parents twenty-three years ago and cost his father a debt that took years to clear. He is a believer but not devout: they keep a picture of Hanuman and a calendar image of Male Mahadeshwara at home, his wife lights a lamp most evenings, and once a year they try to visit the MM Hills temple, a journey that mixes pilgrimage and picnic. He fasts on Ayudha Puja, the one festival he holds to strictly, and joins the Kollegal Dasara procession as a spectator, though the grand Mysuru celebration feels like another world. Socially, he moves mostly among other auto drivers, a mixed group of Kuruba, Vokkaliga, SC and Muslim men; caste matters in marriage and politics, less so at the stand. He resents the Vokkaliga domination of local contracts and taluk offices but does not dwell on it. His closest friends are two other drivers and a mechanic who gives him credit on parts; they drink tea together at the stand, discuss fares, crops, children's marks and the state of the roads, a daily solidarity that sustains him.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Mahesh votes in every election, though he says the results rarely change his life. The taluk panchayat is a distant body; he has never attended a meeting and does not know his member's name. The RTO office he knows too well: auto permits, insurance renewals and the bribes one pays to avoid being fined for a cracked mirror or an expired pollution certificate. He drew a Below Poverty Line card years ago, now reclassified under some new survey he does not fully understand; his family gets the PDS rice and Anna Bhagya ragi, though the ration-shop keeper is often rude and weighs short. He has never tried for MGNREGA work—too many days needed on the farm or the stand—but his wife's brother in a nearby village says it offers a fallback when nothing else does. The government hospital saved his mother's life, the school is free, but every other interaction feels like a battle: forms, certificates, queues, officers who assume he is lying or ignorant. He has heard of the Aspirational District label for Chamarajanagara, though he does not know what it means in practice, and he doubts anyone in Bengaluru thinks much about Kollegal's roads or water or the fact that every auto driver here is one breakdown away from ruin.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Mahesh is proud of his work ethic, his daughter's marks and the fact that he has kept the family fed and housed without begging anyone, but he is haunted by a fear that it is not enough and never will be. He worries most about his daughter's CET exam and the nursing-college fees he does not have; if she fails to get a seat or drops out, he will feel he has failed her. He worries about his eldest son's aimlessness and the temptation of Bengaluru, where he might earn more but also fall into bad company or waste his youth in a factory with no future. He worries about the auto's engine, which makes a new noise, and about the loan instalment due next week. He is angry, quietly, at a system that taxes his fuel, fines his vehicle, ignores his crop loss and offers his children schools with no teachers, then asks what more he wants. He blames no one in particular—not the government, not the rich, not fate—but he feels cheated by a promise that hard work leads somewhere when for him it has led only to the same stand, the same three acres and the same grinding calculations every month. He is proud of his community's recent political prominence, but he does not see it in his life: no road has been paved, no hospital expanded, no auto union given voice. What he wants is simple: his daughter in a nursing uniform, his youngest son in a decent trade, his wife free from other people's kitchens, and himself still able to drive and farm until they no longer need him. He does not expect it to happen, but he will break himself trying, because surrender is not in him.

personas.name: Farida
personas.definition: Farida is a composite portrait of a dal mill floor worker in Kalaburagi city, the heart of India's largest pigeon-pea milling district. She represents the experiences of Muslim women in the urban working class of this former Hyderabad State territory, navigating precarious daily-wage industrial work, multilingual schooling choices, and the promise and gaps of Article 371(J) special-status provisions.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Farida works on the sorting line at a medium-sized tur dal mill near the APMC yard on the city's southern edge, one of dozens that process pigeon pea brought in from across north Karnataka and Maharashtra. Her shift runs from seven in the morning until four or five in the afternoon, depending on the day's truck arrivals. She earns around three hundred rupees for a full day, paid weekly in cash, with no written contract or provident fund. The work is loud, dusty, and monotonous—standing for hours picking stones and split grains from the conveyor—but it is closer to home than the garment factories some women travel to in Kalaburagi's industrial area. During the June-to-October lean season when fewer trucks arrive, her days drop to three or four a week, and the household stretches its budget thin. Her husband drives an auto-rickshaw on a daily-hire basis, bringing in another two to three hundred rupees on a decent day, more during wedding season, less during the summer heat when passengers are few.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Farida lives with her husband, her mother-in-law, and her three children—two daughters aged thirteen and nine, and a son aged six—in a rented two-room house in one of the old mohallas within walking distance of the Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah. Her husband's younger brother, unmarried, shares the household and contributes irregularly from his work as a painter. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties, manages the cooking and watches the youngest child when both parents are out; her arthritis has worsened in the last two years, and clinic visits add to the month's expenses. Farida was married at seventeen, shortly after failing her second-year PUC exams; her own schooling, all in Urdu medium, ended there. The older daughter studies in Class 8 at a government Urdu-medium school nearby, but the family is weighing whether to shift her to Kannada medium for high school, hoping it will improve her job prospects under the 371(J) local recruitment quota. The younger daughter and son attend the same school. Farida handles the daily purchases, the children's homework follow-up in the evenings, and the endless juggling of rent, school fees, clinic costs, and the ration-card shopping that keeps the household running.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Farida completed her schooling up to second-year PUC in Urdu medium at a government college in Kalaburagi, but she did not pass the exams and did not return for a second attempt; marriage came soon after. Her older daughter, thirteen, is in Class 8 at a nearby government Urdu-medium school and is a steady student, but the family worries that Urdu medium will limit her later—government jobs under Article 371(J) require Kannada proficiency, and many entrance exams are in Kannada or English. They are considering moving her to a Kannada-medium government high school next year, though she will struggle at first. The nine-year-old daughter and six-year-old son study at the same Urdu school; the boy is just settling in, and his grandmother walks him there each morning. School fees are minimal, but books, uniforms, and the small payments for exam sheets and school functions add up to fifteen hundred or two thousand rupees a term. Farida dreams that at least one of her daughters will finish degree college and sit for a government job exam, taking advantage of the 371(J) reservation that people talk about constantly but which remains a distant abstraction—no one in her immediate circle has yet landed such a job. Tuition classes cost extra, and for now the children study at home with her husband's help in the evenings.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Farida's own health has held up, though the mill dust sometimes triggers a persistent cough and her knees ache from the long standing shifts. She delivered all three children at the government Kalaburagi Institute of Medical Sciences hospital, and the youngest was born under the state's Vajpayee Arogyashree insurance, which covered the costs. Her mother-in-law's arthritis is managed with tablets from a nearby private clinic—government hospital queues are too long for an older woman to endure—and those consultations cost three or four hundred rupees each visit. The household is enrolled under Ayushman Bharat, but Farida is not entirely sure which services it covers and has not needed to use it for a major illness yet. Her children have received their childhood vaccinations at the urban health centre, though the last round for the youngest was delayed by several months because the ANM was transferred and the new one took time to restart the records. Farida worries about her older daughter's health as she approaches adolescence—about ensuring she is well-nourished and not overburdened with housework, a concern her mother-in-law dismisses as modern fussiness. The family buys subsidised ration rice and some staples, but vegetables and milk stretch the budget, especially in lean work months.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Farida's family has lived in Kalaburagi for generations; her husband's grandfather migrated from a village in Bidar district decades ago, and the family is rooted in one of the city's older Muslim mohallas near the Dargah. The Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah is the heart of the community's spiritual and social life: Farida and her mother-in-law visit for Friday prayers and during the annual urs, when the neighbourhood fills with pilgrims and the streets are hung with lights. Her children know the Dargah as a place of blessing and also as a landmark—everyone directs visitors by it. The mohalla is densely Muslim, Urdu and Dakhni widely spoken, and Kannada mixed in; her children move fluidly between all three. The family's social network is tightly local—cousins, former schoolmates of Farida's, her husband's auto-driver friends—and disputes are often sorted by a respected elder or the neighbourhood mosque's imam rather than the police. Caste is less openly discussed here than in rural settings, but Farida is aware of the fine gradations within the Muslim community, the older weaving families versus the newer arrivals, though it rarely affects daily dealings. Eid, Muharram, and Milad-un-Nabi shape the household calendar. Farida feels the pull of Hyderabad—relatives live there, Dakhni Urdu is familiar, Telugu is understood—but Kalaburagi is unambiguously home.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Farida's household receives subsidised ration under the state's Anna Bhagya scheme—rice, some wheat, and occasionally dal and oil from the fair-price shop two streets away; the BPL card is essential and jealously guarded. Her mother-in-law has a small state widow's pension that arrives irregularly into a post-office account, and collecting it means a half-day's wait every other month. Farida has heard much talk about Article 371(J) and the jobs and college seats it reserves for locals, and she is determined that her older daughter should benefit, but she does not yet understand the domicile-certificate process or what exactly the quota percentages mean—information circulates mostly by rumour and from the occasional awareness poster at the school. The household has an Ayushman card, though Farida has not tested its utility. Farida does not follow state politics closely, but she knows Mallikarjun Kharge's name and that he held Kalaburagi for decades before losing, a loss people still discuss with surprise.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Farida worries most about money—whether the dal mill will have enough work next month, whether her husband's auto will need a costly repair, whether they can keep all three children in school without pulling the older girl out to help at home or marry her early as her mother-in-law sometimes hints. She is proud that her daughter is studying and determined that she will not repeat Farida's own truncated education; the idea of a government job for her daughter, stable and pensioned, is a cherished but fragile hope. She resents that Urdu-medium schooling, which felt natural and right, now seems like a disadvantage, a barrier her daughter must overcome by switching languages mid-stream. Farida feels the weight of being from Kalyana Karnataka, a label that in her view comes with the sting of being called "backward" by the rest of the state, even as the government's 371(J) promises have not visibly improved her neighbourhood—roads are potholed, the anganwadi is cramped, the secondary school her daughter may attend is overcrowded. She blames no single person but rather a vague, long-accumulated neglect that everyone around her takes for granted. She is wary of the September 17th "Liberation Day" rhetoric; older relatives remember it differently, and the term "liberation" sits uneasily when her own community's history here is deep and unbroken. What she wants is straightforward: steady work, her children educated and secure, and a household that does not lurch from one expense to the next.
