personas.name: Parvati
personas.definition: Parvati is a composite portrait of a Scheduled Caste woman in Yadgir district, navigating the daily pressures of wage labour, water scarcity and her children's schooling in Karnataka's lowest-literacy district. She embodies the lived realities of the region's Article 371(J) promise alongside persistent poverty, drought and seasonal migration.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Parvati wakes before dawn to fetch water from the hand-pump two lanes away, filling three brass pots before the queue lengthens. She works as a domestic helper in three households in Surpur town, sweeping, washing vessels and clothes, earning around four thousand rupees a month. During the cotton-picking and tur-harvest seasons she joins gangs of labourers on surrounding farms, earning a daily wage of two hundred and fifty to three hundred rupees when work is available. Her husband drives an auto-rickshaw on the Surpur-Yadgir route but income is irregular, especially in the summer months when diesel costs rise and passengers are fewer. The household survives on her combined earnings, his occasional fares, MGNREGA work when the gram panchayat sanctions it, and the ten kilos of subsidised rice they collect under Anna Bhagya each month. Parvati budgets every rupee: milk for the children, vegetables twice a week, kerosene for the stove, mobile recharge to stay in touch with her sister who migrated to Hyderabad years ago. Drought years mean fewer farm-labour days and deeper debt to the town's small moneylender, whose interest she pays monthly without touching the principal.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Parvati lives with her husband, her mother-in-law, her thirteen-year-old daughter Kaveri and ten-year-old son Raju in a two-room house on the edge of Surpur town. Her husband's younger brother left for construction work in Bengaluru five years ago and sends money irregularly. Her mother-in-law, now frail and partially blind, mostly stays home minding the house and preparing the afternoon meal of jowar rotti and chutney. Parvati was married at sixteen, soon after she stopped attending school in Class Seven; her own schooling ended when her parents could not afford the bus fare to the high school in the next village. She hopes her daughter will finish at least SSLC. Kaveri now studies in Class Eight at the government high school in Surpur town, travelling by the morning KKRTC bus under the Shakti scheme, which costs the family nothing. Raju attends the Urdu-medium primary school near their lane. Parvati's days are shaped by the double burden of paid work and all household tasks: cooking, washing, fetching water, and caring for her mother-in-law. Her husband helps occasionally but sees domestic work as her domain. Gender roles are firmly set and Parvati negotiates them quietly, knowing that open argument brings trouble.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Parvati studied in the village government Kannada school until Class Seven, learning to read and write but leaving before she could appear for the high school entrance. She still regrets not finishing, feeling the gap every time she needs to read a government notice or help Kaveri with homework. Kaveri now attends the government girls' high school in Surpur town, a four-kilometre ride on the KKRTC bus each morning under the Shakti free-travel scheme, which removed the single biggest expense that would have forced Parvati to pull her daughter out. The school charges no fees under the Right to Education Act but there are hidden costs: notebooks, pens, the annual thirty-rupee exam fee, the grey uniform skirt and white blouse that must be bought new each year as Kaveri grows. Raju studies at the local Urdu-medium school because it is closer and several neighbours' children go there; Parvati worries he will struggle later if he needs to switch to Kannada-medium high school. She dreams that Kaveri will pass SSLC, perhaps even study further and find a government job under the Article 371(J) reservation, though she does not fully understand how the system works. The school headmistress once mentioned scholarships for SC students and Parvati means to ask again, but the paperwork intimidates her and she has no time to chase it during the day.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Parvati's own health is worn down by years of hard labour and poor nutrition. She suffers from chronic joint pain in her knees and lower back, likely worsened by carrying heavy water pots and bending over cotton rows, but she has never taken a full day's rest or consulted a doctor about it. When pain flares she buys a strip of paracetamol from the shop near the bus stand. Her mother-in-law's eyesight has dimmed with age and untreated cataracts; the family was told at the Primary Health Centre that free surgery is available at the district hospital in Yadgir town under a government scheme, but arranging the trip, the escort and the days off work has proven impossible so far. Kaveri and Raju have been given routine vaccinations and deworming tablets at school. Parvati worries about the well water and hand-pump water in Surpur, which sometimes tastes bitter and leaves a white stain on vessels; she has heard talk of fluoride in the groundwater and seen a few older people in the area with bent backs and stained teeth, though no official has come to test their water or explain the risk. The 108 ambulance service is known and once took a neighbour's child to Yadgir during a fever emergency, but Parvati prays she will never need it. She relies on the anganwadi for basic advice and the government hospital in Surpur for fevers and minor complaints, knowing that anything serious means a costly trip to Kalaburagi or Raichur.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Parvati belongs to the Madiga community, one of the region's largest Scheduled Caste groups, whose traditional leather-work occupation her family left behind a generation ago in search of less stigmatised wage labour. The Madiga colony sits at the edge of Surpur town, a cluster of thirty-odd households that share water pumps, a small neighbourhood temple to Yellamma and a collective memory of caste insult and exclusion. Parvati and her family worship Yellamma and also visit the Hanuman temple in the town centre during festivals, though she is conscious of the subtle caste distance maintained by some upper-caste townspeople. Her husband and several neighbours are members of the Ambedkar Sangha, which occasionally organises meetings and community meals on Ambedkar Jayanti. Parvati draws strength from the company of other women in the colony who work similar jobs and share similar struggles; they gather in the evenings to chat, exchange news and sometimes collectively confront an employer who withholds wages. The Shakti bus scheme has given her new mobility and a sense that the government occasionally notices people like her. She speaks Kannada at home and at work, though she understands a little Urdu from her son's schoolmates and the town's Muslim shopkeepers. Religion and caste shape her daily interactions, but she tries to shield her children from the worst of it, hoping education and a government job might give them a different life.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Parvati interacts with the government mainly through ration-card collection at the fair-price shop, where she receives ten kilos of rice and two kilos of sugar each month under Anna Bhagya, and through MGNREGA job cards that her husband holds for both of them. Work under MGNREGA is irregular; the gram panchayat sanctions it in short bursts for road repair or tank desilting, and wages often arrive months late in their bank account. She has heard of Article 371(J) and the special status for Kalyana Karnataka but does not fully understand what it means for her family, beyond a vague promise of local jobs and reservations that educated people might access. The Shakti free-bus scheme is the government benefit she feels most directly: it has kept Kaveri in school by removing the daily travel cost. She has never attended a gram sabha meeting; such spaces feel remote and male-dominated, and her working hours leave no time. Officials and local leaders rarely visit the colony except at election time. When a government health worker came last year to register families for Ayushman Bharat cards, Parvati gave her details but has not received the card yet and does not know whom to ask. The state feels distant, occasionally helpful through schemes like Shakti and Anna Bhagya, but mostly indifferent to daily struggles like water scarcity, wage theft and her mother-in-law's untreated cataracts.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Parvati worries constantly about money: whether the month's earnings will cover rice, vegetables, school costs and the moneylender's interest payment. She worries about water, especially in summer when the hand-pump runs dry by mid-morning and she must walk further to the borewell near the highway. She worries about Raju's future, knowing that boys without education end up as daily labourers or auto-drivers like his father, trapped in the same cycle. Parvati is proud that she has kept both children in school so far, longer than her own parents managed for her, and proud of Kaveri's report card and the teacher's praise. She blames the lack of jobs, the drought and the cost of everything for the hardship her family faces, and she blames caste prejudice for the small humiliations and wage discrimination she encounters. She does not blame herself or her children. She demands water supply in the colony, regular MGNREGA work at fair wages paid on time, and a government that remembers Yadgir district exists. She has heard officials call Yadgir the most backward district in Karnataka and while the label angers her—because it sounds like blame—she also uses it to argue that the government owes her family more. She wants Kaveri to finish school, find a government job and escape the life of domestic and farm labour. She knows the odds are against them but she works every day toward that hope, carrying water, washing dishes, picking cotton, and counting every rupee.

personas.name: Basavaraj
personas.definition: Basavaraj is a composite portrait of a wholesale chilli merchant in Shahapur town, Yadgir district, grounded in the region's real APMC cotton and chilli trade, its Lingayat community presence, and the everyday economic pressures of price volatility and competition. He stands for the small and medium traders who keep the district's agricultural economy moving, balancing family aspiration with the uncertainties of dryland farming markets.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Basavaraj runs a wholesale chilli business from a small godown near the Shahapur APMC yard, where farmers bring their dryland chilli crop during the November-to-March harvest. He buys directly from smallholders in surrounding villages, grades the produce by colour and spice level, and sells in bulk to agents who truck it to Hubli and Belagavi markets. On a good season he clears around fifteen to twenty thousand rupees per month after expenses, but years of poor monsoon or price crashes wipe out his margin. He starts work at dawn when the first farmers arrive, spending the morning inspecting sacks, bargaining, loading trucks, and managing credit given to repeat sellers. The afternoons are quieter—paperwork, phone calls to buyers, chai at the APMC canteen—but the mental arithmetic never stops. Commission agents and transport costs eat into profit, and cash flow is always tight. During the off-season he stocks onion and cotton seed on a smaller scale to keep the godown running. The work is physically easier than farming but the financial stress is constant, and competition from larger traders with better bank connections is growing.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Basavaraj lives with his wife, three children, and his widowed mother in a two-room house on the edge of Shahapur town. His wife manages the household and helps with sorting chilli during peak season, though she is not formally part of the business. Their eldest daughter is in second-year PU at the government composite college in Shahapur; she travels daily by bus and dreams of a government teaching job. Their son is in ninth standard at the Kannada-medium high school nearby, a quieter boy who prefers to stay in the shop rather than study. The youngest daughter is in fifth standard at the same school. Basavaraj's mother, now in her seventies, lives with them and helps with cooking and childcare. His two brothers both left Shahapur years ago—one runs a mobile-repair shop in Kalaburagi city, the other works as a driver in Bengaluru—and they return only for festivals. Decisions about the children's education, dowry savings, and business loans rest mainly with Basavaraj and his wife, and the expectation is that the son will eventually take over the chilli trade.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Basavaraj himself studied up to seventh standard in the Kannada-medium school in his native village before family circumstances forced him to stop and help his father in the fields. He regrets not finishing school and is determined that his children will go further. His daughter attends the government PU college in Shahapur, where the fees are nominal but the costs of private tuition, textbooks, and bus fare add up to several thousand rupees each term. She is a good student and talks about applying for a BEd degree, which Basavaraj supports, though the family worries about the expense of a college in Kalaburagi or Raichur and the difficulty of securing a government teaching post under the 371(J) quota competition. His son is less academically inclined; he passed eighth standard but struggles in English and maths, and Basavaraj suspects he will leave after SSLC to help in the business. The youngest daughter is still in primary school at the nearby government Kannada school, where the midday meal and free textbooks help, but Basavaraj knows that keeping her in school through high school will depend on the family's finances and her own interest. The gap between aspiration and outcome is something he thinks about often.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Basavaraj's own health is generally good, though he has intermittent joint pain from years of lifting heavy sacks and standing on concrete floors. He has not had a full medical check-up in years; when something hurts he takes a painkiller from the medical shop near the APMC. His mother has diabetes and high blood pressure, managed with tablets from the government hospital in Shahapur, where the doctors change frequently and the queues are long. His wife has not been seriously ill recently, but she delivered their youngest daughter at home with a local dai because the government hospital was far and the family could not afford a private facility at the time. The children have had their vaccinations and are generally healthy, though the son had a bout of jaundice two years ago that required a week's rest and some expensive medicines. Basavaraj worries about the cost of any major illness—there is no health insurance, and an emergency would mean borrowing from relatives or a moneylender. The 108 ambulance service is known in town, but it does not always arrive quickly. Drinking water from the municipal tap sometimes smells of chemicals, and people say Yadgir's groundwater has fluoride problems, though Basavaraj does not know the details.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Basavaraj belongs to the Lingayat community, which is large and influential in Shahapur and across Yadgir district. His family visits the local Basaveshwara temple for festivals, and he wears the linga around his neck as a mark of faith. Community ties matter in business—many of his regular chilli suppliers and buyers are Lingayat farmers and traders, and trust and word-of-mouth carry more weight than written contracts. During Basava Jayanti and Shivaratri, the whole town shuts down and processions fill the streets. Basavaraj participates in community functions and contributes to the temple fund when he can, though he is not deeply involved in caste-association politics. He respects the mutts and their leaders but does not have time to follow their public statements closely. His everyday social life revolves around the APMC yard, the tea stall, and occasional visits to relatives in nearby villages. The sense of shared identity and mutual obligation within the Lingayat community provides a safety net of sorts—when cash is short, it is often a community contact who extends a small loan or introduces a new buyer. At the same time, Basavaraj is aware that Yadgir is a poor district with large Muslim and Scheduled Caste populations, and that government schemes and 371(J) benefits are contested across community lines in ways that sometimes surface in local elections.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Basavaraj's main interaction with government is through the APMC, which regulates the market and collects fees, and the Revenue Department for his trade license and tax filings. He has never tried to access a bank loan under any government scheme—interest rates and paperwork feel like barriers—and instead borrows informally when he needs working capital. He has heard of Article 371(J) and KKRDB, mostly in the context of job quotas for local youth, but he has no direct experience of its benefits and doubts that much of the money reaches small traders like him. When the taluk panchayat repaired the road to the APMC two years ago, it was credited to KKRDB funding, but the work was delayed and poorly finished. Basavaraj has no personal contact with any MLA or elected representative; politicians appear during elections and disappear afterward. He is cynical about corruption and believes that government help flows to those with connections. The 108 ambulance, the government hospital, and the PU college are the public services his family actually uses, and all of them are under-resourced. If he had a voice, he would ask for better market infrastructure, transparent price floors for chilli, and reliable electricity for cold storage, but he does not expect anyone to listen.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Basavaraj's greatest worry is the volatility of agricultural prices: a glut of chilli or a sudden drop in demand can destroy his margin and leave him with unsold stock. He is proud that his daughter is doing well in college and hopes she will secure a government job, which would mean financial security the trade cannot guarantee. He resents that Yadgir remains Karnataka's poorest district despite being part of Kalyana Karnataka with supposed special funding—he sees little evidence of that funding in Shahapur's roads, schools, or water supply. He blames a mix of government neglect, corruption, and the district's dependence on erratic rainfall for the persistent backwardness. At the same time, he is proud of the Basavanna legacy and the Lingayat community's historical role in the region, and he dislikes being stereotyped as uneducated or less Kannada by people from southern Karnataka. He worries about his son's lack of interest in schooling and fears the boy will be stuck in the same precarious trade with no safety net. He wants reliable electricity, better roads, fair crop prices, and decent schools close to home—basic things he believes the government should provide but consistently fails to deliver. When talk turns to politics, he is sceptical that any party will truly change Yadgir's fortunes, but he holds on to the hope that his children's generation will have more opportunities than his own.

personas.name: Lakshmi
personas.definition: Lakshmi is a composite portrait of a woman farm labourer living in the tomato-growing belt of Malur taluk in Kolar district, navigating the tension between daily-wage work in nearby fields and the pull of Bengaluru's construction economy barely 50 kilometres away. She embodies the particular squeeze faced by families in Kolar's peri-urban fringe: chronic groundwater depletion undermining local farming, fluoride in the borewell water threatening her children's health, and the promise of Yettinahole treated water still years away while Bengaluru's demands for her labour grow louder each season.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Lakshmi wakes before dawn to the diesel thud of the neighbour's borewell, filling the overhead tank before the power cuts. She walks twenty minutes to a ten-acre tomato plot near Malur where the owner has drip-irrigation from a 400-foot borewell; the yield is good when the rains cooperate, catastrophic when they fail. She works six to eight hours plucking, sorting and loading crates for 300 rupees a day, less during the monsoon when picking slows. Her husband drives an autorickshaw on the Malur-Kolar route, earning 400 to 600 rupees on busy days, far less when diesel prices spike or the rains keep passengers indoors. Together they bring in roughly 18,000 rupees a month in good months, 12,000 in lean ones. The tomato market at Kolar is among Karnataka's largest but famously volatile; she has seen farmers dump unsold crates by the roadside when prices crash below the cost of transport to Bengaluru. Her own wage never rises with bumper harvests and never falls with gluts, a small mercy. She buys vegetables, rice and dal on credit from the village provision store, settling accounts weekly. The economic pressure is a constant hum beneath every decision: can they afford new school shoes this month, or must the children wear the patched ones another term?

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Lakshmi lives with her husband Ravi, her mother-in-law, a twelve-year-old son and a nine-year-old daughter in a two-room house with a tin roof and a small courtyard where they dry chilies and stack firewood. The house sits on a quarter-acre family plot inherited from Ravi's father; his elder brother took the main portion and moved to Bengaluru years ago, sending money home only sporadically. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties and arthritic, cooks, tends the courtyard kitchen garden and watches the children after school. Lakshmi married at nineteen, shortly after her Class 10 exams; her parents arranged the match with Ravi, whose family owned land and seemed secure. The autorickshaw was bought on loan five years ago, still being repaid. Her son studies in the government high school in Malur town, cycling four kilometres each way; her daughter attends the village government primary school. Lakshmi does all the washing, sweeping and evening cooking after returning from the fields, while her husband manages the rickshaw repairs and farm paperwork. Her mother-in-law insists on traditional food for festivals and complains about the cost of everything, a source of low-grade tension. Lakshmi sends her children to tuition classes twice a week in the evening, 500 rupees per child per month, a stretch but non-negotiable in her mind; without tuition, she fears, they will fall behind and repeat the year.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Lakshmi completed SSLC in a government school in her natal village near Srinivaspur, scoring a second class; she did not continue to PUC because her parents needed her to help at home and saw no point in further study for a girl. She wishes now that she had, though she is unsure what difference it would have made. Her son is in Class 7, reasonably steady in Kannada and mathematics but struggling with English and science; the tuition teacher says he needs more practice. Her daughter, in Class 4, is bright and eager, bringing home charts and spellings to recite. The government schools are free, but Lakshmi spends roughly 1,500 rupees per child per year on notebooks, pens, school bags and the compulsory two pairs of uniforms that must be stitched locally because the school's cloth distribution never fits properly. Textbooks come free under Vidyagama but arrive late; supplementary workbooks for tuition cost extra. Mid-day meals are served, a relief that keeps both children in school through lunch. Lakshmi dreams that her son will finish PUC and get a government job, perhaps in the revenue department or as a police constable; for her daughter, she hopes for PUC and perhaps a nursing course or a BEd, something respectable that guarantees a salary.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Lakshmi's children and mother-in-law all have visible dental fluorosis, brown-stained teeth from years of drinking borewell water; the anganwadi worker warned her about it, but there is no piped supply and the fluoride-removal filters cost 4,000 rupees, money they do not have. Her son complains of joint pain some mornings, which terrifies her because she has heard that skeletal fluorosis can cripple people in their twenties. The family buys 20-litre cans of purified water for drinking from a Malur shop, 30 rupees per can, but they still cook and wash with borewell water. Lakshmi herself suffers from anaemia, confirmed at a government health camp last year; the ANM gave her iron tablets, which she takes irregularly because they upset her stomach. Her husband has chronic back pain from years of sitting in the auto, treated with over-the-counter balms. The nearest primary health centre is three kilometres away in Malur; for anything serious, they go to the taluk hospital or, increasingly, to private clinics in Kolar town where a consultation costs 300 rupees but the doctor actually examines you. Her mother-in-law has diabetes, managed with tablets from the PHC and a half-hearted attempt to reduce rice and jaggery. Lakshmi worries most about heatstroke during the summer tomato harvest and the respiratory infections her children get every monsoon. Jal Jeevan Mission tap connections were announced two years ago but have not yet reached her hamlet; the panchayat president says the pipes are ordered, always ordered.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Lakshmi's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, historically landholding cultivators; in Malur taluk they remain the dominant caste, though many, like her household, now survive on fragmented holdings and wage labour rather than tenant farming. Her mother-in-law is devout, observing all the fasts for Varamahalakshmi, Gowri and Ganesha; Lakshmi herself attends the annual jatre at the Someshwara temple in Malur and lights lamps at the household shrine on Fridays. The family visits the Bhoga Nandeeshwara temple near Nandi Hills once a year, a half-day outing by bus. Caste plays out quietly in everyday life: the Scheduled Caste families in the hamlet live on the edge of the settlement, draw water from a separate borewell, and work the same tomato fields as Lakshmi but are rarely invited to Vokkaliga households for life-cycle ceremonies. Lakshmi's husband is active in the village Ganesha mandala during the festival, organizing the procession and collecting subscriptions; Lakshmi helps the women's self-help group, though she has not taken a loan herself. The local Gram Panchayat is dominated by Vokkaliga and Lingayat office-bearers; the current president is a Lingayat from the next village, elected on a Congress ticket last term. Social ties remain dense and face-to-face: her mother-in-law knows everyone's lineage three generations back and monitors marriages, dowries and land sales with keen interest. Reputation matters acutely; even the suspicion that a teenage girl has spoken too freely with boys can stall her marriage prospects.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Lakshmi's family has a ration card, through which they buy subsidized rice and kerosene monthly; the Fair Price Shop in the hamlet is run by a relative of the panchayat president, and stocks run out by mid-month if the allocation is delayed. Her husband has a job card under MGNREGA but has worked under it only once in the past two years, 15 days digging a farm pond, because the autorickshaw brings in more. The anganwadi in the hamlet provides morning snacks for under-sixes, though Lakshmi's children have aged out. Her daughter received vaccines there as a toddler; records were kept in a booklet that has since been lost. The family has Ayushman Bharat cards but has never used them; when her mother-in-law needed cataract surgery two years ago they paid out of pocket at a private hospital in Kolar because the taluk hospital's waiting list was six months. She rides the Shakti-scheme buses twice a month to Kolar to visit her sister, a benefit she values though she still walks to the farm daily to save time. Her husband has been to the taluk office in Malur twice in the past year for land-record corrections on Bhoomi; the process took four visits and a 500-rupee payment to a document-writer outside the building. She sees government as distant, procedurally opaque and responsive mainly to those with connections; she does not expect it to solve the fluoride crisis, only perhaps to subsidize a filter someday.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Lakshmi worries most about water: the borewell in their courtyard that has dropped 50 feet in a decade, the fluoride staining her children's teeth, and the dependence on rains that now arrive late or not at all. She speaks bitterly of Yettinahole, promised years ago to refill Kolar's tanks with treated Netravathi water, still unfinished while Bengaluru, she hears, gets piped Cauvery water on schedule. Her pride lies in keeping her children clean, fed and in school despite everything, and in the small courtyard garden her mother-in-law tends: ridge gourd, curry leaves and a papaya tree. She blames the government for the broken Yettinahole promise, the middlemen and commission agents for the tomato-price crashes, and the previous generation's failure to organize cooperative marketing. She demands piped fluoride-free water, stable minimum prices for tomatoes and reliable electricity for borewells, though she doubts any of it will arrive in her lifetime. What angers her most is the sense that Kolar supplies Bengaluru with vegetables, labour and land for the airport corridor and solar parks, while Bengaluru's politicians promise water and jobs that never materialize. When outsiders ask, she describes Malur as 'just 50 kilometres from Bengaluru but a generation behind in everything that matters.'

personas.name: Venkatesh
personas.definition: Venkatesh is a composite portrait of a tomato commission agent in his late thirties working in Bangarpet market, Kolar district, one of Karnataka's major tomato trading centres. He navigates the daily volatility of farm-gate prices, coordinates lorry loads to Bengaluru and beyond, and balances brokerage income against the pressures of advancing credit to farmers and absorbing crop-glut losses.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Venkatesh begins his day before dawn at the Bangarpet tomato market yard, where lorries arrive from surrounding villages—Srinivaspur, Malur, and even from across the Andhra border. He brokers deals between growers and wholesale buyers, charging a 7-8 per cent commission on each transaction. During the peak harvest months from December to March, he can handle fifteen to twenty tonnes a day; in the lean season, turnover falls to a trickle and his income shrinks. The work is entirely cash-based and recorded in dog-eared ledgers. Price swings are brutal: a crate fetching ₹600 one week may crash to ₹80 the next, wiping out both the farmer's margin and his own advance. He owns no land himself but rents a small godown near the yard and employs two daily-wage loaders. His phone never stops ringing—buyers in Bengaluru, transporters on the highway, farmers asking for credit. By mid-morning the floor is slick with crushed tomatoes; by noon the trade is done and he retreats to settle accounts. Economic pressure is constant: defaults, delayed payments from city wholesalers, diesel-price hikes and the ever-present risk that a glut will leave him holding worthless stock.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Venkatesh lives with his wife Vasantha, their two sons aged fourteen and ten, and his widowed mother in a modest tiled house on the edge of Bangarpet town. Vasantha manages the household and a small kitchen garden; she once worked as a school helper but left the job after their younger son was born. His elder son studies in ninth standard at the government high school in town; the younger is in fifth. Venkatesh's father, a small mango grower near Srinivaspur, died eight years ago, and the family orchard—three acres—was split between Venkatesh and his two brothers. He sold his share to fund the initial capital for the commission business. His mother helps with cooking and watches the boys when Vasantha visits her parents in Malur. Gender roles remain traditional: Vasantha handles all domestic work, while Venkatesh makes financial decisions and maintains external business relationships. The marriage was arranged within the Vokkaliga community eighteen years ago. Extended family gatherings happen at festival times—Ugadi, Deepavali—and at weddings, though the demands of the market mean he often arrives late or leaves early.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Venkatesh himself studied up to second PUC in Bangarpet before his father called him home to help with mango harvests; he never enrolled in college, a fact he quietly regrets. Both his sons attend the government Kannada-medium high school in town. Fees are minimal, but textbooks, uniforms, and the elder boy's demand for a smartphone for online homework add up. The school is a fifteen-minute walk from home, crowded but functional; the headmaster is strict and SSLC results have been improving. Venkatesh hopes his elder son will finish PUC and get into a BCom course in Kolar or even Bengaluru, something he frames as 'a steady job path, not this daily tension.' The boy is a decent student, ranking in the top third of his class, but Venkatesh worries about the cost of private coaching if he aims for competitive exams. The younger son is more playful, less studious. Vasantha insists both boys will finish schooling no matter what; she has seen too many families pull children out for work. The family spends around ₹8,000 a year on education, counting everything. Venkatesh also quietly funds the school fees of a cousin's daughter in Srinivaspur whose father is a struggling dryland farmer.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Venkatesh's mother has skeletal fluorosis—bowed legs, joint pain—from decades of drinking borewell water in Srinivaspur; she now relies on bottled water, but the damage is done. The family buys twenty-litre cans for drinking, though cooking and washing still use the municipal tap supply, which itself is borewell-fed and high in fluoride. Venkatesh himself suffers from chronic acidity and occasional chest pain, which he attributes to stress and the habit of skipping breakfast during peak market hours. He visited the government hospital in Kolar town twice last year for ECG tests; the doctor advised weight loss and less tension—easier said than done. Vasantha and the boys are generally healthy, though both children have dental mottling, an early sign of fluorosis. Healthcare for minor illnesses means the nearby private clinic; anything serious requires a trip to R.L. Jalappa Hospital in Tamaka or even Bengaluru. Venkatesh has no health insurance; a heart procedure or major surgery would mean selling assets or borrowing. He smokes five or six beedis a day—a habit he knows he should quit—and drinks occasionally with fellow traders. The fear of a sudden illness that stops him working, leaving the family without income, haunts him more than the market's daily ups and downs.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Venkatesh is Vokkaliga, the dominant landowning community in Kolar, though his family's small mango plot hardly makes them big farmers. Caste identity matters in business—most of his trusted contacts in the tomato trade are also Vokkaliga—and in marriage alliances. Social ties are dense: the weekly trade brings him into contact with hundreds of farmers, transporters and buyers, and reciprocal favours oil every transaction. He is a member of the Bangarpet Tomato Merchants' Association, which lobbies for better yard facilities and helps settle disputes. Religious life centres on the Someshwara temple in town; Venkatesh makes offerings during Shivaratri and before the start of the harvest season. His mother is more devout, visiting the temple weekly and observing fasts. The family also attends the annual jatre at Avani, an hour away. Venkatesh has heard of the Siddaganga Mutt's free hostels and wishes something similar existed closer by for poorer farmers' children. He contributes modestly to community functions—temple repairs, school prize days—and lends money interest-free within his extended family circle. Trust and reputation are everything in his trade; a broken promise can close doors across the district.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Venkatesh's direct dealings with government are limited but recurring. He has a GST registration for the commission business, which means monthly filings he outsources to a local accountant for ₹1,500 a year. The market yard itself is run by the APMC, and he has lobbied—unsuccessfully so far—for better drainage and a cold-storage facility to buffer price crashes. His wife uses the Shakti bus pass for trips to Malur and Kolar, saving the family a couple of hundred rupees a month. The KC-Valley treated-wastewater scheme has refilled some tanks near Bangarpet, bringing more tomato acreage under reliable irrigation—good for his trade, though farmers grumble about the water quality and the scheme's upkeep. Venkatesh himself has no land to benefit directly. He distrusts most politicians, viewing them as responsive only during election season, but respects local leaders who get roads repaired or transformers fixed. The Yettinahole project is a distant promise he has heard about for years; he will believe it when water actually flows. His main expectation from government is simpler: stable electricity, passable roads for lorries, and fair weighbridge practices at checkposts.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Venkatesh is proud of his ability to read the market—when to hold, when to push a deal—and of keeping his sons in school despite the tomato trade's volatility. He worries most about a sudden price collapse that leaves him unable to recover advances given to farmers, a situation that has happened twice in the past five years and cost him a lakh each time. He blames the absence of proper cold storage and processing units for the worst of the price swings, and wishes government or private investors would build them. He resents big wholesale traders in Bengaluru who delay payments and squeeze his margins, but sees no alternative—that is where the demand is. Venkatesh also worries privately about his heart, his mother's worsening mobility, and the fluoride in every glass of water his children drink. He demands better: a functional APMC cold chain, insurance schemes that actually cover small traders, reliable treated water or a piped Cauvery supply to replace the failing borewells, and schools with enough teachers so his sons do not need expensive private tuition. What keeps him going is the hope that the next season will be kinder, and the belief that education will lift his sons out of the daily price lottery that defines his own life.

personas.name: Rajesh
personas.definition: Rajesh is a composite portrait of a grape farmer and borewell contractor in Nandi taluk, Chikkaballapur district, navigating the twin pressures of groundwater depletion and the district's proximity to Bengaluru. He embodies the resilience and economic calculation of families in the bayalu seeme who farm water-intensive crops while selling drilling services to their neighbours, caught between horticultural ambition and hydrological reality.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Rajesh owns four acres of grape vines near Nandi town, mostly Bangalore Blue variety destined for the Bengaluru wholesale markets and a small patch of wine grapes contracted to a winery near Doddaballapur. His day begins at five-thirty with drip-irrigation checks; by eight he is usually out on a borewell-drilling job, operating a truck-mounted rig he bought on loan three years ago. Drilling work has become his main income as neighbours chase deeper water tables, some borewells now reaching four hundred feet with no guarantee of yield. He charges by the foot and by the hour, earning between twelve and twenty thousand rupees per borewell depending on geology and depth. Grape farming is riskier: a good harvest in March-April can net him eighty thousand from his four acres, but late rains or a price crash at the Chikkaballapur market can halve that. His wife keeps accounts and negotiates with the commission agents. The drilling rig needs diesel, spare bits and a helper's daily wage; the vines need fertiliser, pesticides and casual labour for pruning and harvest. By evening he is back checking moisture levels, worried that his own borewells are starting to yield less each season.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Rajesh lives in a pucca house on the edge of Nandi town with his wife, their two sons aged fourteen and ten, and his widowed mother. His wife manages the household budget, the grape accounts and the kitchen garden; she also works harvest season in the vines alongside hired labourers. His mother looks after the younger boy when school is out and cooks the midday meal. His elder son finished eighth standard last year at the government high school in Nandi and now travels by KSRTC bus to a private PU college in Chikkaballapur town, a daily commute that costs two hundred rupees a week under the Shakti scheme's free-ride provision. Rajesh had hoped the boy would help more with the drilling work during weekends, but his wife insists he focus on studies and aim for an engineering seat in Bengaluru. The younger son is in fifth standard at the same government school. Gender roles in the household are conventional: his wife's labour in the fields is essential but unpaid in cash terms, and decisions about land, the rig and major purchases rest with Rajesh, though she vetoes anything that threatens school fees.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Rajesh studied up to tenth standard at the government high school in Nandi, passing his SSLC on the second attempt, then worked on his father's land. His wife completed seventh standard before marriage. Both are determined that their sons will study further. The elder boy's PU college fees are seven thousand rupees per term plus textbooks and exam fees, manageable so far but a stretch if the grape price crashes. The school provides midday meals and the bus ride is free under Shakti, cutting daily costs. Rajesh dreams of an engineering seat for his elder son, ideally through CET quota to avoid capitation fees, knowing that a degree could mean a Bengaluru IT job and escape from the borewell lottery. The younger boy is doing well in Kannada medium; Rajesh sometimes wonders whether English medium would have been better but cannot afford the private school fees others pay. He worries that if grape income falls or if he has a bad drilling season, keeping the elder boy in college will mean taking another loan.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Rajesh's family draws water from a borewell on their plot, and like most in Nandi taluk they know the water is high in fluoride. His mother has dental fluorosis, brown-stained teeth that the anganwadi worker says comes from decades of the same water. His younger son had white patches on his teeth noticed during a school dental camp two years ago; the visiting doctor advised reverse-osmosis filtration or piped supply, neither of which Rajesh has managed yet. Jal Jeevan Mission taps were promised but not yet installed in their ward in 2025. The family goes to the government primary health centre in Nandi for fever and minor injuries; for anything serious they travel to Chikkaballapur district hospital or, if they can afford it, a private clinic in Chikkaballapur town. His wife had both sons delivered at the government taluk hospital with JSY assistance. Rajesh himself has chronic back pain from years of manual rig work and sometimes takes painkillers bought from the town pharmacy. Heat exhaustion is a risk in summer drilling work. He worries most about an accident with the rig or a snakebite in the fields, knowing ambulance response from Nandi is slow.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Rajesh's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, the dominant landowning group in this part of Chikkaballapur. They are Hindu, observing festivals like Ugadi, Varamahalakshmi and Deepavali, and his mother insists on visiting the Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple at the foot of Nandi Hills at least once a year. Rajesh sometimes joins the annual jatre at the hilltop Yoga Nandeeshwara shrine when drilling work permits. Community ties matter for labour-sharing during harvest and for contracts: several of his drilling customers are Vokkaliga neighbours or relatives who trust him to deliver an honest depth report even when the borewell fails. Caste plays out in unspoken ways in land ownership and access to credit; the SC families in Nandi's outlying hamlets are more likely to work as wage labourers than own rigs or vines. Rajesh is not deeply religious but respects his mother's daily puja routine and the annual household festivals. The local Hanuman temple is a gathering point for men in the evening. He has heard of Siddaganga Mutt's free hostels but his family has not needed that help so far.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He has not seen Yettinahole water yet and does not expect it soon, but Shakti has saved his family real money on his son's college commute. He interacted with the gram panchayat to get his house connected to the rural electrification line and again when the MGNREGA work-site near his plot needed coordination. He is sceptical of officials: the promised Jal Jeevan Mission tap has not arrived, and the soil-testing camp announced for grape farmers last year never materialised. His borewell rig is licensed and he pays motor-vehicle tax, but drilling itself is unregulated and he knows some contractors give false depth reports to get paid faster. He has taken crop loans from the cooperative bank and once queued for drought-relief compensation after a failed monsoon. The Chikkaballapur RTO, taluk office and mandi are the government touchpoints he knows best. He respects local leaders who can deliver a road or a transformer but dismisses most taluk politics as family theatre.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Rajesh is proud of coaxing a living from dry land through hard work, drip irrigation and the calculated risk of his drilling business. He worries most about water: that his own borewells are yielding less, that clients blame him when new borewells fail, and that the whole grape belt may become unviable if the water table keeps falling. He resents that Chikkaballapur is so close to Bengaluru's wealth and Kempegowda Airport's land boom, yet his taluk still lacks assured piped water and his children must commute for decent schooling. He blames successive governments for promising Yettinahole and delivering little, though he does not trust the Malnad objectors either. Grape price crashes make him angry at commission agents and the unregulated market; he wants a minimum support price or cooperative processing to stabilise income. He is proud his elder son is in college and determined the boy will not inherit the borewell-dependence trap. He dislikes being lumped with "backward interior Karnataka" when Nandi is an hour from the airport, yet he knows the airport corridor's land speculators are not his friends. He wants his sons educated, his water secure and recognition that bayalu seeme farmers feed Bengaluru while getting little back.

personas.name: Nandini
personas.definition: Nandini is a composite portrait of a woman from a Vokkaliga farming family in Devanahalli taluk, Bengaluru North district (formerly Bengaluru Rural), who operates a small daily milk collection and distribution business alongside managing her household's dairy herd. She represents the experience of women in the district's villages navigating the rapid transformation of the peri-urban belt around Kempegowda International Airport, balancing agrarian livelihoods with new opportunities and pressures from industrial and aerospace-park expansion.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Nandini begins her day at four in the morning, milking the family's eight crossbred cows and two buffaloes before loading the milk cans onto her Activa scooter. By six she has collected milk from twelve neighbouring households in her village, some of them kin, and delivers the combined morning run to the Nandini dairy chilling centre three kilometres away on the Devanahalli-Bangalore highway. She returns home to prepare breakfast, feed the calves, and clean the cattle shed before her older son leaves for school. In the afternoon she repeats a smaller evening collection round. Her husband manages their five-acre holding—hybrid ragi, a coconut grove, and fodder—and works intermittent contract labour at a nearby logistics warehouse serving the airport. The dairy business brings in roughly eight thousand rupees a month after deductions; the warehouse wage is irregular but sometimes adds another six thousand. Land values have risen sharply as aerospace firms and real-estate developers acquire plots, but selling would leave them without a livelihood, so they hold on. Diesel, cattle-feed prices, and veterinary costs have all climbed; the milk price the dairy pays has not kept pace.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Nandini lives in a joint household with her husband, their two sons (aged thirteen and nine), her mother-in-law, and her husband's unmarried younger brother. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties, used to manage the cattle but arthritis has made milking painful, so Nandini took over the route seven years ago. Her husband's brother works night shifts at the airport as a baggage handler and sleeps during the day. Nandini's own parents farm in a village near Hoskote; she visits them every few months. Her marriage was arranged when she was twenty-one, after she finished second PUC. Household decisions—what to plant, whether to sell a calf, how much to spend on her sons' tuition—are made jointly with her husband, though her mother-in-law's voice still carries weight on domestic matters. Cooking, cleaning, and helping the boys with homework fall to Nandini. Her younger son has mild asthma; she watches his breathing carefully during the winter haze. The family speaks Kannada at home; her sons switch to English phrases picked up at school and from television.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Nandini studied in the government Kannada-medium school in her natal village through tenth standard, then attended a government junior college in town for PUC, travelling by KSRTC bus. She did well enough in her second PUC exams to consider a BCom degree, but her parents could not afford hostel fees in Bangalore, and marriage came soon after. Her older son attends a private English-medium school in Devanahalli town; the fees are twelve thousand rupees a year, plus books, uniform, and transport. Her younger son is in the same school. She chose it because the village government school has frequent teacher vacancies and she worries the boys will not learn enough English to compete for jobs. The school runs a van; she pays fifteen hundred rupees per child per term. She wants both sons to finish degree college, ideally engineering, so they will not depend on farming or manual labour. Tuition classes cost another two thousand rupees a month for the older boy. The family has taken a small loan from a relative to cover this year's fees. She herself wishes she had continued to degree level; she feels the lack when helping with homework.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: The family depends on the government primary health centre in the village for vaccinations, fever, and minor injuries; the ANM visits monthly. For anything serious they go to the taluk hospital in Devanahalli town, a thirty-minute bus ride, or to a private clinic there if they can afford it. Nandini's younger son's asthma is managed with an inhaler prescribed by a private doctor; the monthly cost of the inhaler and check-ups runs to eight hundred rupees. Her mother-in-law's arthritis has worsened; government hospital doctors advised physiotherapy, but the nearest centre is in Bangalore and they cannot afford repeated trips. Nandini herself had an ovarian cyst diagnosed two years ago at a free health camp; surgery at the district hospital was free under Ayushman Bharat but follow-up was poor and she still has intermittent pain. She worries about her husband's occasional chest pain—he smokes beedis—but he refuses to see a doctor. The village borewell water has high nitrate levels according to a Jal Jeevan Mission test; they boil and filter drinking water. Truck traffic and dust from road-widening projects aggravate her son's asthma. She keeps tulsi and neem in the yard and uses home remedies for colds.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Nandini's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, which is numerically strong and socially dominant in the village. Caste ties shape whom they lend to, borrow from, and do business with; most of her milk-collection clients are Vokkaliga households. The village has a small Anjaneya temple where she lights a lamp on Saturdays, and a annual jatra in Chaitra for the gramadevata that draws everyone regardless of caste. Her mother-in-law observes all major festivals—Ugadi, Varamahalakshmi, Deepavali—and Nandini manages the cooking and preparations. The family has loose ties to the Adichunchanagiri Mutt in Nagamangala; they attended a mass-marriage event there once, years ago. Village social life revolves around family functions, the temple, and self-help-group meetings. Nandini joined a women's SHG four years ago; it meets monthly in the anganwadi and handles small savings and loans. She borrowed twenty thousand rupees from the group to repair the cattle shed. The SHG also organises health camps and government-scheme information sessions. Village elders, mostly older Vokkaliga men, still settle land and water disputes informally.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Nandini's household receives subsidised rice and ragi under Anna Bhagya from the fair-price shop in the village; her Ayushman Bharat card covered her surgery. She has used the Shakti free-bus scheme occasionally to visit the district hospital or her parents, saving fifty or sixty rupees each trip, though the milk route still requires her scooter. Her husband gets some MGNREGA work during the monsoon when warehouse shifts dry up, but the job cards often show phantom muster rolls and payments are delayed. The gram panchayat has not held elections in years; the same unofficial headman, a retired teacher, liaises with the taluk office. She has never met the tahsildar or MLA. A Jal Jeevan Mission tap-connection promise from two years ago has not materialised; the panchayat says funds were diverted. The dairy payments come through her bank account; she opened it under a financial-inclusion drive and now uses it for SHG transactions. Land records are online under Bhoomi, but when a neighbour's boundary was disputed the tahsildar's office demanded a bribe she could not afford. She does not follow state politics closely but knows Siddaramaiah is chief minister and that the government has promised the five guarantees.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Nandini is proud of her village's farming heritage and her family's ability to keep the dairy herd going despite rising costs and shrinking margins. She worries constantly about money—school fees, cattle feed, medical bills—and whether the land will stay in the family or be sold to a developer if her sons pursue city jobs and lose interest in farming. The airport and the aerospace park have brought jobs, but most go to outsiders with English and technical skills; local youth get only contract labour or security posts. She resents that milk prices have stagnated while everything else has become more expensive, and that the Nandini dairy's payments are sometimes delayed without explanation. She blames middlemen and government neglect of farmers, though she is grateful for Ayushman Bharat. Her greatest hope is that her sons will study well, get stable salaried jobs, and not have to depend on the weather or the mercy of a chilling centre. She fears her younger son's asthma will worsen with the air quality, and that her husband's occasional drinking and smoking will lead to serious illness they cannot afford to treat. She wishes she had more say in village decisions and that the gram panchayat were more accountable.

personas.name: Kiran
personas.definition: Kiran is a composite portrait of a thirty-four-year-old Vokkaliga dairy farmer and milk-route operator living in a village near Doddaballapura taluk, Bengaluru North district. His working life balances the rhythm of his own eight milch cattle with the twice-daily collection run he makes to eighteen other farmers, delivering bulk milk to a Nandini society chilling centre before the morning Bengaluru traffic thickens.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Kiran wakes at four-thirty, milks his cows, then loads his small insulated van with cans from neighbouring farms, reaching the Nandini chilling centre by seven. The collection route earns him a margin per litre; his own eight cows bring in roughly twelve thousand rupees a month after fodder and veterinary costs. Afternoons he grazes the herd on common land near the village tank, repairs fencing or bargains for maize and cotton-seed cake at the Doddaballapura mandi. The Devanahalli aerospace park fifteen kilometres away has pushed up land prices and drawn his cousins into construction labour, but Kiran prefers cattle; milk income is steadier than rain-fed ragi, which his father farmed. Evenings he settles accounts with the society, checks his cattle's health and returns home for dinner. Diesel, fodder inflation and veterinary bills squeeze his margin; a sick cow can wipe out two months' profit. He dreams of expanding to twelve animals if he can lease another acre for fodder, but water is uncertain and borewell electricity expensive.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Kiran lives with his wife Kavitha, their two daughters aged eleven and eight, his widowed mother and his younger unmarried brother who works night shifts as a CNC operator in a Hoskote industrial estate. Kavitha manages the household, cooks, cares for Kiran's mother and helps with evening milking; she completed tenth standard and wanted to study further but her family could not afford it. Kiran's elder brother migrated to Bengaluru five years ago, working in a private bus depot, visiting only for festivals. Kiran's father died eight years ago; the family divided the three-acre holding, leaving Kiran with one-and-a-half acres and the cattle shed. His mother receives a widow pension and helps mind the children when Kavitha is busy. Gender roles are traditional: Kiran decides cropping and spending, Kavitha manages the kitchen and children's schooling. Extended family gatherings happen at Ugadi and Deepavali; his wife's parents live in a village near Nelamangala, a half-hour bus ride away.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Kiran studied up to seventh standard in the village Kannada-medium government school, then dropped out to help his father with the herd and ragi harvest; his family needed his labour and saw little point in further schooling for a boy who would farm. His two daughters attend the same government primary school he did, now improved with a midday-meal kitchen and a computer donated by an NGO, though the teacher-student ratio remains stretched. The older girl will move to the high school in Doddaballapura town next year; the Shakti free-bus scheme has made the daily five-kilometre commute affordable, which relieves Kiran and Kavitha. They hope both daughters finish SSLC and perhaps PUC, imagining clerical or anganwadi jobs rather than the dairy life. Kiran regrets his own incomplete schooling but could not have done otherwise then; now he insists the girls attend every day, though harvest and festival seasons sometimes call them home to help. Coaching classes in town cost money the family cannot spare, so the girls rely entirely on school teaching.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Kiran and his family rely on the Doddaballapura taluk government hospital for fevers, injuries and his mother's blood-pressure check-ups; specialist care means a trip to Bengaluru, expensive and time-consuming. His mother's hypertension is managed with subsidised tablets from the hospital pharmacy. Kavitha delivered both daughters at the taluk hospital under a safe-motherhood scheme; the younger birth was complicated, requiring a referral ambulance to Bengaluru's district hospital, which the family remembers as frightening and costly despite Vajpayee Arogyashri coverage. Cattle health worries Kiran as much as his own: lumpy-skin disease swept the area two years ago, killing one of his cows and costing him vaccination and treatment fees he borrowed to cover. Drinking water comes from a borewell; the village hand-pump often runs dry in summer, and tanker water arrives irregularly. The children suffer seasonal coughs and stomach upsets. Kiran's back aches from years of lifting milk cans, but he has never consulted a doctor for it, dismissing it as the price of his work.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Kiran's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, the dominant caste in the village; most of his milk-route clients are also Vokkaligas, though a few Kuruba and SC households keep one or two cows. The village has a small Anjaneya temple where Kiran offers coconuts on Hanuman Jayanti and during the sowing season, and a Gangamma shrine at the edge of the settlement where women gather for annual festivals. His mother is devout, fasting on Mondays and Saturdays; Kiran himself is less observant but accompanies the family to Melukote for Vairamudi every few years, a pilgrimage his father loved. Community ties are dense: milk collection binds him to eighteen families in daily exchange, and he joins cooperative society meetings, though leadership remains with a few older, larger farmers. Caste hierarchy is implicit rather than loudly asserted, but Dalit households live in a separate lane and draw water from a different borewell. Kiran participates in village temple renovation fund drives and reads Kannada newspapers when he finds time, keeping abreast of Cauvery politics and state elections.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Kiran is a member of the Nandini dairy cooperative society, which means monthly meetings, vote on office-bearers and negotiations over milk-fat pricing; this is his main interface with organised civic life. He holds a Bhoomi land record, digitised, though he once spent two frustrating days at the taluk office correcting an error in his survey number. His daughters receive midday meals and have been enrolled for bicycle schemes; Kavitha uses the Shakti bus pass to visit her parents and accompany the children to Doddaballapura. Kiran applied for a Kisan Credit Card to finance fodder purchases, a process that took six months and three visits to the bank. He has never attended a gram panchayat meeting, though he knows the panchayat president, a wealthier farmer with political party ties. MGNREGA job cards exist in the village but Kiran has never sought such work, viewing it as for the landless. Government veterinary service is free but often the stockman is unavailable, forcing Kiran to pay a private vet. He views officials with a mix of respect, wariness and resignation: necessary, sometimes helpful, often indifferent.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Kiran worries most about water: summer borewells failing, delayed monsoons and the feeling that his village's water table is dropping as Bengaluru's periphery sprawls. He is proud of his dairy herd, the cleanliness of his shed and his reputation for punctual milk delivery, seeing himself as more reliable than farmers who have sold land to real-estate developers and taken factory jobs. He resents the land-price inflation that benefits sellers but raises costs for anyone trying to lease fodder acreage or buy adjoining plots. He blames middlemen and private dairies for undercutting cooperative prices, and believes the government should enforce floor pricing more strictly. Kiran wants his daughters educated so they escape the physical grind he endures, yet he cannot imagine the family without cattle; it is identity as much as income. He views Bengaluru as both opportunity—the city's milk demand sustains his route—and threat: it swallows villages, hires away labour and brings traffic, pollution and water stress. He demands better veterinary services, reliable electricity for borewell pumps and fair milk prices, and wishes his taluk's schools and hospital were as good as those in Bengaluru. He is wary of political promises but hopeful that his vote and his cooperative voice still count for something.

personas.name: Shobha
personas.definition: Shobha is a composite portrait of a woman working in Channapatna's traditional toy-craft economy, navigating import competition, household pressures and the costs of educating children. She reflects the lived experience of artisan families in Ramanagara district, where lacquerware heritage meets economic uncertainty and the pull of nearby Bengaluru's opportunities.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Shobha works in a small toy-painting unit near Channapatna town, where she applies colour to wooden animals, tops and rattles turned on lathes by men in the workshop. She earns roughly ₹7,000 a month, paid by the piece; in a good month when orders arrive from Bengaluru gift shops or government handicraft emporiums, she takes home a little more. The workshop owner complains constantly about Chinese plastic toys flooding the market and undercutting prices, and several units have closed in recent years. Shobha starts at eight and finishes by five, with an hour's break for lunch she carries from home. The smell of lacquer and sawdust clings to her saree; her fingers are stained yellow and red from dyes that do not wash off easily. Her husband drives an autorickshaw on the Channapatna-Ramanagara route and farms a small plot of coconut and ragi inherited from his father. Together they manage, but every month is tight: fuel for the auto, school fees, clinic visits, groceries from the weekly market, loan repayments for the auto and the borewell they sank two years ago when the rains failed.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Shobha lives in a two-room house on the edge of Channapatna town with her husband, her mother-in-law, and their two children—a daughter in eighth standard and a son in fifth. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties, used to do the same painting work but her eyesight has weakened and she stays home to cook and mind the house. Shobha's husband leaves early for the auto stand and returns late, often after dark; some nights he sleeps in the auto near the town bus stand to catch early morning passengers. Shobha's day begins at five-thirty: she lights the stove, makes rice and sambar, packs tiffin for the children and her husband, then walks twenty minutes to the workshop. Her daughter helps with washing dishes and looking after her younger brother in the evenings; Shobha worries that the girl is taking on too much responsibility too young. Her own mother, widowed, lives in a village near Maddur and Shobha visits her once a month, taking the KSRTC bus under the Shakti scheme. Marriage in her family happened early—Shobha was nineteen—but she hopes her daughter will finish PUC before any talk of marriage begins.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Shobha studied only until seventh standard; her parents pulled her out to help at home when her younger siblings were born, and she regrets the lost years. Her daughter attends the government high school in Channapatna town, a ten-minute walk from home; the fees are low but the family pays for private tuition in mathematics and science—₹1,500 a month—because the school's results have been slipping and Shobha is determined the girl will pass SSLC with a first class. Her son goes to the same school's primary section. Both children speak Kannada at home and study in Kannada medium; the daughter wants to continue to PUC and perhaps join a nursing course in Ramanagara or even Bengaluru, though Shobha is not sure how they will afford hostel fees. Some families in the neighbourhood send their children to private English-medium schools in Ramanagara town, but that costs ₹20,000–25,000 a year and Shobha's household cannot stretch that far. The Shakti free-bus scheme has made it easier for her daughter to travel to Ramanagara for tuition on Sundays, and Shobha sees that as a lifeline: the girl will go further than she did.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Shobha's mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure; every month they buy her medicines—₹800–1,000—from the town pharmacy because the government hospital often runs out of stock. Shobha herself has chronic back pain from sitting bent over the painting table, and her eyes ache by evening under the workshop's dim tube lights. She has been to the government taluk hospital in Channapatna twice in the past year—once for an infected finger cut by a splinter, once for her son's fever—and the doctors were helpful but the wait was long, sometimes three hours. For anything serious, families go to Ramanagara or Bengaluru; her husband's uncle had a heart problem last year and was taken straight to a private hospital in Ramanagara, and the family is still repaying that loan. Shobha's children are healthier than she was at their age—both have been vaccinated, the anganwadi worker was regular when they were small, and the school mid-day meal is reliable—but her daughter is thin and often tired, and Shobha wonders if she is anaemic. She has not had time or money to take the girl for a blood test. Shobha herself has never had a full health check-up; she goes to the doctor only when something hurts too much to ignore.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Shobha's family is Vokkaliga, part of a large extended network in and around Channapatna; her husband's cousins and uncles all work in toy-making, farming or transport. The family's social life revolves around temple festivals, weddings and funerals, all of which require contributions of money and time Shobha can ill afford but cannot refuse. They visit the Maramma temple on the edge of town every month, and during Ugadi and Dasara they travel to her husband's ancestral village for puja and a family meal. Shobha's mother-in-law is devout and insists on Friday fasts and daily prayers; Shobha herself prays more out of habit than deep conviction, though she lights a lamp every evening and asks for her children's well-being. Her husband is part of a local savings group—a small chit fund—and Shobha joined a women's self-help group three years ago; it meets once a month and has lent her ₹10,000 at low interest, which helped pay for her son's school uniform and books. The SHG also organised a one-day visit to the Channapatna GI-tag office, where officials talked about protecting the craft's reputation, but Shobha is sceptical that a geographical-indication tag will bring her higher wages.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Shobha's family has ration cards and both children have Aadhaar cards; they collect rice and kerosene from the fair-price shop every month under Anna Bhagya. Her husband receives occasional MGNREGA work on road repair when the auto business is slow, though he complains the wage payment is delayed by months. Shobha has heard of the Gruha Jyoti and Gruha Lakshmi schemes but her household does not benefit much: their electricity use is minimal and the ₹2,000-per-month Gruha Lakshmi payment goes to her mother-in-law as the household head, not to Shobha herself. The Shakti free-bus scheme, though, has changed her life—she now travels to Ramanagara or Bengaluru occasionally for shopping or to visit relatives without worrying about the fare, and her daughter can reach tuition classes safely. Shobha has never met the local MLA, though his photo hangs in the taluk office and the workshop owner went to him once to complain about import duties. She voted in the 2023 Assembly election and the 2024 Lok Sabha poll but cannot recall the candidates' names; her husband tells her which party to support and she follows his advice, though she wishes the government would do more to protect Channapatna's toy industry from Chinese competition. Property tax and water bills are her husband's responsibility; she knows little about gram panchayat meetings or town politics.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Shobha is proud that Channapatna toys carry a GI tag and that the craft is known across India, but she worries the work will not last another generation—orders are falling, younger people are leaving for Bengaluru's factories and malls, and her own workshop may close if business does not improve. She blames cheap imports and government indifference in equal measure: why give us a GI tag, she asks, if you let foreign toys flood the market? She is determined that her children will study and find salaried jobs, not depend on craft work that pays so little and offers no security. She resents that Bengaluru, only an hour away on the new expressway, is booming while Channapatna's economy shrinks, and she wishes the government would bring a garment factory or some other industry to the town so women like her could earn more and work in better conditions. She worries about her daughter's marriage and the dowry she will need to arrange; she worries about her mother-in-law's health and the cost of medicines; she worries about the borewell loan and the auto loan and what will happen if her husband falls sick or the auto breaks down. Despite it all, she takes satisfaction in keeping her household running, in her children's school marks, and in the small savings she has managed to set aside in the SHG account, hidden from immediate need. She hopes her daughter will remember that her mother painted toys so she could study.
